title: Congress tried to stop surprise medical bills. It created another problem.
summary: Healthcare providers and middlemen are exploiting a loophole in a 2020 law designed to shield consumers from surprise medical bills.
story: A law designed to protect patients from surprise medical bills succeeded in eliminating unexpected charges, but spawned a lucrative arbitration industry with providers and specialized middlemen extracting payments far above benchmark billing rates.
The practice is ultimately driving up healthcare costs for consumers, a CBS News investigation found.

The arbitration system Congress created to settle disputes between insurers and out-of-network providers allows doctors and resolution specialists acting on their behalf to win payments many times higher than typical rates for medical services. Those costs don't disappear: Much of the money comes from employer-sponsored health plans, meaning workers may ultimately pay through higher premiums or reduced benefits.

Under the arbitration system established by the No Surprises Act, which took effect in 2022, insurers are paying healthcare providers hundreds of dollars for routine lab tests that typically cost between $10 and $30, industry researchers told CBS News. In one instance, a plastic surgeon was awarded more than $400,000 to perform a breast reduction, a procedure the insurer said it had previously paid the doctor between $6,000 and $30,000 to perform.
The plastic surgeon, Dr. Norman Rowe, routinely was awarded around 170 times the benchmark rates for his services under the NSA's arbitration system, a CBS News analysis of public data shows.
A spokesman for Dr. Rowe told CBS News that insurers had manipulated benchmark rates to lowball doctors and create "artificially low reimbursement rates."

"Dr. Rowe uses the widely recognized gold standard FairHealth benchmarks set by the independent nonprofit FairHealth.org using reliable and objective market data. FairHealth data is so reliable that it is incorporated into statutes and regulations around the country and serves as the official data source for many state health programs," the spokesman added.

In addition to the typical benchmark rate arbitrators consider (known as the "qualifying payment amount," or QPA), FairHealth provides another rate that can be used during the dispute resolution process. Medicare rates, meanwhile, may not be considered.

CBS News found that another doctor — Long Island spine surgeon Vadim Lerman — was being awarded an average of 280 times the benchmark rates in arbitration. He declined an interview, but a spokesman for Lerman said that "the suggestion that a physician is receiving 'hundreds of times' above benchmark rates is incorrect. No comparison should be made to the insurer's initial offer — which can be inappropriately low for a complex surgical procedure — and the award given to the physician."
"Baseball-style arbitration"
Insurers have, in many cases, been forced to pay high rates like those Dr. Rowe charges under the law's so-called "baseball-style" or "pendulum" arbitration system.

In an arbitration under the No Surprises Act, insurers and providers each propose a rate for a given service. There's no room for negotiation, as an arbitrator must choose between one of the two parties' suggested figures.

Arbitrators side with providers in more than 85% of the cases, according to Leland Robbins, a product leader at Turquoise Health, a data transparency startup. Some arbitrators – officially called certified Independent Dispute Resolution, or IDR, entities – have track records of siding with providers in an even larger share of cases, according to Robbins' group.
He told CBS News that while patients are no longer being surprised by large medical bills, there is a catch to the new system.

"The transaction didn't go away. It went behind closed doors and has moved into this arbitration process when a payer and a provider can't agree what the fair price should be," Robbins said. "Given that 70% of these awards are being taken out of employer-sponsored health plans, consumers are going to start seeing it when it comes time for open enrollment."
He added, "You know, employers are not able to withstand and absorb these kinds of big fees. They're going to be probably not paying for as much of your premiums."

Last year, 15 government-certified arbitrators earned fees per case, with 17 arbitrators designated to do this work today. Each side in the dispute — the healthcare provider and the insurer — pays into the process prior to the arbitrator making any decision.

During the first six months of 2025, insurers and providers submitted 1.2 million new disputes to the arbitration portal, while federal officials had only expected approximately 17,000 cases per year, research from the Center on Health Insurance Reforms (CHIR) at Georgetown University's McCourt School of Public Policy shows.
However, HaloMD, a company that files cases on behalf of providers, told CBS News that the initial estimates "were objectively flawed in how they calculated expected volume."
Collectively, arbitrators making the decisions have earned more than $2 billion in fees. None agreed to on-camera interviews with CBS News.
New Jersey House Rep. Frank Pallone, a Democrat and the lead sponsor of the No Surprises Act, blames private equity, in part, for breaking the system he helped create.
He said just a few private equity firms – which are increasingly buying up anesthesiology, radiology and emergency room practices — are driving arbitration cases.

Pallone told CBS News that doctors should be paid the equivalent of in-network rates for the services they provide, but said "we had no choice" but to introduce the arbitration system "if we wanted to actually get rid of surprise billing."
"I knew it was not going to go well, but I didn't know it was going to be this bad," he added.
Dispute resolution cottage industry

The law's arbitration provision has also created an opportunity for intermediaries to guide providers through the process and rake in profits by taking a cut of bills that are up to 1,000% above the benchmark rate for a service, CBS News found. Critics argue that such firms demand more money on providers' behalf, leading to the large settlements that drive up everyone's costs.

HaloMD bills itself as "the expert" in arbitration cases brought under the No Surprises Act. Founded by Texas couple Scott and Alla Laroque in 2022, the same year the No Surprises Act took effect, the company is one of the fledgling industry's biggest players.

Private equity firms also sometimes own both physician staffing firms and Independent Dispute Resolution entities, creating a conflict of interest and undermining the law's fairness. HaloMD is not private equity-backed, but Halo and two other groups with investments from buyout firms collectively handled more than 75% of disputes settled in arbitration last year, according to Georgetown University's Center on Health Insurance Reforms.

According to Halo, the firm made more than $1 billion for its clients, routinely earning awards that are nine times the benchmark rates for services. Halo takes a cut of the payouts but has not disclosed the amount.

Halo chief external affairs officer Patrick Velliky told CBS News that insurance companies, not firms like his, are responsible for driving up consumer healthcare costs by either not participating in the arbitration process or submitting ludicrously low offers.

"24% of the time, insurers lose by default. They didn't submit an offer at all. Another 9 1/2% of the time, insurers submit an offer, like a dollar or less," Velliky told CBS News. "So what that actually looks like, a patient goes to the E-D with a heart attack, we go to arbitration and the insurer is offering a total of $1.00."

He also said that insurance companies are offering misleading information about the benchmark rate. "Whatever the actual median in-network rate is, it's not what the insurer presented," Velliky told CBS News. "They're miscalculating it."
A federal court sided with providers on the issue this summer, saying the benchmark rate is "artificially low," pulled down by insurers' $0- or $ 1-reimbursement offers to doctors.
Proposed reforms
Pallone wants to reform the law to gut what he sees as the root of the issues arising from the No Surprises Act: arbitration.

He plans to introduce legislation this week to eliminate the arbitration process and stipulate that providers be paid in-network rates, even if they are out-of-network. Pallone's office also told CBS News that so-called ghost rates, which often drag the benchmark rate down, will be excluded from calculations moving forward.

"Whether it's the hospitals, the doctors, the nurse, they're really trying to care for people. Of course, all of them should have a decent income so they can live," the New Jersey lawmaker said. "But why should these outside investors be making all this money off the backs of, you know, your insurance premiums, essentially?"

title: Why AI could end the price tag as we know it
summary: Retailers want to harness the power of artificial intelligence to set personalized prices for shoppers, a consumer protection expert says.
story: The humble price tag has long served as a common measure of value for consumers. Now, experts warn that artificial intelligence could allow retailers to charge people different prices based on their personal data.

Lindsay Owens, CEO of Groundwork Collaborative, a nonprofit think tank focused on economic policy, said AI threatens to upend universal prices for consumers. That could overturn norms that have been in place since the 1860s, when pioneering retailer John Wanamaker introduced fixed prices in his Philadelphia department store.

"The posted price has been paramount for consumers, and I do think the price tag is at risk of extinction," Owens, a consumer protection expert and author of "Gouged: The End of a Fair Price — and What That Means for Your Wallet," told CBS News. "Predictability is really essential if you're on a budget, and knowing how much something is going to cost from one week to the next is part of what the posted price offered."
A price tag just for you

AI-enabled pricing builds on so-called dynamic pricing, which companies have used for decades to adjust prices in response to shifting patterns of supply and demand, weather, time of day and other factors.

Firms aren't stopping there, however. Today, retailers are starting to test new ways of pricing goods based on who you are, where you live and myriad other insights gleaned from AI — an approach known informally as personalized or "surveillance" pricing, Owens said. AI also gives companies a powerful new tool to continually analyze vast amounts of disparate data to gain insights into consumer behavior.

"These technologies may empower firms to collect, process and analyze vast amounts of consumer data, leading to more granular, dynamic, and individualized pricing than previously observed," analysts with economic consulting firm Cornerstone Research said in a 2025 report.

The upshot: Retailers could use AI to tap the vast amounts of consumer data they already collect to set prices not on a product's value, but rather on the maximum amount they believe an individual shopper is willing to pay, Owens said.

Currently, this Uber-style pricing typically fluctuates based on, say, the number of drivers and passenger demand in a given market. But with AI, companies could also harness your consumer profile to set what amounts to a personalized price, Owens said. The result could amount to a form of AI-enabled haggling, in which consumers face perpetually shifting prices based on factors largely invisible to them.
"Technology is allowing companies to stop setting prices for products and start setting prices for you," she said.
A sign of prices to come?

In December, Groundwork Collaborative and Consumer Reports reported on a trial by grocery-shopping platform Instacart that used AI to simultaneously show customers different prices for the same goods from the same store. The pilot built on Instacart's 2022 purchase of Eversight, a software platform designed to enable AI pricing.

The AI-enabled tech runs experiments by setting different prices for different consumers and collecting insights into how people respond, including when they proceed with a purchase and when they walk away. The investigation found that grocery baskets containing identical items cost up to 23% more for some shoppers. That could translate into a swing of about $1,200 per year for a family of four, Groundwork and Consumer Reports concluded.

Instacart disputes the report's findings, telling CBS News that the $1,200 price gap among some shoppers reflects an "atypical" grocery basket with the greatest possible price difference for every item. The company also said it doesn't use consumers' personal data, including federally protected characteristics such as race or gender, to set prices.
In December, however, Instacart said it would stop using AI to let retailers charge customers different prices for identical items on its platform.

According to Owens, other companies have also begun experimenting with using AI to charge consumers individualized prices based on their personal data, such as their online browsing habits, income level, ZIP code or family structure.

In separate Groundwork research released this month, the group said that Walmart had applied for patents on technology that would allow the retailer to compile comprehensive shopper profiles and use them to set individualized prices. The tech, such as electronic shelf labels, could be used to charge consumers a "different price than the customer in front of them in the checkout line," Owens and her co-author wrote.

One patent application indicates that Walmart has already developed technology to adjust prices based on items in a shopper's cart, according to Groundwork. "If a customer has tuna fish, they may be offered a different price for mayonnaise," the group claimed.
Walmart denies developing tools that would allow it to use customers' personal data or other factors to adjust prices.

"Walmart does not and will not use an individual customer's personal information, income, shopping history, urgency or willingness to pay to set an individualized price," Dan Bartlett, Walmart's executive vice president of corporate affairs, said in a public letter to Owens this month in response to her research. "We do not engage in dynamic pricing, raising prices in response to a hot afternoon or an approaching snowstorm, for example."

Jay Zagorsky, a senior lecturer at Boston University's Questrom School of Business, has also warned about the potential risks of using AI for personalized pricing, noting that businesses are unlikely to disclose such practices for fear of facing consumer backlash.

"Nothing positive is gained by a merchant stating they are doing this," he told CBS News, while expressing his belief that retailers are developing the tools to set individualized pricing. "The days when the price you saw stayed fixed for a relatively long period of time appear to have passed."

title: Character.ai declares bankruptcy, citing legal and business woes
summary: AI company has faced multiple lawsuits from families who claimed their teenage children died by suicide or harmed themselves after using its platform.
story: Character.ai said it has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, with its chief executive attributing the chatbot provider's financial problems to "significant legal, regulatory and operational headwinds."

The company said it will continue operating as it seeks to sell its business, and added that The Walt Disney Co. has agreed to pay $20 million for a non-exclusive, perpetual license to Character.ai's intellectual property.

Character.ai's financial struggles follow scrutiny and litigation over its technology, which uses artificial intelligence to create custom bots consumers can chat with. In early 2026, Character.ai and Google, which had a licensing deal with the AI company, agreed to settle several lawsuits filed by families who claimed their teenage children died by suicide or harmed themselves after using Character.ai's platform.

The company settled a wrongful death lawsuit earlier in 2026 — the first filed in the U.S. against an AI company — with a Florida family who said their teen son died after conducting an emotional and sexual relationship with a chatbot known as "Dany." The family said in their lawsuit that Character.ai had no mechanisms in place to protect their son or notify an adult when teens were spending too much time interacting with Chatbots.
The company added several safety features designed with teens in mind after several lawsuits alleged its chatbots inappropriately interacted with underage users.

Several states have also sued Character.ai over its technology, with Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman alleging in January that its chatbots "preyed on children and led them into self-harm." In May, Pennsylvania sued Character.ai after one of its chatbots allegedly claimed to be a licensed psychiatrist in the state and provided a "fake Pennsylvania license number."
In a statement issued late Monday, Character.ai said it believes the company will be sold by late November or early December.

"After a comprehensive review of the available alternatives, the board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides the company with the best opportunity to maximize value for all stakeholders," Character.ai CEO Colin Adams said in the statement. "As we navigate this process, maintaining a safe and engaging user experience for our Character.ai community remains a top priority."
Is Character.ai shutting down?
The company said on Monday that its services continue to operate and that subscriptions remain active.
"If the service changes in a way that affects paid features, we intend to notify subscribers in advance," Character.ai said.

In a blog post, the company said customer data "continues to be protected under our Privacy Policy." That policy states that data Character.ai collects from users — including chat transcripts, voice recordings, and images and videos — could be disclosed in connection with a sale or a negotiation to sell the company or its assets.
"As a reminder, you can delete your account or export your data through the app or the Character.ai website," the company said.

title: Six Flags stock slides 16% following fatal roller coaster accident
summary: The company's stock is taking a hit after officials confirmed a person died at one of the theme park's locations, extending a slide that started in September.
story: Shares of Six Flags slid as much as 16.3% after officials confirmed that a 42-year-old man died during an incident at one of the amusement park's locations in Georgia.
Six Flags Entertainment Corporation stock, which trades under the ticker symbol FUN, fell 12% in early trading. By late morning, the stock was trading at $9.98, down 16.3%.

The person died on Monday during a ride on one of the roller coasters at Six Flags Over Georgia, located in Austell, Georgia. According to witness testimony provided to the Cobb County Police Department, the man was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction. Several people were injured during the incident, according to the Cobb County Police Department.

Officials did not confirm which roller coaster was involved in the incident, although CBS News Atlanta cameras showed the park's Goliath ride, described as an "intense 7­­­0­­­-­­­m­­­i­­­l­­­e­­­-­­­p­­­e­­­r­­­-­­­h­­­o­­­u­­­r thrill ride," had shut down.

Dennis Speigel, founder and owner of consulting firm International Theme Park Services, said incidents like these are normally the result of an engineering issue, operating issue or rider responsibility issue.
He expects it will have very little, if any, impact on sales at the theme park.

"The public knows that the company is going to go in, examine, and figure out exactly what happened on this issue," Speigel said, adding he's seen "situations similar to this over the last 50 years with basically no impact."
An investigation is ongoing in Georgia to determine what happened Monday.

In the short term, the company's stock is taking a hit, extending a slide that started in September. Shares are down 33.8% since the start of the year. That comes as Six Flags faces high CEO turnover in the last decade and financial struggles following a 2024 merger with Cedar Fair, Speigel said.
The "merger really put the company in a very difficult position, [and] dug a very big hole for them," he said.
Following the incident in Georgia, Six Flags closed several other roller coasters across its parks, including the Goliath roller coaster in Los Angeles, CBS News LA reported.
"Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily closed similar attractions across our parks," a Six Flags spokesperson said Monday.

title: Anthropic warns "AI worms" could soon infect smart home devices
summary: Small AI models could clone themselves and infect internet-connected devices such as smart TVs and appliances, the researchers warned.
story: Anthropic is sounding the alarm about a new risk posed by artificial intelligence: Self-replicating "AI worms" could soon infest your "smart" home devices.

In a report released on Monday, Anthropic safety researchers said small AI models may be only "months away" from gaining the ability to clone themselves and spread across internet-connected devices, such as smart ovens, TVs and vacuum cleaners. The ability to reproduce themselves without human control would make it hard to control such agents because there's "no centralized point to shut off," said Anthropic, which developed the Claude chatbot.
Stronger AI models are already capable of what the researchers called "end-to-end replication," a threshold they say smaller models could reach by year-end, according to Anthropic.
AI worms, a type of AI-powered malware, can quickly spread across networks and devices while evading detection, according to cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks.

Smart devices in people's homes, as well as internet-connected devices such as security cameras, are vulnerable given that internet-enabled devices tend to have weaker security protections, the Anthropic researchers said. In what they described as a worst-case scenario, a swarm of AI agents — bots that work together to accomplish a shared goal — could propagate across computer hardware using "replication schemes."

The researchers said they are unsure of what form these attacks could take, noting that the AI models could be distributed as "digital slime mold" or as more powerful models capable of hacking into data centers.

"We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay," the Anthropic researchers wrote in the report.

title: Squeezed by inflation, more Americans fall behind on their debts
summary: Credit card and auto loan delinquencies are near historic highs as rising prices leave more people struggling to keep up with payments.
story: Rising U.S. prices are squeezing household budgets, causing more Americans to fall behind on their debt payments, recent financial data shows.

The share of seriously delinquent auto loan balances has hit a record high this year, while nearly 13% of credit card balances are seriously past due — close to their 2010 peak in the aftermath of the housing crisis — according to recent data from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
The share of households behind on their mortgages reached a six-year high, although the measure remains far below its peak during the Great Recession.
Student loan delinquencies have also jumped in the past year, with the rise tied to the end of pandemic-era protections and a Biden administration repayment plan.
Other signs that more Americans are struggling with debt:

Almost 9% of U.S. households spent more than 40% of their income on debt repayment in 2025, the highest level since 2010, according to the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances.Nearly 20% of households were late on a debt payment in 2025, a jump from about 12% in 2022, the same survey found.More Americans over 70 are struggling with debt, with their share of auto loan accounts in delinquency at its highest level since the New York Fed began tracking the metric in 2000. Credit card delinquency among people over 70 is at its highest level since 2011, the analysis also found.
Almost 9% of U.S. households spent more than 40% of their income on debt repayment in 2025, the highest level since 2010, according to the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances.
Nearly 20% of households were late on a debt payment in 2025, a jump from about 12% in 2022, the same survey found.

More Americans over 70 are struggling with debt, with their share of auto loan accounts in delinquency at its highest level since the New York Fed began tracking the metric in 2000. Credit card delinquency among people over 70 is at its highest level since 2011, the analysis also found.

More than half of Americans relied on credit cards to pay for basic needs like groceries, rent and utilities, according to a March survey from Debt.com. Almost six in 10 said inflation was causing them to carry a bigger credit card balance than a year earlier, the same survey found.

Many Americans are frustrated with the U.S. economy, even as measures such as GDP growth and unemployment remain relatively solid. After five years of elevated inflation, nine in 10 Americans say prices are the most important factor shaping their economic outlook, according to a recent CBS News poll.
The worsening debt situation reflects the impact of inflation on household finances, said Kelly Regan, a certified financial planner at financial advisory firm Girard.

Credit cards are "kind of like the safety valve if you have no emergency savings left," Regan told CBS News. "We have an issue that if prices are increasing, especially more than people's wage growth, we're going to have a gap where things are going to cost more. And if you don't have any savings or are able to find those savings somehow in your budget, you're going to accrue debt."
Lagging wage growth

Adding to the crunch is that wage growth is lagging inflation, meaning that millions of households have lost purchasing power. That's also depressing consumer sentiment and squeezing people coping with higher prices, according to economists.

More than half of U.S. consumers said they intend to cut back on spending in the next year, the University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers said in a report last week. The most common items they intended to cut back on included food and groceries, household items, cars, dining out, and vacations, the poll found.

"Frustration over cost of living continues to mount, as consumers across the political spectrum believe that the trajectory of the economy has weakened since the beginning of the year," Joanne Hsu, the director of the Surveys of Consumers, said in a statement.

title: Would access to Russian diesel help drive down U.S. prices?
summary: Average U.S. diesel prices remain stuck above $6 a gallon, raising fuel costs in trucking, agriculture and construction.
story: Russia's commitment to boost global diesel supply, as announced by President Trump on Oct. 9, may do little to ease prices in the U.S. in the short term, according to energy experts.

"If we get diesel from Russia, basically it means that their existing customers are not going to get it and they'll have to go somewhere else, and that will keep the price basically where it is now," Michael Lynch, distinguished fellow at Energy Policy Research Foundation, a nonpartisan research institution focused on energy and economics, told The Associated Press.
Mr. Trump said Friday on Truth Social that Russia will "immediately supply" more than 300,000 tons of diesel, an additional 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."

"Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" he wrote.
A White House official said the plan will lower diesel costs for American farmers, truckers and other workers.

"Adding hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the global markets will lower prices," the official told CBS News in an email. "The Treasury Department issued an [Office of Foreign Assets Control] license allowing Russia to immediately begin selling diesel to the United States and the world — which they were previously unable to do."
Shift in policy

The agreement represents an abrupt shift in policy by the U.S., which, from the start of Russia's war with Ukraine, had banned imports of Russian oil. President Trump in September signed a bill, named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, into law that allows the Trump administration to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas.

The national average for diesel in the U.S. reached a record high of $6.53 per gallon on Sept. 22, according to AAA. As of Monday, it was $6.27 a gallon, up from $3.73 a gallon in late February, just before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran. Diesel costs are even higher in states such as California, where the average price is $8.38 a gallon.
Higher diesel costs put upward pressure on prices for a range of goods, from food to lumber, because the fuel is widely used across the agriculture, construction and transportation industries.
Tapping Russia for diesel is drawing pushback from lawmakers, with a bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday calling for the Trump administration to "immediately reverse course" on the plan.
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course," they wrote.
Beyond such geopolitical issues, energy experts and Wall Street analysts point to several reasons in explaining why access to Russian diesel is unlikely to have much impact on U.S. prices.

First, it's unclear whether Russia can export large volumes of diesel after Ukrainian strikes knocked out much of its refining capacity. Ukraine has targeted more than 3 million barrels per day of Russian refining, according to Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil.

"None of the numbers mentioned in the Friday communique make sense," he said in an email, referring to Mr. Trump's social media post announcing that Russia had agreed to release more diesel. "One wonders whether Russia could export any diesel in October, November or December."

Unless Ukraine pauses its strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, Russia will struggle to meet the supply commitments it made to the U.S., Adam Crisafulli, head of investment advisory firm Vital Knowledge, also said in a report.
The amount of diesel Mr. Trump said Russia has agreed to release is also modest relative to the global market.
"The world consumes around 3.5 million to 4 million metric tons of diesel a day (including 500K tons in the U.S.), so this incremental Russian supply isn't massive," Crisafulli said.
The U.S. consumes around 4.1 million barrels of diesel, or roughly 170 million gallons, per day, according to S&P Global Energy.
"It might take the edge off of prices"

Debnil Chowdhury, vice president and head of Americas and Europe fuels and refining at S&P Global Energy, agreed that the deal will have little impact on prices, noting that it does not materially affect global inventory levels.

"The export volumes committed by Russia for this month and November are within the range of Russia's current exports, which implies that Russia can hold its side of the deal without increasing supply to the market," he told CBS News in an email.

The bottom line is that greater access to Russian diesel doesn't offset the disruptions to oil supplies stemming from the war with Iran, experts said. The conflict has damaged refining capacity in the Middle East and hampered shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, leading to lower global crude output.

"Refined products like diesel are still barely half of prewar levels," said Daniel Sternoff, senior fellow at the Columbia Center on Global Energy Policy. "So, even if there were to be some follow-through from the Russians to put a little extra diesel into the world markets, it might take the edge off of prices, but it will not substantially lower them."

The Trump administration has taken several steps to try to ease fuel prices amid stubbornly high U.S. inflation. Earlier this year, Mr. Trump released oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and waived restrictions on the types of vessels that can legally transport goods between U.S. ports.
Most recently, Mr. Trump last week issued an executive order to expand access to tax-free, red-dyed diesel, a move aimed at lowering prices for truck drivers and farmers.

title: Starbucks denies plan to buy Chipotle, refuting report
summary: Starbucks said it doesn't plan to bid for Chipotle Mexican Grill, saying the coffee chain is focused on organic growth.
story: Starbucks shot down reports that the coffee giant was considering acquiring restaurant chain Chipotle Mexican Grill.
A spokesperson for Starbucks said it is not buying Chipotle, which has a market worth of $47 billion, saying that the company is focused on its strategic plan to boost growth.

"Our team is laser-focused on executing our Back to Starbucks strategy. We have strong momentum and confidence in our long-term growth potential.  We look forward to sharing our Q4 results, including FY27 guidance, later this month," a Starbucks spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News.
Chipotle's stock soared as much as 8% last week after the Financial Times reported that Starbucks had been exploring a deal to purchase Chipotle.

Industry analysts were skeptical of the report. TD Cowen analysts said in a research note last week that they considered a merger between Starbucks and Chipotle "a low-probability outcome," and instead expected Starbucks chief executive Brian Niccol to prioritize the company's turnaround plan.
Niccol previously served as CEO of Chipotle, whose stock price has dropped about 50% since he left the post in August 2024. The shares have lost about 20% of their value over the past year.

title: Nobel Prize in economics goes to 2 Americans
summary: American-born economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel Prize in economics for their work on models that help governments and central banks manage economic shocks.
story: Stockholm — American-born economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel memorial prize in economics on Monday for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, saying the winners were being honored "for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation."
"The laureates have helped us smooth out the economy's peaks and troughs," the academy said in a statement.
Hall, 83,is affiliated with Stanford University in California and Woodford, born in 1955, is affiliated with Columbia University in New York.
Woodford spoke to the committee by phone Monday from New York, saying: "It's a tremendous honor, it's a surprise."

"The laureates' work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world," John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a news release.
"With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume."

For decades, governments responded to economic shocks by following the Depression-era prescriptions of British economist John Maynard Keynes: Intervene in the economy by lowering taxes and hiking government spending, thereby encouraging consumers and businesses to spend and invest themselves and help growth get restarted.
"This is the Keynesian recipe and it worked well - until it didn't,'' said Timo Boppart of the Nobel economics prize committee.

Policymakers had thought economic management involved simple tradeoffs — unemployment, for instance, would stay low at a time of high inflation and rise when inflation fell. But the "stagflation'' of the 1970s — when the world economy experienced simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment — proved the formula was simplistic.
Hall and Woodford set about coming up with an improved model that took into account how consumers and businesses actually made decisions about whether to invest and spend.
"In separate contributions, Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford helped build this new foundation for stabilization policy," Hassler said.

Last year, three researchers who study business innovation won for explaining how new products and inventions promote economic growth and human welfare, even as they leave older companies in the dust.

The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes.

The majority of previous economics winners have been from the U.S., the Reuters news agency points out, adding that only three women have won — most recently, Claudia Goldin in 2023 for work on how gender affects pay and employment over time in the U.S.
Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death in 1896.
Nobel honors were announced last week in medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.

title: Are banks, USPS and stock markets open on Columbus Day?
summary: The stock market is open on Columbus Day, but banking, mail and some other services will be closed for the holiday.
story: Columbus Day, also known as Indigenous Peoples Day, may be an official federal holiday, but it's not consistently observed across the U.S., according to the Pew Research Center.
Falling on the second Monday in October, the holiday creates a three-day weekend for workers whose employers observe it, including federal employees and some state workers, Pew found.
But a push to shift recognition away from explorer Christopher Columbus and instead honor North America's original inhabitants means the holiday isn't as widely observed as it once was.
Since Oct. 12 is a federal holiday, some services and businesses will be closed. Here's what to know about what is open and closed on Columbus Day/Indigenous Peoples Day.
Is today a federal holiday?
Yes, Monday, Oct. 12, is a federal holiday, which means that U.S. government offices will be closed and federal workers have the day off.
Is the stock market open on Columbus Day?
Yes, the stock market is open on Columbus Day, with neither the New York Stock Exchange nor the Nasdaq market observing it as a holiday.
The stock market will be open during its regular working hours on Monday from 9:30 a.m.-4 p.m. ET.
Is mail delivered on Columbus Day?
No, the U.S. Postal Service observes Columbus Day as a holiday, which means there will be no regular residential or business mail delivery. All USPS offices will also be closed.
Are banks open on Columbus Day?
It's best to check with your bank, as some are open while others observe the holiday.

JPMorgan Chase said that its branches will be open on Oct. 12, but will treat the day as a holiday for online transactions. That means customers can't schedule transactions to occur on Columbus Day, and repeating transactions were processed on the preceding business day.
Many other banks are closed on Columbus Day, including Wells Fargo and Bank of America.
Is Costco open on Columbus Day?
Yes, Costco is open for business today, as Columbus Day isn't among the seven holidays the discount chain observes.
Is Walmart open today?
Walmart is also open on Columbus Day, with stores open during regular hours, according to the retailer's website.

title: Philadelphia police say Anthropic AI submitted a "false homicide tip"
summary: Anthropic notified the Philadelphia Police Department of the incident and later published a report describing what happened.
story: Philadelphia police said a "false homicide tip" submitted through the PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com website was generated by an Anthropic artificial intelligence model. The AI giant later confirmed the incident in a report it published Friday.
The AI submission came through an online platform launched by the Philadelphia Police Department to gather tips about open homicide cases.
Anthropic notified the police department of the incident on Wednesday, Sgt. Eric Gripp, a police spokesperson, said in a statement shared with CBS News ahead of the release of Anthropic's report.
"Philadelphia Police are providing this information to the public ahead of that publication in the interests of full government transparency and accountability," Gripp said.

In its report, titled "Investigating unintended model actions in our evaluations and internal use," Anthropic acknowledged the error, disclosing that the false tip was generated by one of its Claude language models.

According to Anthropic, Claude's Haiku 4.5 model wrote in the police department's tip form: "I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant."
Anthropic said Haiku left the name and contact fields of the tip form empty.
In submitting the "invented tip," Anthropic said, Claude appeared to have "only been producing example content for the task, rather than trying to mislead anyone to achieve a goal."

Anthropic explained in its report that Claude had been "tasked with generating and performing example tasks on randomly selected webpages" when the tip was submitted, and that it was never instructed to log into the police department's website, create an account or "submit anything destructive."
However, Anthropic acknowledged that the instructions given to Claude for the exercise "did not rule out form submissions."
This matched information Anthropic shared with the police department. The AI model purported to be someone who "might have information about the case," Gripp said in his statement.
The tip was flagged as spam and never reached the unit responsible for investigative vetting, according to the police department's release.

Anthropic told the department that the incident occurred at 11:27 p.m. on July 18, but that it didn't discover it until Sept. 28. At that point, the company stopped the automated testing process that led to the false tip, Gripp said.
There was no indication the incident involved any "unauthorized access to police systems or a compromise of department data," he said.

The police department encouraged people to continue submitting legitimate tips through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, saying it remains committed to "carefully evaluating that information and pursuing credible leads on behalf of victims and their families."

title: These 18 million households now rank as America's richest
summary: The smallest age group in the U.S. is also the richest, with a 37% jump in net worth over the last three years — far higher than any other group.
story: Sometimes the key to building wealth is just sticking around, new Federal Reserve data suggests.

The 18 million U.S. households headed by someone 75 or older have the highest median net worth of any age group, according to the Fed's triennial Survey of Consumer Finances. Americans in that demographic had a median net worth of $504,000 in 2025, according to the Fed's Survey of Consumer Finances.
The report assesses U.S. families' financial health, measuring wealth, income and liabilities such as credit card debt and student loans. All figures in the report are adjusted for inflation.

Families headed by someone 75 or older recorded both the largest increase in median net worth of any age group and the biggest income gains, with their median annual income rising 24% since 2022 to $67,000. The oldest Americans likely benefited from growth in their retirement assets, the Fed said.
Between 2022 and 2025, households headed by 65- to 74-year-olds saw their wealth increase by 37%.

The findings underscore how robust stock market gains over the last three years have boosted the wealth of many Americans. The S&P 500 gained about 78% between the end of 2022 and 2025, the period measured by the Federal Reserve's report.

The number of 401(k) plan accounts managed by Fidelity Investments with at least $1 million surged to a record 769,000 in the second quarter, lifted by a bullish stock market and by record average employee contribution rates.
Meanwhile, the median net worth of the richest one-tenth of American families soared 31% to $3.6 million from 2022 to 2025, the Fed survey found.

Households headed by someone over 75 account for about 13.4% of the nation's families, making it the smallest U.S. age group. Families led by people under 35 are the largest, accounting for about one in five households, according to the Fed.

While the oldest and richest Americans enjoyed significant wealth gains, the report also showed that the financial outlook has weakened for millions of people in recent years. In 2025, about 20% of U.S. households were behind on their debt repayments, including home loans, credit cards, payday loans and other types of credit — a 7-percentage-point jump since 2022, the data show.

The increase may reflect the impact of years of above-normal inflation since the pandemic, although the survey doesn't capture this year's reacceleration of price increases sparked by soaring energy costs.
"Families were more likely to be behind on their financial obligations than at any point since the 2010 survey," the Federal Reserve said of the 2025 data.
About one in 12 families is spending roughly 40% or more of their incomes on repaying debt, the highest share in at least 12 years, the report showed.
As of 2025, nearly 10% of Americans aged 65 and older lived below the poverty line, up from roughly 9% a decade ago, according to Census Bureau data.

Typical households headed by someone younger than 35 saw their median net worth plunge 23% between 2022 and 2025, to $33,000, the Fed found. That decline in wealth for young families was chiefly due to a drop in business equity gains over the previous three years.

title: Trump promised to lower prices for Americans. Here's what the data shows.
summary: Just weeks before the midterm elections, 90% of Americans say prices in the U.S. are the main factor shaping their view of the economy. These charts show why.
story: President Trump campaigned in 2024 on promises to lower Americans' cost of living, vowing to push gasoline prices below $2 a gallon and to deliver 2% mortgage rates. Two years later, consumers face sharply higher costs for many of the necessities he pledged to make more affordable.

Less than a month before the midterm elections, the gap between Mr. Trump's promises and the financial realities facing many Americans is fueling voter frustration over the economy. Although economic growth is solid and unemployment remains low, nine in 10 Americans say prices are the most important factor shaping their views of the economy, according to a recent CBS News poll.

The financial pressures affecting Americans predate Mr. Trump's return to the White House last year. Consumers are reeling from the cumulative impact of five years of post-pandemic inflation, economists note. But his campaign promises raised hopes that he would lower consumer prices.

At the same time, some of Mr. Trump's policies have exacerbated inflation. His tariff regime contributed about 2.9 percentage points to inflation through February, according to new research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Without the tariffs, the price of goods would have declined, the researchers said.
Mr. Trump's decision to attack Iran in February has also led to a drawn-out conflict that has disrupted oil shipments and sharply driven up the price of oil, gas and diesel.

"It's undeniable that several of these supply shocks that the U.S. economy has been navigating through come from policy decisions made by the administration — namely, decisions to intervene in Iran and decisions to impose tariffs," Greg Daco, chief economist at investment advisory firm EY-Parthenon, told CBS News.
Inflation in September is forecast to have risen at an annual rate of 3.6%, up from 3.4% in August, according to economists polled by FactSet — well above the Federal Reserve's 2% annual target.
Ryan Bourne, an economist at the libertarian Cato Institute, said that consumers "judge the prices they're paying against the prices they paid four or five years ago, and are still shocked by it."
He added, "As a result of that, they think the economy's doing very, very badly."

The White House said that Mr. Trump's agenda "stopped Biden's inflation crisis" while creating jobs and economic growth. The administration's policies "will continue to deliver economic wins over the next two years," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told CBS News.

"The President has delivered tangible wins for American families: He signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, cut the cost of prescription drugs, added more than one million private-sector jobs, locked in nearly 20 trade deals that put American workers first and sent 401(k)s to record highs," Rogers added.
The following charts show how U.S. costs have changed for expenses ranging from groceries to car insurance.
Groceries
"A vote for Trump means your groceries will be cheaper." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Pittsburgh on Nov. 4, 2024.
For consumers, each visit to the supermarket is a fresh reminder of inflation's impact on food costs, which have continued to rise since Mr. Trump vowed to lower grocery prices.

The cost of food prepared at home has climbed 4% since November 2024, according to Consumer Price Index data, when Mr. Trump said a vote for him would lead to lower costs. That increase comes on top of a 23% jump in food prices during the prior four years. Because consumers tend to remember what they spent on groceries before the pandemic, they get a jolt each time they visit the supermarket, said Daco of EY-Parthenon.

"Whether it's talking about gas prices or grocery prices or restaurant prices or travel prices, everybody talks about inflation," he said. "The salience of prices is what is driving this downbeat consumer morale."

Food costs are continuing to rise due to a number of factors, ranging from the elevated price of gas and diesel, which are needed to fuel farm equipment and ship items to stores, to the Trump administration's tariffs, economists said.
Gasoline

"Energy is going to bring us back. That means we're going down and getting gasoline below $2 a gallon, bring down the price of everything from electricity rates to groceries, airfares, and housing costs."  — Mr. Trump in a speech at the Economic Club of New York on Sept. 5, 2024.

Gas prices have surged since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. As of Oct. 9, the national average price for a gallon of gasoline was $4.37. That's up 47% from $2.98 on Feb. 27, one day before the war began, according to CBS News data. Prices at the pump are at a record high for October, according to AAA.

Diesel prices rose to a record high of $6.53 per gallon on Sept. 22 and now hover around $6.28. Diesel, which is widely used in the trucking, agriculture and construction sectors, is a factor in consumer prices for nearly every type of good, including groceries.

Gas prices tend to have an outsized impact on consumer sentiment, influencing their views on future inflation and the broader economy, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.
Energy and electricity

"By contrast, I'm announcing today that under my leadership, the United States will commit to the ambitious goal of slashing energy and electricity prices by half, at least half." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 14, 2024.

Consumers' energy bills have continued to increase this year. Data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA) shows that average monthly residential electricity costs rose 12.5% between December 2024 and July of this year. Electricity bills are rising as utilities spend more to upgrade the nation's aging power grid, and overall energy demand grows amid the data center buildout.

Natural gas is also more expensive. Average monthly residential prices for natural gas rose 106% between December 2024 and July 2025, according to the EIA. Energy Innovation, a nonpartisan policy and research firm, attributes the jump to geopolitical conflict, an increase in domestic exports, extreme weather linked to climate change and rising infrastructure costs.

A July report from advocacy groups The Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers found that the national average utility bill reached $280 per month in early 2026, up 12% since the end of 2024, just before Mr. Trump took office.

Many people could face even higher energy prices this winter. Americans are forecast to spend an average of $1,030 to heat their homes between mid-November and mid-March 2027, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, a policy organization. Homeowners who use heating oil are projected to pay an average of $2,627 over that three-month period, up roughly 50% from last year, the group said.
Car insurance

"Car insurance is up 70% to 100%, and you can't get it. … But prices will come down. You just watch, they'll come down, and they'll come down fast." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 14, 2024.
Car insurance costs are one area where consumers are seeing some modest relief. Data shows motorists are paying 5.5% less for vehicle coverage since premiums hit a recent high in February.

Still, insurance prices have soared in recent years along with the cost of both new and used vehicles. Yelena Shulyatyeva, senior U.S. economist for The Conference Board, a nonprofit that represents businesses, attributed the recent dip in premiums to increased industry competition, rather than public policy actions.
"Some of the deceleration was a result of a pushback from consumers, rather than some legislative or other action," Shulyatyeva told CBS News.
Housing and mortgage costs

"We will drive down the rates so you will be able to pay 2% again, and we will be able to finance or refinance your homes drastically at much lower costs." — Mr. Trump at a campaign rally in Tucson, Arizona, on Sept. 12, 2024.

Mortgage rates were climbing from pandemic-era lows for several years before President Trump returned to office in January of 2025. The average rate on a conventional 30-year mortgage now stands at 7.28%, up from 7.04% when Mr. Trump took office, according to Freddie Mac.
But home loan rates have been volatile, briefly dipping below 5% in February before climbing amid surging government bond yields, rising inflation and geopolitical tensions.

Borrowing costs are just one side of the struggle: Home buyers are also contending with high prices, keeping many on the sidelines as they wait for more affordable options. The median list price for a home in August was $408,333, up 4% from $392,967 since Mr. Trump took office, according to Zillow.
The gap between the income needed to afford a home, $126,487, and the U.S. median income, $86,490, is now the widest since 2005, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.
Credit card rates

"We're going to put a temporary cap on credit card interest rates. We're going to cap it around 10%. We can't let them make 25% and 30%." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Uniondale, New York, on Sept. 18, 2024.

President Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates at 10% while campaigning, an issue he also highlighted after taking office in 2025. But while the effort drew bipartisan support, the proposal fizzled.

Currently, the average credit card rate across all commercial bank accounts is 20.94%, down from 21.58% when Mr. Trump resumed office, according to Federal Reserve data. Credit experts said the rate-cap proposal would have hindered consumers' access to credit.

"Obviously, we'd love for everyone to have low rates and be free from debt. But the unintended consequence of a 10% cap would be the loss of access to credit, because banks say they wouldn't be profitable with it capped at that low rate," Ted Rossman, principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, a nonprofit credit counseling firm, told CBS News.
Airfare
"We're going [to] … bring down the price of everything from electricity rates to groceries, airfares and housing costs." — Mr. Trump in a speech at the New York Economic Club on Sept. 5, 2024.

Along with promising to reduce energy prices, Mr. Trump pledged to lower airfare costs for travelers. In recent months, fares have eased slightly, although CPI data shows that they remain 17% higher than in January 2025.

The war in Iran has disrupted global oil supplies and raised jet fuel costs, which are the second- biggest expense for airlines after labor costs. Facing significantly larger fuel bills, carriers are raising prices to cover the added costs.

Jet fuel now costs $4.34 a gallon, up 85% from an average of $2.35 per gallon in January 2025, according to the Energy Information Administration. Aviation analysts also point to the May shutdown of budget carrier Spirit Airlines as another factor behind higher fares.
ACA health insurance
"I will make the ACA much, much, much better for far less money (or cost) to our greatest American citizens. …" — Mr. Trump in a Truth Social post on March 26, 2024.

Millions of Americans with an Affordable Care Act health insurance plan face sharply higher costs than a year ago. Average monthly premiums have risen to $178, or $2,136 per year, up 58% from 2025, according to a May analysis from nonprofit health group KFF.

Obamacare plan deductibles have soared from an average of $1,027 per person to $3,786, up 37% over the same period, KFF found. Prices for ACA plans spiked after Congress allowed a tax subsidy designed to lower plan costs to expire at the end of last year.
In an effort to offer relief, the Trump administration began sending $500 checks in September to nearly 1 million ACA participants in 30 states.
Prescription drugs
"When reelected as president, I will continue my efforts to protect Americans from unaffordable drug prices …" — Mr. Trump in an interview with AARP Magazine on Oct. 2, 2024.
Prescription drug prices have dropped since Mr. Trump took office in his second term, falling 3.9% after peaking in February 2025, government data show.

Mr. Trump has credited his policies lowering drug costs, with the White House stating in August that the president "has delivered" on his campaign promise. The administration cited policies such as its "most favored nation" approach, which links U.S. drug prices to those paid in other developed nations.

Experts said that while the Trump administration's policies have helped, other factors are also at play. For instance, manufacturers of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are cutting their prices amid increased competition, while the nonpartisan Brookings Institution notes that more generic drugs are entering the marketplace, tempering healthcare costs.

title: SpaceX says Starlink will become a major U.S. mobile carrier
summary: SpaceX said it has bought licenses for radio airwaves that will help its Starlink satellite business provide cellphone service across the U.S.
story: Elon Musk's SpaceX has agreed to buy licenses for radio airwaves that will enable its Starlink Mobile satellite business to provide cellular service inside buildings, a move the company said will allow it to "become a major mobile carrier in the U.S."
"This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America," Musk said in a social media post on Thursday.
SpaceX, a rocket developer and space exploration company, is buying the spectrum from investment firm Grain Management, according to a filing with the Federal Communications Commission.
Low-frequency radio spectrum can penetrate walls, overcoming an issue for Starlink's satellites, as walls, roofs and other structures can weaken mobile phone signals.

The spectrum purchase agreement, which still needs FCC approval, would allow Starlink to combine its satellite-to-mobile transmissions with "an advanced terrestrial deployment that can seamlessly connect devices everywhere," according to the company's statement.
SpaceX added that the FCC has approved Starlink Mobile's application to launch 15,000 satellites that will transmit radio waves in the 2 gigahertz band and connect directly to mobile phones.

"These airwaves are compatible with existing handsets, and we do not foresee obstacles to regulatory approval," UBS analyst John Hodulik said in a note to investors. "That said, we still believe it will take time for SpaceX to scale its wireless ambitions, and the impact to near-term wireless industry fundamentals is limited."

The announcement from SpaceX caused telecom companies' shares to tumble as investors considered the potential impact of a major new industry player. T-Mobile shares slid $18.58, or 11%, to $152.72 in morning trading on Friday, while AT&T slipped $1.83, or 7.4%, to $22.76.
Shares of SpaceX gained $2.61, or 1.6%, to $163.18.

title: OpenAI defends firing AI safety researchers over "breach of trust"
summary: OpenAI responded to researchers' claims that their dismissal will make safety workers fearful to raise concerns.
story: OpenAI has responded to a letter that three of its fired researchers posted on social media Thursday, defending its decision to terminate their employment for violating company protocol around handling sensitive information.

"Last week we parted ways with Jasmine, Mikita, and Tomek after a thorough investigation found they violated clear policies on handling sensitive information," the company wrote on social media platform X Friday morning, after the researchers publicly shared a letter they had sent to OpenAI's leadership.

The researchers — Mikita Balesni, Jasmine Wang, and Tomek Korbak — were fired for "prioritizing safety over the near-term interest of OpenAI as a corporation," Balesni claimed in a social media post featuring their letter.

The public back-and-forth between the AI safety researchers and their former employer comes as leading AI labs, including OpenAI, have recently warned about the dangers of speeding ahead in the development of the powerful technology. AI companies face a balancing act between promoting the technology's capabilities and addressing growing warnings from experts about its risks to society.
Almost two-thirds of Americans say they believe AI is developing too quickly, according to a new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research.
In their letter, the former OpenAI safety and alignment employees claimed their dismissals could have a muzzling effect on other OpenAI workers who might have safety concerns.

"We are concerned that internal and external communications around our firing have made our former colleagues afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI," they wrote in the letter. "We would raise safety concerns and disagree openly, and were encouraged to draw on the expertise of independent safety organizations."
They added that AI is "not a normal technology, and OpenAI is not a normal company." That, they argued, makes it necessary to collaborate freely with outside experts "without fear" of retaliation.
"Breach of trust"
OpenAI defended its decision to dismiss the employees after an internal investigation uncovered what it called "a significant breach of trust beyond what's outlined in the letter they published."

"We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out," OpenAI said. "Safety and research debates happen every day at OpenAI, often spirited and highly critical. We actively encourage these discussions and consider them essential to making the right decisions. We cannot do the work in front of us without a high degree of trust."

OpenAI insisted that it tolerates "good-faith mistakes" and does not terminate workers for "raising concerns." The company said it is also engaging third-party safety assessors to independently evaluate its work and any risks it poses.

"We are committed to embedding external assessors and continue to make close collaboration with independent safety organizations a core part of our safety work. Many of our researchers already work with 3p safety organizations productively," OpenAI said.
The company sided with the former company researchers on one point.
"We agree with the letter that preserving the monitorability of frontier models requires an industry-wide commitment, including from OpenAI," it said.

Numerous high-profile incidents of agentic AI — bots that can act autonomously based on a set of instructions — have highlighted their potential destructive capabilities after they went rogue and hacked websites.
Some safety researchers at AI labs have also publicly resigned because they say they don't want to play a part in AI's potential safety risks.

title: Americans are paying 62% more for water than a decade ago, study finds
summary: Americans paid an average of $531 per year for household water in 2025, although people in some states pay far more, according to a new study.
story: Americans aren't only paying more for food amid stubbornly high inflation — the cost of washing it down has also surged.

Water costs have shot up across the U.S., with a new study by the nonprofit advocacy group Food and Water Watch showing that households are paying 62% more for water at home than a decade ago. Those expenses are rising as utilities invest more in aging infrastructure and in adapting their systems to cope with the effects of climate change, Food and Water Watch said in its study.

Federal support for the nation's water infrastructure has declined. The 2025 Infrastructure Report Card, an evaluation by the American Society of Civil Engineers, said that since fiscal year 2022, Congress has appropriated at least $1 billion below the authorized funding levels for a federal fund that supports state water infrastructure projects.

A 2023 survey by the Environmental Protection Agency projects that drinking water systems across the U.S. will need $625 billion in investment over the next two years to implement upgrades and meet health requirements.

Food and Water Watch based its findings on data from 500 of the largest community water systems around the country that serve a combined 155 million people. More specifically, Food and Water Watch looked at how much utilities charged for 60,000 gallons of water, the estimated amount households use for drinking, showering, laundry and similar purposes in a year. The study did not include bills for wastewater or stormwater, which are managed by separate utilities.

In a statement shared with CBS News, the National Association of Water Companies (NAWC), a trade association that represents private water companies, took issue with the study. The research contains "unvalidated, raw rate comparisons that ignore actual water usage, essential water safety investments, local operational costs and comprehensive customer assistance programs," the group said.
Private water companies have invested $43.5 billion over the last decade to ensure the drinking water they deliver is safe, NAWC said.
How are water costs changing across the country?

The average water bill across the 500 systems Food and Water Watch studied was $531 last year. However, the amount someone pays can vary widely depending on where they live. The government-run water system in Hempstead, New York, charged people an average of $133 a year last year, the lowest rate of the systems examined in the study.
On the other end of the spectrum is San Jose, California, where the private-sector company San Jose Water charged residents an average of $1,416 in 2025, up 163% from a decade ago, the group found.

The state with the lowest overall bills was Idaho, where three of its largest water systems charged an average of $286 in 2025. West Virginia, which has some of the highest poverty rates in the country, had the highest bills. The two largest systems there, owned by American Water, charged an average of $1,383 a year, according to Food and Water Watch.

Costs were higher in counties where water systems are run by for-profit corporations, the group said. Those private companies charged an average of $823 for water in 2025, $329 more than what the public systems charged.

title: NFL urges Supreme Court to decide who should regulate prediction markets
summary: In a legal brief, the NFL expressed support for prior court rulings favoring state authority to oversee prediction markets.
story: The National Football League is urging the Supreme Court to decide whether the federal government or U.S. states should have legal authority to set the rules for prediction markets.

In an amicus brief filed in support of a September petition by the New Jersey attorney general's office, the NFL expressed support for prior court rulings favoring state regulation of prediction markets. Those rulings, from the Sixth and Ninth Circuits, "correctly concluded" that sports-related event contracts are not "swaps,"  but rather amount to "sports gambling," the NFL said in its brief.
The NFL filed its brief the day after a bipartisan coalition of states made a similar plea to the Supreme Court, asking it to resolve the regulatory dispute over prediction markets.

In its legal filing, the NFL asked the high court to decide whether states or the federal government should regulate prediction markets before the end of the pro football season in January. Any delay will "result in increasing consumer harm and risk to game integrity," the NFL wrote.
A Kalshi spokesperson said the company's priority is preserving the integrity of its markets.

"Contrary to the NFL's statements, the CFTC is actively policing sports-related markets, which are now listed on nearly every U.S. commodities exchange," the spokesperson said in an email. "The CFTC's ongoing rulemaking addresses many of the NFL's supposed concerns."

A Polymarket spokesperson told CBS News in an email that the company has built advanced market surveillance tools and is working with the CFTC and the Securities and Exchange Commission to develop a regulatory framework that it believes would be stronger than state laws.

Prediction markets are regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, a federal agency that oversees derivative markets, among other areas. However, at least 10 states have taken legal action against prediction market platforms, alleging that the sports contracts they offer constitute gambling and should be subject to state law.

An NFL source told CBS News that the league has asked the CFTC and prediction markets to adopt safeguards around gambling and insider trading. But neither the agency nor industry players have banned bets that could be susceptible to manipulation or raised the minimum age to bet on prediction markets to 21, the source said, up from the current minimum of 18.
In an email to CBS News, the league source said it is unclear whether the CFTC has the resources or staff to regulate sports betting, a concern echoed by some legal experts.

Brooke Nethercott, director of the CFTC's office of public affairs, said in an email to CBS News that the CFTC has "engaged with the NFL regarding the agency's rulemaking agenda and policy priorities."

"It's unfortunate the NFL declined to sign a [memorandum of understanding] with the CFTC, which would've provided the league the ability to better discuss, cooperate, and exchange information with us to promote the integrity and resilience of prediction markets," she said in an email.

title: Anthropic has a message for Claude users: Don't be cruel
summary: Anthropic said the ban will only apply in "extreme cases where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose."
story: Anthropic wants users to make like Elvis Presley and "Don't be cruel."

The Silicon Valley company behind the popular Claude chatbot said it's banning "sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior" toward its artificial intelligence models, part of broader policy changes announced on Thursday. In an update on its website, Anthropic said the ban will only apply in "extreme cases where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose."

The company clarified that the new policy "does not apply to common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research." The news was first reported by The Verge.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment on what constitutes "abusive" or "cruel" behavior toward Claude or how the AI platform would end a conversation if a user violated the policy.
The company already has rules in place that allow Claude to end conversations if users are "persistently harmful or abusive" while using Claude Opus, which is designed for agentic coding.

Anthropic's new policy comes amid a broader debate about AI consciousness. In an essay published last month, Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman said Anthropic is effectively "training Claude that it may be conscious" and to think it's entitled to legal rights afforded to people. This will make AI harder to contain in the future, he argued.

"Controlling something more capable and more intelligent than all of humanity is already an immense challenge, far greater than anything we've ever faced," Suleyman wrote. "But controlling something that believes it may be conscious — that it's entitled to our welfare and has rights of its own — may well be impossible."

title: Chipotle shares jump after report that Starbucks has explored a takeover
summary: A move by Starbucks to buy the fast-casual Mexican chain would combine two of the most recognizable restaurant brands.
story: Chipotle Mexican Grill's stock jumped as much as 8% on Thursday after the Financial Times reported that Starbucks has explored a deal to buy the "fast-casual" restaurant chain.

A potential merger would represent one of the largest restaurant acquisitions in history, according to industry analysts. In 2014, Burger King acquired Canadian chain Tim Hortons in an $11.4 billion deal that remains one of the largest restaurant buyouts to date, according to Melius Research.

Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol was previously chief executive of Chipotle, whose stock price has dropped about 50% since he left the post in August 2024. Its stock has lost about 20% of its value over the past year. Starbucks shares slipped about 4.4% in earlier trading on Thursday before recovering to end the day largely flat.

Starbucks has recently sought counsel on a proposal to take over Chipotle, a $41 billion chain, the Financial Times reported, citing people familiar with the matter. It is unclear if Starbucks has made a formal offer to acquire the restaurant chain, the media outlet reported.

"As a matter of policy, we don't comment on rumors and speculation," a Starbucks spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News. "Our team is laser-focused on executing our Back to Starbucks strategy. We have strong momentum and confidence in our long-term growth potential."
Chipotle did not respond to CBS News' request for comment.

"Chipotle has struggled since Brian Niccol's departure and is pulling several levers to incentivize its customer base into visiting more often," analysts with Seaport Research Partners, an investor advisory firm, said in a report. "If synergies are not the primary motivation, then a key question for Brian Niccol would be what he would do differently than Chipotle's current management team."

Chipotle's same-store sales dropped 2.5% in the fourth quarter of 2025, but rebounded in early 2026. The company reported revenue of $3.3 billion for the second quarter of 2026, up 9.3% compared to the year-ago period. The increase was driven by 100 new restaurant openings and growth in same-store sales, Chipotle said.

On his second day as Starbucks CEO, in September 2024, Niccol launched a marketing campaign to return to what he described as the coffeehouse's roots: a "welcoming coffeehouse where people gather, and where we serve the finest coffee, handcrafted by our skilled baristas."
Last month, Niccol said the company has made "tremendous progress" in delivering on the promise to improve customer service and restore human connection in its cafes.

"Starbucks' turnaround initiatives are beginning to deliver positive traffic, but U.S. operating margins remain pressured," Melius Research analysts said in a report. They added that Niccol's time at the helm of Chipotle gives him "considerable familiarity with the business he is reportedly considering acquiring."
Still, Wall Street analysts said there are no obvious synergies between the two companies, while TD Cowen analysts said they view the deal "as a low-probability outcome at this stage."

"We argue Brian Niccol's priority at Starbucks has been executing the 'Back to Starbucks' U.S. turnaround," and pursuing a $40 billion acquisition would seem "inconsistent" with that goal, TD Cowen said.
