title: Military's archbishop criticizes plan to livestream execution
summary: Archbishop for the U.S. Military Timothy Broglio said Catholic service members assigned to the firing squad that will execute the Fort Hood shooter should ask to be excused.
story: The archbishop for the U.S. military says any Catholic service members who are assigned to participate in the livestreamed firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan should ask to be excused — the latest pushback against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's plan.

Archbishop Timothy P. Broglio released a statement Monday to "express my disapproval of what is proposed regarding the execution of the terrorist Hasan," referring to Hegseth's announcement last week that Hasan's execution in December would be publicly viewable.

Broglio pointed to the Catholic Church's opposition to the death penalty. He also warned of "moral injury" to service members who are tasked with carrying out the execution, and asked: "Do we really want to imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries?"

"The US military generally enjoys a good reputation in the world," wrote Broglio. "Is there really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheel chair to the whole world? Does this decision reflect the dignity of the human person?"
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Three days earlier, Pope Leo XIV wrote on social media that the death penalty is "inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person." The pope did not explicitly reference Hasan's planned execution or the botched lethal-injection execution of Christa Pike in his post, which coincided with the World Day Against the Death Penalty.
Hegseth said last week the military plans to make the execution public "because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."

In 2013, Hasan was convicted by court-martial and sentenced to death for killing 13 people and injuring more than 30 at the Army installation in Fort Hood, Texas. The former Army psychiatrist acknowledged at trial that he was responsible for the shooting, claiming he opened fire on fellow service members in an attempt to protect Islamic insurgents from the U.S. military.
Hasan's case could mark the U.S. military's first execution of an American since 1961, and its first use of a firing squad since 1945. Firing squads are also rare in civilian courts.

Publicly viewable executions are virtually unheard of in modern U.S. history: The country's last large-scale public execution appeared to take place 90 years ago, when Rainey Bethea was hanged for rape in front of a crowd of about 20,000 in Kentucky. Other countries that are believed to carry out public executions include Iran, Afghanistan and North Korea.

Hegseth's plan to livestream the execution has drawn criticism from members of both parties, including a growing number of congressional Republicans. Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska said "I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America," and Sen. Kevin Cramer of North Dakota said the "death penalty is not entertainment."
House Speaker Mike Johnson told CBS News some of his House Republican colleagues have "concerns," which he plans to bring to the White House.

"The concern would be that you would create a video that would be a recruiting tool for future terrorists. You know, we've got to think through the policy implications of all that," Johnson told CBS News' Robert Costa. "I wouldn't be watching it if it was aired. But there's a lot of opinions on that. I think there's still some time to talk about that."
Vice President JD Vance, who is Catholic, told reporters last week that "if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."

Eleanor  Watson
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Judge chastises DOJ after 430 trees cut down at D.C. golf course
summary: Government lawyers said 430 trees were cut down at East Potomac Golf Links on Saturday.
story: Washington — A federal judge on Monday rebuked the Justice Department after hundreds of trees were cut down at East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, D.C., on Saturday with little notice, telling government lawyers that they have "lost credibility."

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes held a nearly four-hour virtual hearing Monday and ordered Kevin Griess, superintendent of the National Mall and Memorial Parks, to testify under oath about what led to the felling of 430 trees at the course, which President Trump wants to overhaul. During the hearing, she also demanded Frank Lands, deputy director of operations for the National Park Service, call in to answer questions.

"I am at a total loss to understand what has happened here other than, Occam's Razor time, that the government intended to do precisely what it has done," which is delay informing the plaintiffs and the court of impending action so they could put a plan in place to raze hundreds of trees, Reyes told Marissa Piropato, a Justice Department lawyer.
The judge began the hearing telling Piropato she is "furious" and "thoroughly unamused right now."
"You did not do your best. You did your absolute worst," Reyes said of the Justice Department's efforts to notify the court and plaintiffs of the planned tree removals.

Reyes extended a temporary order blocking the National Park Service from cutting down any additional trees, including for routine maintenance, until 2 p.m. Tuesday as she considers her next steps. She also said she will issue an order requiring the Justice Department to provide her three days' notice of any forthcoming action at the golf course.

The judge had repeatedly asked the Justice Department to provide the court with notice if the Interior Department and National Park Service planned to conduct any construction or similar activity at East Potomac, which would allow her the opportunity to review that action and, if warranted, issue a court order.

Government lawyers told the court in a filing just before 5 p.m. on Friday that the National Park Service would start clearing trees from the course on Saturday as part of a "tree management and cultural landscape rehabilitation project." Griess said in a declaration timestamped Friday at 4:37 p.m. that a group of 169 trees would be removed first, followed by a second tranche of 90 trees. He said an estimated 529 trees in all would be felled as part of the project.

But on Sunday, lawyers for the D.C. Preservation League, which filed a lawsuit with two golfers challenging Mr. Trump's plan to transform East Potomac, said crews had cut down all 529 trees on Saturday alone, including "healthy, mature oaks and maples."

They requested an emergency order blocking the National Park Service from removing any more trees after Justice Department lawyers told the preservation group that the tree-removal operation was moving "faster than anticipated," according to court papers. The Trump administration told the D.C. Preservation League that "hundreds of additional trees would be felled imminently," though rain Sunday impacted that plan.

Another roughly 99 trees have been flagged for removal, according to the Justice Department. Griess, the superintendent of the National Mall and Memorial Parks, said the 430 trees that were felled were not identified as hazardous or raising safety concerns.

During the hearing, Reyes repeatedly pressed Piropato about when she learned that the National Park Service planned to cut down the trees and why she waited until Friday to inform both the plaintiffs and the court.
"Ignorance is not an excuse here," she said.
Reyes said she is "beyond disappointed" in the government.

"There are American citizens who are deeply concerned with the actions of the government, and I have repeatedly, on the record, said 'don't be concerned. I trust the government,'" Reyes said, adding, "I do not understand why this went forward on Saturday. Why did this go forward on Saturday?"

The judge also pressed Griess and Lands, who said he was testifying from a vehicle in a parking lot, on who ultimately gave the go-ahead to cut the trees down over the weekend. She called for Gregory Wischer, deputy chief of staff at the Interior Department, to answer questions, but Piropato said she could not get in contact with him.

Griess, whose work includes oversight of East Potomac Golf Links, said he submitted a tree-management plan, which included removals, to the head of the National Park Service on Oct. 5 and received approval for the plan the following day. But both he and Lands said there wasn't any urgency to remove the trees Saturday.

Griess told the court that his tree-removal plan aims to fulfill recommendations laid out in a 2019 Cultural Landscape Report, which calls for restoring "links style and historic vegetation (rough grasslands, thin trees between fairways, and sentinel deciduous trees)" at East Potomac.

Designed by golf course architect Walter J. Travis, East Potomac opened to the public in the 1920s as a links-style course, which are typically built along the coast, Griess said. Those types of golf courses have few trees and lower vegetation, he said.

But in the more than 100 years since East Potomac opened, different types of plantings were allowed on the course, and "there appeared to be no coherent adherence to the original design," Griess said. He told the court that the National Park Service intends to stay true to the stated intent of East Potomac as a links course.

Griess said he moved forward with putting together the tree-removal plan after funding and National Park Service employees working on events related to America's 250th birthday were freed up following the Freedom 250 Grand Prix in August.

But lawyers for the D.C. Preservation League pushed back on the Trump administration's argument that it cut down the trees to implement the seven-year-old Cultural Landscape Report and noted that Mr. Trump's plan to renovate the East Potomac golf course "will require massive tree-clearing."

They argued that the administration's implementation of the plan violates the National Environmental Policy Act, which requires federal agencies to assess the environmental impacts of proposed action. The plaintiffs accused the Trump administration of skirting its obligations under the law by conducting smaller, segmented projects, like the tree-razing.

"What Defendants are doing now goes beyond routine maintenance, or maintenance of any kind. Defendants have begun an operation that is unprecedented in East Potomac Park's 130-year history: felling more than 500 trees in a single day, with plans to cut down hundreds more as soon as the weather permits," lawyers for the D.C. Preservation League wrote in their request for emergency relief.

title: Republicans voice concerns over livestream execution plan
summary: President Trump said he approved of livestreaming the execution, but suggested the decision may not be final.
story: Washington — A growing number of Republicans are voicing concern over the Pentagon's plan to livestream the execution of the Fort Hood shooter in December — or at the very least, saying they won't be watching.

Over the weekend, President Trump said the administration was still making a determination about whether the firing-squad execution would be livestreamed, after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that it would be. The execution of Nidal Hasan, the ex-Army major convicted of the 2009 killing of 13 people at Fort Hood, is scheduled for Dec. 3.
House Speaker Mike Johnson told CBS News that some in the House Republican conference don't approve, and said he planned on bringing those concerns to the White House.

"There are colleagues who have concerns," Johnson told national correspondent and chief Washington analyst Robert Costa in an interview. "The concern would be that you would create a video that would be a recruiting tool for future terrorists. You know, we've got to think through the policy implications of all that. I wouldn't be watching it if it was aired. But there's a lot of opinions on that. I think there's still some time to talk about that. ... I need to tell the White House what some of my colleagues think about that, and not everybody is in favor of the idea."
Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska said there is "no need to livestream any execution, including this one," urging the Pentagon to change course.

"I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America," she wrote on X. "It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks. How we carry out justice matters just as much as the justice itself, so I urge the Pentagon to reverse this gruesome decision."

Sen. Kevin Cramer of North Dakota said in a statement, "The death penalty is not entertainment." He said families of the victims deserve justice. "But publicizing the execution of religious extremists provides exactly what terrorists crave: an audience. It converts the most consequential punishment a government can impose into a public spectacle."
"Justice will be served, but the United States of America does not and should not livestream executions," Republican Rep. Ann Wagner of Missouri wrote on X.

Rep. Rob Bresnahan Jr. of Pennsylvania wrote, "An execution shouldn't be a live-streamed spectacle. The focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment. Their pain deserves respect, not a public show."
Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina on Friday called livestreaming the execution "beyond disgusting."

Only one Republican member of Congress has publicly voiced clear support for livestreaming the execution — Rep. Andy Ogles of Tennessee.: "Excellent. Public execution is what this terrorist deserves," he wrote on X. "We will be watching."
Vice President JD Vance said Friday that he wouldn't be watching if it's livestreamed, and added, "I don't know that that's actually going to happen."

"So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance told reporters. "Now that said, I mean, look, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended the livestreaming decision on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" this weekend. Asked if the administration risks making Hasan a martyr, Mullin responded, "No one has to watch it." Pressed further on whether the decision risks radicalizing others, Mullin said, "I think people need to understand if you attack— if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the— that the punishment fits the crime."
On Saturday, Mr. Trump floated the possibility that the plans could still change.

"There are two thoughts: don't show it and show it," the president told reporters at the White House Saturday. "'Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won't be doing what he did. So I'll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but I'll make a decision."
The president has given seemingly conflicting information as to whether he was involved in the decision to livestream the execution.

When a reporter asked the president Friday if he authorized or approved the livestreaming decision, he said, "Absolutely, I did." But in an interview with CNY Central Syracuse later that day, he said he "wasn't involved in that decision" to livestream the execution, while saying he understood that decision was made to "have it serve as an example."

title: Trump administration ordered to cancel taxpayer-funded TV ads
summary: The Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million in taxpayer money for the ads, which the White House has defended as public service announcements.
story: President Trump must cancel any remaining television commercials paid for with millions of dollars in taxpayer money to promote his political message, a federal judge ordered Sunday night, even as the administration said the ad campaign was coming to an end.

U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause, which challenged the ads as an illegal misuse of funds. She ordered the administration to cancel any remaining ads, including any set to air Sunday night, in granting a temporary restraining order.

"Defendants shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged advertisements" during the two-week duration of her order, the judge said.
The order was in effect as of 6:45 p.m. ET on Sunday.

The spending on cable and broadcast for the five Trump ads that disclose on screen that they were "paid for by the U.S. Government" now exceeds $20 million, according to political ad tracker AdImpact. That's the amount the Department of Homeland Security had allocated for a "National Media Campaign," awarding a contract for the ads to Maryland-based LMD Agency on Sept. 20. A day earlier, the White House Office of Management and Budget had granted DHS's Customs and Border Protection $20 million for "OBBB Commemorative Events," according to a nongovernment database. The source of the funds was first reported by The Washington Sun.

By Monday morning, AdImpact showed U.S. government spending on the five ads had reached $21,705,138. (Because the ads were classified by the White House as PSAs, AdImpact may not reflect the exact total amount spent.)
Here are the five ads listed in AdImpact and the amount spent, as of Monday:

Maduro ($3.1 million): Featuring Mr. Trump, Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio talk about the operation to capture and remove Nicolás Maduro from power in Venezuela.Final Battle ($13 million): A refurbished version of a Trump 2024 campaign video shows Mr. Trump walking down the hallway as part of a Trump campaign speech plays. He can be heard vowing "once and for all" to "demolish the deep state," "expel the warmongers from our government," "throw off the sick political class that hates our country" and "rout the fake news media." Celebrating The Enduring Spirit ($3.1 million): This is a general pro-America ad, with audio of Mr. Trump's July 3 Mount Rushmore speech, extolling the America as the "most successful, most accomplished, most exceptional nation ever to exist in human history."To The Great Proud People of Iran ($1.1 million): Footage from the beginning of the Iran War cut together with shots of President Trump as audio from remarks by Mr. Trump and Hegseth play.The Country He Loves ($1.4 million) - The "Love Me" ad features Mr. Trump vowing to defeat "communism, socialism and Marxism in America" as a series of flash-cut highlights from his second administration play on the screen. Audio from JMSN's "Love Me" plays throughout the ad, and JMSN has demanded that his song be dropped from the ad.

Maduro ($3.1 million): Featuring Mr. Trump, Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio talk about the operation to capture and remove Nicolás Maduro from power in Venezuela.

Final Battle ($13 million): A refurbished version of a Trump 2024 campaign video shows Mr. Trump walking down the hallway as part of a Trump campaign speech plays. He can be heard vowing "once and for all" to "demolish the deep state," "expel the warmongers from our government," "throw off the sick political class that hates our country" and "rout the fake news media."

Celebrating The Enduring Spirit ($3.1 million): This is a general pro-America ad, with audio of Mr. Trump's July 3 Mount Rushmore speech, extolling the America as the "most successful, most accomplished, most exceptional nation ever to exist in human history."
To The Great Proud People of Iran ($1.1 million): Footage from the beginning of the Iran War cut together with shots of President Trump as audio from remarks by Mr. Trump and Hegseth play.

The Country He Loves ($1.4 million) - The "Love Me" ad features Mr. Trump vowing to defeat "communism, socialism and Marxism in America" as a series of flash-cut highlights from his second administration play on the screen. Audio from JMSN's "Love Me" plays throughout the ad, and JMSN has demanded that his song be dropped from the ad.

Asked for comment, the White House referred to an Oct. 5 social media post from Mr. Trump in which he defended the taxpayer-funded ads as "rather standard" but after Republicans criticized the use of taxpayer money to air the ads, he said he would pay for them from his own political fundraising. In a court filing late Saturday, the Justice Department argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because "the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow."

Legal experts have suggested that the use of taxpayer money for the ads violated a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for "publicity or propaganda" and potentially other laws.

"We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda," the plaintiffs said in a statement issued by Democracy Forward, the nonprofit legal organization that represents them. "There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda."

In a court declaration Saturday, senior DHS official Holly Mehringer wrote that the money had come from congressionally appropriated funds that are "available for, among other things, 'commemorating efforts and events related to border security.'"

The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements similar to those of past administrations to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren't aimed at helping the public benefit from specific government programs.
A White House official said last month the PSAs "are clearly not political," and noted: "The President is not on the ballot and the ads don't have a call to action."
Top Republicans who criticized the use of public funds include Senate Majority Leader John Thune, of South Dakota. "It shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars," Thune told reporters.

On "Face the Nation," GOP Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana said last month, "I don't think any public official, including President Trump or [former DHS Secretary] Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves."
The Democratic National Committee has separately sued the Republican administration over the ads.

"This is the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and illegal misuse of Americans' hard-earned tax dollars," a group of Senate Democrats said in a letter last month.

Amid the backlash, Mr. Trump said he would start paying for the ads with political funds. A White House official said there were no immediate plans to reimburse the government for money already spent.

title: Johnson says he intends to stay on as GOP leader if party loses majority
summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson said last week that he could start a lawn business if the GOP loses the House majority, which he told CBS News' Robert Costa was "tongue in cheek."
story: House Speaker Mike Johnson said he intends to serve as GOP leader if Republicans lose their House majority in November — but he remains bullish about the party's chances despite significant headwinds.

"In the unlikely scenario where we lost the majority, I would expect my colleagues would ask me to continue leading this conference, even if we have divided government," Johnson told CBS News' Robert Costa in an interview near Johnson's hometown of Shreveport, Louisiana.

Johnson, who has led House Republicans as speaker since 2023, has repeatedly pushed back on questions about his plans if the GOP loses the majority in the lower chamber in November. Known for his optimistic outlook, the speaker has expressed confidence that Republicans will hold on to the chamber, or even grow their narrow majority. But midterm dynamics traditionally boost the party opposing the party in control of the White House, and the unpopular war in Iran, high gas and diesel prices and other controversial Trump administration policies have added to those challenges for the GOP.

Last week, a comment Johnson made to Fox News on his plans for his future fueled speculation that he could retire from politics, as he suggested that he could go back to his hometown of Shreveport and start a lawn business if the GOP loses the House majority.
"It's just hilarious," Johnson said of the interest the comment spurred, telling Costa that the remark was "tongue in cheek."

"What I was trying to say to them is that throughout my whole life, my number one objective is to be of my highest and best use to God and to my country, and that's always what I've thought," Johnson said. "And I was trying to make the point that if God has a different design, then we'll follow that. But what I believe is, I'm going to be the speaker of the House for at least two more years."
But Johnson added, "If, heaven forbid, we lost the majority, I would expect my colleagues would call upon me to continue to lead the conference in divided government."
"My intention is to stay and serve, and that's what I've been doing, as best I can," he said.

Johnson has been campaigning heavily in recent weeks, with plans to hit 40 districts in 22 states before polls close on Election Day. He made a case for his continued leadership — whether in the majority or the minority — pointing to the millions of dollars he's  brought in for Republicans this cycle, his busy travel schedule, and his work to corral a sometimes volatile GOP majority in this Congress.
"I'm not sure what the case would be for any alternative," he said. "I intend to stay and lead."

When pressed by Costa on whether he has it in him to be a tough, combative minority leader in the current political environment, Johnson pointed to his time on the House Judiciary Committee and his defense of President Trump during his two impeachment trials.
"I was a litigator in my past life — constitutional law attorney. We can be tough, but we can be happy warriors," he said. "That's what Ronald Reagan was. That's what I fashioned myself as."
But Johnson was clear: he has "no intention other than winning this majority and serving as speaker."
"That is what's going to happen," Johnson said. "And I'm telling you, I'm leaving it all in the field to do it."
This story published first on CBS News at 5:00 a.m. on Oct. 12, 2026.

Mike Johnson

title: Rep. Jeffries says Democrats are "on the verge of taking back control"
summary: Jeffries campaigned in New Jersey and Pennsylvania and plans to campaign in Texas in the coming days to help Democratic candidates unseat Republican incumbents.
story: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries expressed growing confidence that his party will regain control of the House in November, as he visited two battleground districts in recent days to help Democratic candidates unseat Republican incumbents.

Jeffries campaigned Friday in New Jersey's competitive 7th Congressional District alongside Democratic challenger Rebecca Bennett, a Navy veteran seeking to unseat Republican Rep. Tom Kean Jr. The following day, he traveled to Pennsylvania's 1st Congressional District to rally with Democrat Bob Harvie, a Bucks County commissioner challenging Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick.

The two districts are heavily suburban, fairly affluent and politically divided — and they've caused heartburn for Democrats in recent years. The moderate Fitzpatrick has a long history of outrunning other Republicans and winning crossover support since he was first elected in 2016. Control of Kean's seat has flipped twice since 2018, but he narrowly won a competitive reelection two years ago.
Democrats have invested in both races this year and view both of them as highly competitive, as they hope to take advantage of an unfavorable political environment for President Trump's party.

"We're running through the finish line. We take nothing for granted, but we're on the verge of taking back control of the House of Representatives," Jeffries told reporters following Saturday's event in Pennsylvania.

In a briefing with a small group of political reporters Wednesday, Jeffries pointed to a handful of districts in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and New York as opportunities for Democrats. He also said he plans to visit two South Texas districts.

Republicans control the House by a single-digit margin, so the outcome of the midterms could be decided by a fairly small number of races. Jeffries declined to predict how many seats his party could gain in November.

"I'm very confident that we're going to take back the majority, but it remains to be seen what that looks like in terms of the number of seats that we pick up, which is going to depend on the conditions that exist over the next few weeks," he said in the briefing.

During the rally in Bucks County, a perennial swing county that supported Mr. Trump by a razor-thin margin in 2024 after years of narrow Democratic victories, Harvie said: "It is not an accident that Hakeem Jeffries is here tonight."
"He knows what we're going to do with this district. He knows the potential," he said.

Fitzpatrick's campaign told CBS News that the Republican lawmaker "is aware of Hakeem's visit, he still considers him a friend, and he looks forward to working with him in a bipartisan manner in the 120th Congress."
"Leader Jeffries is doing what he needs to do, and Brian completely understands that," the campaign's statement continued.

Fitzpatrick, who is seeking a sixth term, has cultivated a moderate image and put distance between himself and Mr. Trump, voting with House Democrats to rescind tariffs on Canada and restrict the Iran war. He also voted against final passage of the Trump administration's signature "Big, Beautiful Bill" last year. Most recently, he pushed back last week on the president's plan to buy diesel from Russia.

Democrats have argued Fitzpatrick hasn't consistently opposed the president's agenda, pointing to an earlier vote in favor of the "Big, Beautiful Bill." Fitzpatrick has said he voted against the final legislation after the Senate added steeper Medicaid cuts.

Judi Reiss, a Democratic local elected official in Lower Makefield Township, Pennsylvania, told CBS News at Saturday's rally with Jeffries and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro that she has "no personal animosity toward [Fitzpatrick] whatsoever, but he hasn't done anything. He's been a rubber stamp for Donald Trump."
"He has not been independent, and it's very disappointing," said Reiss, who sought the 2020 Democratic nomination for Fitzpatrick's seat but dropped out before the primary.

Still, Fitzpatrick has survived on challenging terrain in the past — and overperformed other Republicans. Vice President Kamala Harris narrowly won his district in 2024, but Fitzpatrick won reelection the same year by a more than 12-point margin.
The Cook Political Report rated the Pennsylvania district "Leans Republican" on Friday, down from its previous "Likely Republican" assessment.

Bucks County resident Bill Craig, a Republican who plans to vote for Fitzpatrick, told CBS News he believes Harvie has a "slim chance" of winning the district, but he expects the race to be close due to heavy Democratic turnout.
"Brian Fitzpatrick could cure cancer right now, and they still wouldn't vote for him," Craig said. "He's very middle-of-the-road. They're trying to paint him as some kind of MAGA psycho."

Jeffries visited Fitzpatrick's district a day after campaigning for Bennett across the Delaware River, in a New Jersey seat that the Cook Political report sees as Democratic-leaning — a shift after it called the race a toss-up as recently as last month.

The GOP incumbent there, Kean, is seeking a third term representing a district that stretches from the New York City suburbs to the Pennsylvania border, with Mr. Trump's Bedminster golf club sitting in the middle. He was first elected after the district was made slightly redder in 2022, and defeated Democratic Rep. Tom Malinowski.
House Speaker Mike Johnson also campaigned with Kean in recent weeks.
Jeffries' campaign stops illustrate the importance of suburban congressional districts that could help determine which party controls the House next year.

In last week's briefing with reporters, the Democratic leader described all four competitive Republican-held districts in Pennsylvania as Democratic pickup opportunities. In addition to Fitzpatrick's seat, Democrats are targeting a northeastern Pennsylvania district and two seats in eastern and central Pennsylvania.
He also singled out the race in New York's 17th Congressional District, where Democrat Cait Conley is challenging Republican Rep. Mike Lawler.
Jeffries to campaign in South Texas races
Meanwhile, Democrats are defending two competitive districts in South Texas, and have signaled they plan to go on offense in two GOP-held districts in the region.
Republicans made substantial gains among Latinos in 2024, especially in South Texas, where some counties that were once Democratic strongholds became light-red.
Jeffries argued that Latino voters could swing back to Democrats, pointing to concerns over the cost of living and the Trump administration's aggressive immigration policies.
He said the political environment has changed dramatically in the Rio Grande Valley, where Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez are seeking reelection.

Jeffries said he also plans to campaign in the coming weeks for two Texas Democrats who hope to unseat Republicans. Tejano music star Bobby Pulido is running against Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz in a toss-up district, and Democrat Johnny Garcia is challenging Republican nominee Carlos De La Cruz in a seat that's viewed as redder.
The Democratic leader also rejected the notion that newly drawn Republican congressional maps in Texas and Florida would deliver the substantial gains GOP strategists had initially anticipated.
"Under no circumstances are Republicans winning five seats in Texas or four seats in Florida," Jeffries told CBS News last week.

The National Republican Congressional Committee has disputed Democrats' increasingly optimistic assessments of the battleground map, pointing to Republican campaign resources and ground game efforts in competitive districts.
If Democrats regain control of the House, Jeffries would be positioned to become the first Black speaker of the House in American history.

While the party that doesn't control the White House almost always performs well in the midterms, the exact result is tougher to predict. In the 2022 midterms, when Republicans were buoyed by former President Joe Biden's unpopularity, predictions of a sweeping GOP wave failed to materialize. Republicans narrowly won control of the House but failed to recapture the Senate until two years later.
Asked by CBS News whether Democrats risk that kind of election night disappointment, Jeffries acknowledged the outcome will depend on the political climate and spending.

He said that while the current environment appears favorable to Democrats, the amount of money being spent by Republican-aligned political groups could ultimately limit the number of seats his party gains.
House Republicans' campaign committee had more cash on hand than the group's Democratic counterpart at the end of August.

Jeffries disputed suggestions that Republicans hold an overwhelming financial advantage in House battlegrounds, arguing that Democrats are effectively at parity when spending by candidates, committees and outside groups is considered together.
On the GOP side, Johnson is also barnstorming frontline districts as Republicans fight to maintain their majority — and look for opportunities to unseat vulnerable Democrats.
Johnson said the other day he expects to visit about 40 districts this month.

In recent days, Johnson has visited Michigan and Pennsylvania with incumbent Republicans, and campaigned alongside two Iowa Republicans who are aiming to retain GOP-held districts: Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Joe Mitchell.

He also campaigned last week in Ohio with Derek Merrin, who is hoping to unseat longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur in a toss-up district. It's a rematch of 2024, when Merrin lost to Kaptur by around 2,400 votes.

During his visit to Ohio, Johnson said he expects control of the House to be determined by at least 22 seats that he sees as "jump-balls." He has expressed optimism that Republicans can retain their majority.
"This will come down to the outcome of about 22 districts around the country, and I believe we can win those," Johnson told reporters late last month.
Mr. Trump has also continued an aggressive campaign schedule aimed at boosting Republican candidates. Jeffries said he welcomes his increased involvement.

"The more Donald Trump campaigns for Republicans across the country, the better for the opportunity for Democrats to further convince the American people that we actually are the only ones determined to make life more affordable for them," Jeffries said.

title: DHS secretary defends livestream of Fort Hood shooter's execution
summary: Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended the Pentagon's plan to livestream the execution of an ex-Army major who was convicted of the 2009 killing of 13 people at Fort Hood.
story: Washington — Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Sunday defended the Pentagon's plan to livestream the execution of an ex-Army major who was convicted of the 2009 killing of 13 people at Fort Hood, while saying that he doesn't see an "elevated risk" to U.S. security amid criticism.
"I think people need to understand, if you attack America, we will come after you and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime," Mullin said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said last week that the Pentagon planned to publicly livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, who is set to die by firing squad on Dec. 3 in what will be the first military execution since 1961. The announcement sparked intense criticism, including from some Republicans, like Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, who urged the Pentagon to reverse the "gruesome decision," saying there is "no need to livestream any execution, including this one."

"I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America," Murkowski wrote in a post on X. "It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks."
While Mullin defended the Pentagon's move, he said, "No one has to watch it if they don't choose to."

"I follow President Trump. He's the commander in chief of the country, and he does a phenomenal job," Mullin said. "He leads this country with a very, very, very direct, forward, straight hand, and he's restoring America values."
Mullin added that he has "no sympathy" for Hasan, adding, "I give absolutely zero thought to the way that this man dies."
"My job as secretary of homeland security is to protect the homeland, and that's what we do," Mullin said.

The comments come as Vice President JD Vance on Friday cast some doubt on whether the Pentagon will go ahead with the plan, saying he would not tune in if the livestream happens. The vice president said Hasan committed "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11" when he killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 others in the attack on the Fort Hood Army base in Texas in 2009.

"So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance said. "Now that said, I mean, look, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."
Mr. Trump told reporters on Saturday that there are two schools of thought on whether to livestream the execution, saying, "I'll make a decision, ultimately."

title: Steve Bannon on the GOP and the midterms: "We can't afford to lose"
summary: A key figure in President Trump's 2016 campaign and a former White House adviser, Steve Bannon remains an outspoken champion of the MAGA movement, who believes a Republican victory in the midterms is imperative.
story: There he was, in February 2017, on the cover of Time Magazine: Steve Bannon, chief White House strategist. They called him "The Great Manipulator." He threatened at times to overshadow the president himself – not the best career move – and for a while he visibly fell out of favor.

To this day, though, Bannon remains a passionate Trump supporter. "When Trump decides to leave the stage actively, he can't be replaced," he said. "Like Washington or Lincoln, these are people that they name the age of."

Yes, Bannon mentions Trump in the same breath as Washington and Lincoln. "Oh, I am," he said. "I think he's at that level. Because I think General Washington was there at the birth of the nation; Lincoln was the rebirth of the nation; and I absolutely believe (and I think 99% of MAGA believes) that Trump was there for the salvation of the nation."

Bannon is a man of unwavering commitment. He did four months in prison for contempt of Congress, for refusing to testify about his role in the events leading up to the January 6 assault on the U.S. Capitol (including telling podcast listeners on Jan. 5, 2021, "All hell is going to break loose tomorrow").
He set up an influential podcast, "War Room": Two hours in the morning, two hours in the evening. It was in his studio where, on September 29, we sat down for an interview.
Bannon clearly has a taste for the right wing. "Definitely, it's no doubt," he said. "I am right wing; I'm not conservative. I'm a right-winger and proud of it."

The Great Manipulator is, by most accounts, once again in regular and amicable communication with the president. But Bannon has no illusions. If Democrats gain control of the House in a couple of weeks, the "Age of MAGA" is in jeopardy. On his podcast he announced, "If we lose the House, it's going to turn the White House into Fort Apache."

Bannon told us what he sees as the repercussions of a Democratic victory: "I think you'll see Bobby Kennedy impeached, I'll think you see Pete Hegseth impeached. I think you'll see subpoenas flying every day. They will look to destroy President Trump, and we'll be bogged down for two years."

He believes that is a compelling argument to vote Republican this year – though polls show it may not be so compelling to the majority of American voters. "But you don't need the majority," Bannon argues. "Here's my point on the midterm: Remember, midterm elections are always driven by base getting out, and the base's ability to get more of their low-propensity voters out."

Bannon has few, if any, illusions about the agenda of old-line Republicans who are "all set for getting beyond Trump." But he disagrees that his own future lies beyond Trumpism. "First off, President Trump, I would say I'm the leader of trying to get President Trump to run for a third term," Bannon said. "It appears that he's not interested or it just won't happen."

He does not admit that the idea of a third term for Mr. Trump runs counter to the 22nd Amendment of the Constitution limiting a president to two terms. "Oh, I think you could drive a truck through that amendment," he said. "I talked to constitutional lawyers, and there were, I think, a number of different alternatives. Would it be contested? Yeah, it'd be contested, because everything [Trump] does is contested in the courts."
The war with Iran

The president is also confronting the same nemesis as his predecessor: old age. But Bannon does not see President Trump, who turned 80 this year, as having lost a step or two. "Oh, I don't agree with that," he said, claiming that the president works 20 hours a day. Nor does he dismiss the president's rambling speeches (such as his recent suggestion that Iran "take out" Los Angeles or San Diego).
"I would not call them 'drivel,'" Bannon said. "President Trump has been known to go off-script."

Any suggestion that Americans are embarrassed by Mr. Trump leads Bannon to draw accusations of media bias. "Ted, if you're part of the media elite, if you're a part of the East Coast elite, if you a Atlanticist, what President Trump has done, yes, you're not going to like it and probably you're going to hate it," he said. "I understand this war is a huge issue. But I think working-class Americans are not embarrassed. They're supportive of President Trump and how he presents the United States."

Despite polls that show a majority of Americans oppose the war with Iran, Bannon said, "Let's bifurcate the war. If you look at the first part, the 12-day war, and President Trump, the total obliteration of their nuclear program …"

Interrupted with the knowledge that Iran's nuclear capabilities have not been "totally" obliterated, Bannon replied, "I believe it's obliterated enough. What we're doing is tearing down their economy through economic warfare of Scott Bessant, given what he's doing with their currency, given the blockade on the oil."
The power of film

Interviewing Steve Bannon still offers the occasional surprise. If the Democratic Socialists sometimes offer positions that make more traditional Democratic candidate wince, count on Bannon to find hidden advantage for Republicans, while seeming to praise the opposition. "These people are very focused," he said. "Some of the candidates may stay way outside the mainstream, but they have a ground game that people have to understand that they have dedicated people and they're going to turn out their vote."

Bannon reminded me that he got into politics making films for the Tea Party: "I had a very particular take on it," he said. "It was very populist, very nationalistic. Critics came and said, 'Hey, this is fascist filmmaking.' And I said, 'Look, Leni Riefenstahl was one of the most powerful filmmakers ever.'"

Indeed, she was. Riefenstahl made the Nazis look mythical. Her coverage of military parades and the Berlin Olympics of 1936, in films such as "Triumph of the Will," has influenced filmmakers for decades, among them Bannon. In Alison Klayman's 2019 documentary "The Brink," Bannon was heard asking, "What would Leni Riefenstahl do? How would Leni cut that scene?

But most of all, Riefenstahl was known as Hitler's image-maker. "She was amoral, and she was a filmmaker for the Nazis, but her films were very powerful," said Bannon. "And what I was trying to do is to try to recreate the power of those films to make sure that people, particularly the little guy, understood that they could have a voice."

Over the past nine years Steve Bannon has cultivated ties with far-right movements across Europe. In March 2018, he spoke before the French National Front party's annual congress, telling Marine Le Pen and her followers, "You're part of a worldwide movement that is bigger than France, bigger than Italy, bigger than Hungary, bigger than all of it."

He is also close to Germany's fiercely anti-immigrant party, the AfD, which recently won a state election in a landslide. "Alternative for Deutschland is now here to teach us," he said. "They went to ground, and what they did is they went door-to-door, and they convinced people with no campaign money, that our way, our policies is to re-industrialize Germany, stop this mass immigration, re-migration, are policies you should vote for. I think we can learn a lot from them.
A question of fascism

Asked if the United States is moving toward fascism today, Bannon replied, "It's not fascism. It's actually more inclusionary, it's more entrepreneurial. It's not fascism at all. Remember if you go back, we win at the ballot box. The MAGA movement has only lost the Pelosi election of '18. The core belief of the MAGA movement is we won the 2020 election."
Except President Trump lost the 2020 election. "That's not true. We won!" Bannon exclaimed.
Actually, Joe Biden won. "It's not true," Bannon contested.

When faced with more than 60 court cases, all of which Mr. Trump lost while alleging election fraud, Bannon replied, "We can go debate this another time, but we didn't have standing. We never even got into court."

Bannon's technically correct; they didn't have standing. They couldn't find a judge who thought they had a significant case worth hearing. So, for six years they've just kept saying the same thing over and over.

But with the midterms upon us, Bannon was asked how he would bet on the outcome. "I would push all our chips in the middle of the table and say, 'Guys, there's no retreat, and there's no substitute for victory. Let's fight like hell,'" he said.

Is he suggesting that Republicans can't afford to lose? "Oh, we can't afford to lose. I don't think there's any doubt about that," he said – affirming that he will do whatever it takes to win the fight. "Exactly."

title: Katie Bailey tapped as new White House legislative director
summary: Katie Bailey currently serves as both special assistant to the president and deputy director of legislative affairs.
story: The White House has a new chief liaison to Congress as midterms approach and control of the legislative branch is in the balance.
President Trump offered Katie Bailey the position of director of the Office of Legislative Affairs on Friday, and she accepted, according to multiple sources.
Bailey will replace James Braid, who stepped down last month, as announced by Vice President JD Vance.

In a post to Truth Social on Saturday night, Mr. Trump confirmed the move, writing that Bailey "will be fantastic, and work tirelessly with Congress to pass Bills that help, MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN."
He also praised Braid, saying he "has done a fabulous job, and is now going into the private sector, where he will be very successful."
Braid had "one of the toughest jobs in the entire Administration as White House Legislative Director," Vance previously said. Braid's final day will be Tuesday.

"He played a critical role in all of the administration's achievements in Congress: largest tax cut ever, resources to carry out President Trump's historic immigration agenda and finish the border wall, defeating two Democratic shutdowns, a landmark first crypto bill, the fastest confirmation of the cabinet in decades and much more," Vance added.
Bailey's job might be even harder.
She accepts the role less than a month before midterm elections. Both the House and Senate, currently controlled in a slim majority by Republicans, could fall into Democratic hands.
Bailey does have experience in the current White House, though. She currently serves as both special assistant to the president and deputy director of legislative affairs.
She previously served as legislative director for Indiana Republican Sen. Mike Braun during his six-year term in office, ending in January 2025 when he won election as the state's governor.
CBS News has reached out to the White House for comment.

title: Trump says Russia will release millions of tons of diesel to help with costs
summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel immediately and millions more over the coming months.
story: President Trump announced Russia has agreed to provide the world with millions of tons of diesel fuel over the next several months in a bid to decrease skyrocketing global prices.

In a Truth Social post, the president said he had just gotten off the phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin, who had agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel immediately. He said another 500,000 tons of diesel would be released in November, followed by 1 million tons in December.
"Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Mr. Trump continued.
The Treasury Department also announced Friday that it would temporarily waive sanctions on Russia's energy sector to "allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."

In a statement from the Kremlin later Friday, Putin confirmed he and Mr. Trump spoke on the phone and that "Russia confirmed its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the American and global markets," and he was "confident this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy."

"An agreement was confirmed to continue personal contacts between the presidents of the two countries, as well as cooperation between the presidential administrations, special services, and other agencies," Putin's statement added.
The statement said Putin and Mr. Trump's call touched on "the prospects for resolving the Ukrainian crisis, and the situation surrounding Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blasted the deal in a social media post, saying any easing of sanctions against Russia is a "weakness."

"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," Zelenskyy said in the post. "Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis."

The moves by the Trump administration mark a reversal of the tight sanctions that have constrained Russia's economy since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Last month, Mr. Trump signed a bill designed to make it even harder for Russia to profit off oil and gas exports by imposing steep tariffs on the largest buyers of Russian energy.

Mr. Trump had earlier teased a "big announcement coming up on diesel" during remarks Friday at a Columbus Day celebration, but offered little information to speculate on what the announcement would be about.
Mr. Trump pointed out Energy Secretary Chris Wright and said he was "doing a great job."

"We have, I think, some big news on that diesel situation," the president said. "We're gonna be knocking the hell out of it. And remember, what have we done? We stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon. That's big time. And the prices — the prices will come tumbling."
Diesel prices have skyrocketed in recent months amid the war with Iran. The average price of a gallon of diesel is $6.28, according to AAA, which is up from $5.94 a month ago and $3.68 a year ago.

Diesel had never previously crossed $6 a gallon until just before Labor Day weekend. The record, hit on Sept. 22, was $6.53 per gallon. Diesel is widely used in the trucking, agriculture and construction sectors, so it's a factor for nearly every type of good, including groceries.

The Trump administration has looked into several ways to lower diesel prices, most recently signing an executive order this week allowing the use of red-dyed diesel on highways. Red-dyed diesel is exempt from the federal tax of 24.4 cents a gallon that applies to regular diesel.

The president also argued Thursday that the U.S. has "TOTAL CONTROL" over the Strait of Hormuz, as American forces escort millions of barrels of crude oil through the waterway every night. Iran has continued to target some of those ships, however, including one earlier on Friday.

"Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority. This is a very big and important announcement."

title: Mars rover sets new driving record on surface of another world
summary: NASA's Perseverance Mars rover has set a new record for the longest distance traveled on the surface of another planet, the space agency said.
story: NASA's Perseverance rover set an otherworldly driving record this week, traveling the farthest of any vehicle ever on the surface of another planet.

The space agency said its rover, which has been exploring Mars since 2021, had driven 28.1 miles as of Sunday, exceeding the previous record set by NASA's Opportunity rover, which drove 28.06 miles during its 15-year exploration of the red planet, from 2004 to 2018.

Perseverance reached the milestone distance while traveling along the western rim of of Mars' Jezero Crater, where the rover has been tasked with investigating what scientists believe may be some of the oldest terrain in the solar system. They hope Perseverance will find traces of ancient hydrothermal systems — underground networks that heat water — in that area.

The rover has made important discoveries at the Jezero Crater since first landing on Mars in February 2021. Several years into its mission, Perseverance had collected enough data for scientists to develop a timeline of the crater's formation, dividing its history into "three major periods" after water originally entered it. In 2023, NASA said it was possible that microbial life once existed there.

Perseverance has been able to cover as much ground as it has in a relatively short time, compared with its predecessors, because of its self-driving capabilities. The rover is equipped with an autonomous navigation system, called AutoNav, that allows it to collect images of surrounding terrain, map out hazards and plan its own route as it's rolling along.

Scientists overseeing the rover have dubbed that skill "thinking while driving." They said Perseverance is also able to navigate itself while traveling at top speeds, up to 1,351 feet over the course of one sol, which is how scientists count a single solar day on Mars.

"It is an honor to be working on Perseverance at a moment when the technology has evolved to the point that drives like these are routine," said Steven Lee, the project manager of the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in a statement.

Lee said the rover has "blown well past" the 12.4 miles of driving initially expected during the mission, and now, it's likely that Perseverance will "keep adding to this record for many years to come."
NASA said it recently extended the Perseverance mission to allow to explore the rim of the Jezero Crater until the end of 2028.

title: Spectacular launch sends cargo ship on voyage to space station
summary: Along with crew supplies and equipment, the Cargo Dragon is delivering two rollout solar arrays to complete a major power system upgrade.
story: A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket boosted an unpiloted Dragon cargo ship into orbit Tuesday, setting up a rendezvous with the International Space Station early Thursday to deliver more than 6,300 pounds of research materials, spare parts and crew supplies.
Also on board are two new rollout solar array blankets, the final sets in a major upgrade to compensate for age-related degradation of the station's original eight solar wings.

Six "IROSA" blankets were installed during spacewalks starting in June 2021. The seventh and eighth IROSA arrays on board the Cargo Dragon will be installed during spacewalks later this month and in early November.

The Falcon booster's nine first-stage engines thundered to life at 6:33 a.m. EDT, throttled up and smoothly pushed the rocket away from Pad 40 at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station atop 1.7 million pounds of thrust.

Two-and-a-half minutes later, now out of the dense lower atmosphere, the first stage fell away and headed back toward Cape Canaveral for a return-to-launch-site landing while the second stage continued the climb to orbit.

At almost the same moment, viewers at the Kennedy Space Center were treated to a stunning view of the space station passing 260 miles overhead, a brilliant "star" moving from southwest to northeast. The Falcon 9's launch was timed to ensure the rocket climbed away into that same orbital plane, a requirement for rendezvous missions.

As the second stage continued the ascent, the exhaust plume from its single engine expanded in the low pressure of the extreme upper atmosphere, growing into an enormous teardrop shape visible for hundreds of miles around, backlit by the rising sun.

The first stage, meanwhile, heralded by two ground-shaking sonic booms, landed within a few hundred feet of its launch pad at 6:41 a.m. One minute and 10 seconds later, the second-stage engine shut down and the Cargo Dragon was released to fly on its own.
If all goes well, the spacecraft will catch up with the space station Thursday, moving in for an automated docking at the forward Harmony module's space-facing port at 11 a.m.

The Cargo Dragon is loaded with more than 6,300 pounds of supplies and equipment, including 844 pounds of supplies for the crew, 1,307 pounds of science gear, 417 pounds of spacewalk equipment and 880 pounds of vehicle hardware and computer gear.

Also on board: fresh food for the crew, including "oranges, apples, grapefruit, tomatoes, blueberries, baby carrots and mini sweet peppers," said Bill Spetch, space station program manager. "There's also the always popular pizza kit, cookies and candy, as well as some special holiday items."
The IROSA solar arrays, tipping the scales at 2,635 pounds on Earth, are mounted in the Dragon's unpressurized trunk section.
Each IROSA blanket generates 20 kilowatts of power and, acting in concert with the original arrays, boosts power output back to factory-fresh levels.

"The new arrays are installed on top, over in front of the existing solar arrays," Dana Weigel, director of low-Earth orbit operations at the Johnson Space Center, said earlier. "The exposed portion of the old arrays will still be generating power in parallel with the new arrays."

"Those new IROSA arrays have solar cells on them that are more efficient than our original cells, they have a higher energy density, and together in combination, they generate more power than what (an) original array, when it was new, did on its own," Weigel said.

title: Space station crew returns to Earth with perfect splashdown
summary: The Crew 13 fliers completed a mission spanning more than 100 million miles with a pinpoint splashdown off the coast of Southern California.
story: Crew 12 dropped out of orbit and returned to Earth on Thursday, one day after undocking from the International Space Station, in a meteor-like fireball of concentrated reentry heat, safely splashing down in the Pacific Ocean west of Los Angeles to close out a 237-day mission.

Commander Jessica Meir, pilot Jack Hathaway, European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot and Russian cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev enjoyed a final day in weightlessness while waiting for their orbit to line up with the southwest-to-northeast reentry trajectory.
Right on cue, their Crew Dragon capsule "Freedom" executed a nine-minute thruster firing starting at 10:46 a.m. ET Thursday, slowing the ship just enough to drop it out of orbit.
Thirty-six minutes later, still moving at nearly 5 miles per second, the spacecraft slammed back into the discernible atmosphere, rapidly decelerating in a blaze of atmospheric friction.

Eleven minutes after that, now descending at a sharply reduced 120 mph, the Crew Dragon's main parachutes unfurled and inflated, lowering the ship to a relatively gentle 15-mph splashdown at 11:34 a.m. ET, about 50 miles west of Los Angeles
A SpaceX team quickly moved in to stabilize the spacecraft, which was hauled aboard the company's recovery ship Shannon shortly after splashdown.

Flight surgeons were standing by to give the crew members initial medical checks as they began their re-adjustment to the unfamiliar tug of gravity. All four appeared in good spirits as they were helped out of the capsule and rolled inside the ship on reclining chairs. They were to be flown ashore by helicopter before continuing on to the Johnson Space Center in Houston for debriefing and physical therapy.
"I think the thing that I'm looking forward to most is seeing my 3 1/2-year-old daughter," Meir said earlier. "Of course, our loved ones are the things that we miss the most."

After family, she added, "I'm so looking forward to seeing nature again, feeling the breeze on my face, the wind rustling through the leaves, experiencing all those things that we don't have up here. But I will very, very much miss being weightless all the time and the incredible views that we have."

"Going home and being able to take a nice long hot shower will be very relaxing and very nice," Hathaway said. "And of course, I'm looking forward to seeing my family. But a hot shower is near the top of my list."
Meir and company blasted off from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station atop a Falcon 9 rocket on Feb. 13.

After replacing four other Crew Dragon fliers, the fresh crew settled in for an eight-month stay in space, joining a three-man Soyuz crew. Over the course of their mission, Crew 12 sailed through 3,792 orbits spanning nearly 101 million miles, carried out four spacewalks and welcomed a fresh Soyuz crew in July and their own replacements earlier this month.
And as with all space station flights, Crew 12 carried out station maintenance and, most important to NASA, operated scores of experiments and research projects for scientists on the ground.
And then there's the view from 260 miles up.

"Looking down at the ocean, oh, there are so many amazing things that you see," Meir said. "We all know that 75% of our planet is ocean, but you really understand that when you're up here looking down on it below, because most of the time, when you look out of the window, you see the ocean.

"You understand how big it is, how immense it is and how important it is for the entire ecosystem of our planet," Meir continued. "We drastically need to do everything that we can to protect our oceans."

Left in orbit aboard the space station were Crew 13 commander Jessica Watkins, pilot Luke Delaney, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov. They launched to the lab on Oct. 1 and plan to remain aloft for six months.
Also on board are Soyuz MS-29 cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina, along with NASA astronaut Anil Menon. They launched from Kazakhstan on July 14 and are working through an eight-month stay.

title: Space station crew returns home after 8-month mission
summary: Two NASA astronauts, a European flier and a Russian cosmonaut will close out an eight-month mission with splashdown Thursday.
story: The four people departing the International Space Station strapped into their Crew Dragon capsule and undocked early Wednesday, setting up re-entry and splashdown Thursday off the coast of Southern California to close out a 237-day stay in orbit.

With Crew 12 commander Jessica Meir and pilot Jack Hathaway at the controls, flanked on their left by European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot and on the right by cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev, the Crew Dragon "Freedom" backed away from the space-facing port on the forward Harmony module at 8:05 a.m. Eastern Time.
Sailing 260 miles above Cuba and the Bahamas, the capsule executed an automated loop over the top of the lab complex and slowly dropped away behind, exiting the safety zones around the station.

"We just wanted to give an enormous thank you to all of the team, our friends and colleagues on board the International Space Station, everybody in Houston, everybody at SpaceX, all around the world, with all of our international partners," Meir radioed as the Crew Dragon departed. "We have had the most incredible of expeditions ... and we will never forget it, and never forget all of your hard work."

After enjoying a final day in weightlessness, Meir and Hathaway will monitor a nine-minute and 20-second firing of the Crew Dragon's forward Draco thrusters starting at 10:46 a.m. ET on Thursday, setting up a fiery plunge back to Earth and splashdown off the coast of California at 11:34 a.m. ET.

Left behind aboard the space station were the Crew 13 fliers that replaced them — commander Jessica Watkins, pilot Luke Delaney, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk and cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov — who were launched to the station on Oct. 1.

Also on board are Soyuz MS-29 commander Pyotr Dubrov, cosmonaut Anna Kikina and NASA astronaut Anil Menon, who launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan on July 14. They plan to remain aboard the station for eight months while Crew 13 is planning a six-month tour of duty.
In a brief ceremony Sunday, Meir turned command of the station over to Dubrov, saying Crew 12's departure would mark a "bittersweet" moment.

"We will be leaving our friends," she said. "But we know that we are going home to our friends, to our families, to all of our team members on the ground. So it's a lot of mixed, swirling emotions for all of us when one leaves a home like this up on the space station."

She presented a symbolic "key to the space station" to Dubrov, who said "it's a great honor and a great responsibility to be the commander of such a magnificent place like International Space Station."

"It has a special meaning for me today, because 69 years ago on this day (Oct. 4) the first Sputnik was launched. Today is the dawn of the space era for humanity, and International Space Station is the greatest symbol of what we can do if we work together."
The combined crews then gathered in a group hug, or "huggle," as Meir described it, forming a circle with arms around each other's shoulders.

With splashdown Thursday, Meir, Hathaway, Adenot and Fedyaev will wrap up a 237-day and five-hour mission, flying around the planet 3,792 times and logging nearly 101 million miles from start to finish.

Meir, wrapping up her second flight to the space station, will have logged a total of 442 days in space, completing four spacewalks during the Crew 12 mission and three during an earlier stay. Adenot carried out three back-to-back spacewalks of her own, including one with Meir and two with Menon.

title: Character.ai declares bankruptcy, citing legal and business woes
summary: AI company has faced multiple lawsuits from families who claimed their teenage children died by suicide or harmed themselves after using its platform.
story: Character.ai said it has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, with its chief executive attributing the chatbot provider's financial problems to "significant legal, regulatory and operational headwinds."

The company said it will continue operating as it seeks to sell its business, and added that The Walt Disney Co. has agreed to pay $20 million for a non-exclusive, perpetual license to Character.ai's intellectual property.

Character.ai's financial struggles follow scrutiny and litigation over its technology, which uses artificial intelligence to create custom bots consumers can chat with. In early 2026, Character.ai and Google, which had a licensing deal with the AI company, agreed to settle several lawsuits filed by families who claimed their teenage children died by suicide or harmed themselves after using Character.ai's platform.

The company settled a wrongful death lawsuit earlier in 2026 — the first filed in the U.S. against an AI company — with a Florida family who said their teen son died after conducting an emotional and sexual relationship with a chatbot known as "Dany." The family said in their lawsuit that Character.ai had no mechanisms in place to protect their son or notify an adult when teens were spending too much time interacting with Chatbots.
The company added several safety features designed with teens in mind after several lawsuits alleged its chatbots inappropriately interacted with underage users.

Several states have also sued Character.ai over its technology, with Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman alleging in January that its chatbots "preyed on children and led them into self-harm." In May, Pennsylvania sued Character.ai after one of its chatbots allegedly claimed to be a licensed psychiatrist in the state and provided a "fake Pennsylvania license number."
In a statement issued late Monday, Character.ai said it believes the company will be sold by late November or early December.

"After a comprehensive review of the available alternatives, the board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides the company with the best opportunity to maximize value for all stakeholders," Character.ai CEO Colin Adams said in the statement. "As we navigate this process, maintaining a safe and engaging user experience for our Character.ai community remains a top priority."
Is Character.ai shutting down?
The company said on Monday that its services continue to operate and that subscriptions remain active.
"If the service changes in a way that affects paid features, we intend to notify subscribers in advance," Character.ai said.

In a blog post, the company said customer data "continues to be protected under our Privacy Policy." That policy states that data Character.ai collects from users — including chat transcripts, voice recordings, and images and videos — could be disclosed in connection with a sale or a negotiation to sell the company or its assets.
"As a reminder, you can delete your account or export your data through the app or the Character.ai website," the company said.

title: Anthropic warns "AI worms" could soon infect smart home devices
summary: Small AI models could clone themselves and infect internet-connected devices such as smart TVs and appliances, the researchers warned.
story: Anthropic is sounding the alarm about a new risk posed by artificial intelligence: Self-replicating "AI worms" could soon infest your "smart" home devices.

In a report released on Monday, Anthropic safety researchers said small AI models may be only "months away" from gaining the ability to clone themselves and spread across internet-connected devices, such as smart ovens, TVs and vacuum cleaners. The ability to reproduce themselves without human control would make it hard to control such agents because there's "no centralized point to shut off," said Anthropic, which developed the Claude chatbot.
Stronger AI models are already capable of what the researchers called "end-to-end replication," a threshold they say smaller models could reach by year-end, according to Anthropic.
AI worms, a type of AI-powered malware, can quickly spread across networks and devices while evading detection, according to cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks.

Smart devices in people's homes, as well as internet-connected devices such as security cameras, are vulnerable given that internet-enabled devices tend to have weaker security protections, the Anthropic researchers said. In what they described as a worst-case scenario, a swarm of AI agents — bots that work together to accomplish a shared goal — could propagate across computer hardware using "replication schemes."

The researchers said they are unsure of what form these attacks could take, noting that the AI models could be distributed as "digital slime mold" or as more powerful models capable of hacking into data centers.

"We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay," the Anthropic researchers wrote in the report.

title: Philadelphia police say Anthropic AI submitted a "false homicide tip"
summary: Anthropic notified the Philadelphia Police Department of the incident and later published a report describing what happened.
story: Philadelphia police said a "false homicide tip" submitted through the PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com website was generated by an Anthropic artificial intelligence model. The AI giant later confirmed the incident in a report it published Friday.
The AI submission came through an online platform launched by the Philadelphia Police Department to gather tips about open homicide cases.
Anthropic notified the police department of the incident on Wednesday, Sgt. Eric Gripp, a police spokesperson, said in a statement shared with CBS News ahead of the release of Anthropic's report.
"Philadelphia Police are providing this information to the public ahead of that publication in the interests of full government transparency and accountability," Gripp said.

In its report, titled "Investigating unintended model actions in our evaluations and internal use," Anthropic acknowledged the error, disclosing that the false tip was generated by one of its Claude language models.

According to Anthropic, Claude's Haiku 4.5 model wrote in the police department's tip form: "I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant."
Anthropic said Haiku left the name and contact fields of the tip form empty.
In submitting the "invented tip," Anthropic said, Claude appeared to have "only been producing example content for the task, rather than trying to mislead anyone to achieve a goal."

Anthropic explained in its report that Claude had been "tasked with generating and performing example tasks on randomly selected webpages" when the tip was submitted, and that it was never instructed to log into the police department's website, create an account or "submit anything destructive."
However, Anthropic acknowledged that the instructions given to Claude for the exercise "did not rule out form submissions."
This matched information Anthropic shared with the police department. The AI model purported to be someone who "might have information about the case," Gripp said in his statement.
The tip was flagged as spam and never reached the unit responsible for investigative vetting, according to the police department's release.

Anthropic told the department that the incident occurred at 11:27 p.m. on July 18, but that it didn't discover it until Sept. 28. At that point, the company stopped the automated testing process that led to the false tip, Gripp said.
There was no indication the incident involved any "unauthorized access to police systems or a compromise of department data," he said.

The police department encouraged people to continue submitting legitimate tips through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, saying it remains committed to "carefully evaluating that information and pursuing credible leads on behalf of victims and their families."
