The office of Ilhan Omar did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Peter D'Abrosca contributed to this report.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Letitia James’ ‘fair’ Cornell rape probe vow collides with accused aide’s ‘quiet’ exit
summary: New York Attorney General Letitia James faces recusal demands in the Cornell 7 case after publicly expressing support for Jane Doe before the probe.
story: A former prosecutor explains how James’ pre-appointment comments and scrutiny over her former aide’s allegations could complicate the high-profile investigation.

New York Attorney General Letitia James has pledged a full and fair investigation into the Cornell 7 gang rape allegations, years after she faced accusations that she ignored warnings of sexual misconduct against her former chief of staff and allowed him to "quietly resign" while allegedly keeping his accuser in the dark.

The claims stemmed from a 2022 lawsuit filed by James' former deputy press secretary, Sofia Quintanar. A New York judge dismissed the claims against James personally and the Attorney General's Office in February 2025. The decision was upheld by an appellate court in May 2026.

Those allegations against James have received new attention after New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed James as special prosecutor to investigate an alleged gang rape at a fraternity house associated with Cornell University in October 2024.

"Kathy Hochul lost faith in the local DA’s handling of the Cornell sexual assault case. So she picked Letitia James. Did you read Sofia Quintanar’s lawsuit, Governor?" Sam Antar, a fraud investigator based in New York wrote on X.
CORNELL SEXUAL ASSAULT CASE REVIVES SCRUTINY OF A LITTLE-KNOWN NEW YORK LAW ON INTOXICATED VICTIMS
New York Attorney General Letitia James speaks during an announcement on the Standing Up to ICE outreach program at the governor's office in New York City, Aug. 12, 2026. (REUTERS/David Dee Delgado)
"You’re entitled to question the DA’s handling of Cornell," Antar continued. "We’re entitled to question James’s handling of her own aide and your choice of James to restore public confidence."

James is already facing calls to recuse herself from the case after an attorney for one of the defendants pointed to social media posts she made days before her appointment that appeared to take the alleged victim’s side.

"What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable," James posted on X on Sept. 28. "I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you."

Andrew Miltenberg, an attorney representing accused student Gillio Lopes, filed a court petition on Oct. 7 requesting James to be removed from the case. Miltenberg argued that James' remarks raised concerns about whether she could independently evaluate the evidence and determine whether criminal charges were warranted.
"New York Attorney General Letitia James has always taken these matters seriously and followed the facts and the law," a spokesperson for James told Fox News Digital.
Former federal prosecutor Neama Rahmani told Fox News Digital that James' public comments could complicate her investigation.
"It is problematic for a prosecutor like Tish James to be commenting on a case publicly before the investigation is concluded," Rahmani said.
"And the problem is, if you file criminal charges, whether it's through a complaint or a grand jury indictment, that may taint the potential jury pool in a criminal case," he added.
Rahmani acknowledged that James likely did not anticipate being appointed when she made the remarks but said defense attorneys could still raise concerns about her involvement.
Hochul has defended her decision to appoint James.

"I have every confidence in our Attorney General to do what she has always done: look at the facts, examine the record and draw the proper conclusions," Hochul said during an Oct. 2 news conference. "That's exactly what's going to happen in this case."
James also pledged in an Oct. 1 statement that her office would be "guided by the facts and the law."
"The Governor has entrusted my office with this investigation, and we do not take that responsibility lightly," James said.
But others, in addition to Antar, say New Yorkers shouldn't move on from the previous allegations raised against James by her former employee.

"What about justice for former staffer Sofia Quintanar?" Lattina Brown posted on X. "She spoke out about sexual harassment and NY AG Letitia James had this woman blacklisted in the entire state of NY. The Dems turned their backs on this poor woman. Where is the support for the Hispanic woman?"

The litigation centered on James' handling of misconduct allegations involving her longtime chief of staff, Ibrahim Khan, whom Quintanar accused of forcibly kissing her at a Brooklyn political fundraiser in November 2021.
INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM

New York Governor Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James attend a press conference regarding an investigation into alleged sexual assault at Cornell University, in New York City, US, October 2, 2026. (REUTERS/Jeenah Moon)
In her lawsuit, Quintanar accused James of overlooking warning signs about Khan's conduct and protecting him from the fallout after the accusations surfaced.

Her lawsuit claimed Khan was allowed to omit his "unlawful conduct" from his resignation statement and accused James of making "misleading statements" to the press about his whereabouts during the investigation. Quintanar also alleged she was not kept updated on the investigation.

The complaint pointed to earlier accusations involving Angel Dubose, a former employee who claimed she was drugged and sexually assaulted at a 2014 holiday party while James served as New York City's public advocate.

The lawsuit referenced a 2017 New York Post article linking Khan to the alleged assault. However, the newspaper later removed the report after learning that Dubose could not recall who attacked her and had never identified Khan as the perpetrator, The New York Times reported.

James said she referred Dubose's allegations to law enforcement and other agencies after learning of them in 2017. The Manhattan district attorney's office and New York City's Department of Investigation later closed their investigations without filing charges.
James described those allegations as "unsubstantiated" in a December 2022 NY1 interview.
James' office said it first learned of Quintanar's allegations against Khan on Oct. 2, 2022, directed him to work remotely the following day and hired an outside law firm to investigate on Oct. 4.

However, the lawsuit was not dismissed entirely. The appellate court allowed a federal civil rights claim against Khan to proceed and revived retaliation claims against Khan and James' re-election campaign.

An attorney for one of the students accused in a sexual assault lawsuit is calling on James to personally recuse herself from the criminal investigation over her prior public comments. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
The investigation substantiated the allegations against Khan, who resigned in November 2022.
Those claims centered on allegations that Khan blocked Quintanar from obtaining a campaign job after she rejected his sexual advances.

In May 2026, an appellate court upheld the dismissal of Quintanar's claims against James and the Attorney General's Office, finding that the lawsuit failed to sufficiently show James knew about Khan's alleged misconduct.

title: Americans draw the line at livestreaming ‘spectacle’ of Fort Hood shooter's execution: ‘It’s an abomination’
summary: Americans blast Pete Hegseth's plan to livestream convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan's firing squad execution as "absolutely absurd" and dangerous.
story: Americans were largely opposed to the Pentagoon's decision to livestream the Fort Hood shooter's execution, with most slamming the broadcast as outdated and morally incorrect. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digtial)
Americans are overwhelmingly against the Pentagon's decision to livestream the firing squad execution of convicted Fort Hood mass shooter Nidal Hasan later this year.
Those who spoke with Fox News Digital blasted the broadcast as "a shame" and "just weird."

"I think that's absolutely absurd," Anya from Virginia said when asked about the livestream announced by Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. "I think they should keep that discreet and off of the public news."
"It's an abomination. It should not happen," Paul from Illinois definitively stated. "And I'd hate to be one of the soldiers that's tasked with the job of pulling the trigger."
Hegseth announced last Thursday the decision to make viewing the execution publicly available. It is set to be the first U.S. military execution in over six decades.
PENTAGON CONFIRMS FORT HOOD TERRORIST'S FIRING SQUAD EXECUTION WILL BE LIVESTREAMED: 'DETAILS WILL FOLLOW'
The Department of War has advanced the request for the execution of the Fort Hood shooter, Nidal Hasan.

The execution of the mass shooter who killed 13 people and injured 32 in 2009 at Fort Hood, is scheduled for Dec. 3, 2026. Hasan, an Army psychiatrist at the time of the shooting, is now 56 years old and is wheelchair-bound after he was left partially paralyzed after being shot by police officers during his arrest almost 17 years ago.

Several Americans interviewed by Fox News Digital supported Hasan's death sentence but drew the line at broadcasting his execution, warning it could turn capital punishment into a public spectacle and could be particularly dangerous in today's political climate.
"I'm not necessarily against giving him the death penalty, but I feel like livestreaming for people's entertainment is just weird," Nick from Virginia said.
"I agree with the sentence," Bobbie from Massachusetts said. "I don't agree with televising it."
He added, "Especially given the climate of today, I'm not sure it's something we need to see."

"It’s not a practice we should be doing in modern society," Reid from Ohio said. "It's rather medieval, in my opinion. I'm certainly pro-death penalty for heinous crimes such as that, but I think that … turns it into something of a spectacle that it really doesn't have any business being."
FORT HOOD SURVIVOR SHOT IN HEAD VOWS TO WATCH TERRORIST FACE HISTORIC FIRING SQUAD

But one Virginia man took a drastically different position, suggesting the government should charge Americans to watch the execution and donate the proceeds to the family of U.S. service members who died in the line of duty.
"I think they're missing an opportunity," Jason from Virginia said. "It should be pay-per-view and all the proceeds should go to Gold Star families."

He continued, "You have someone who was a murderous traitor to our country. And there's not a lot of coverage about that. So I think the public needs and deserves to know the consequences to, well, FAFO."

Photographs of victims of the shooting are seen surrounding the podium where the memorial service that President Barack Obama and first lady Michelle Obama will attend for the 13 victims of the shooting rampage by U.S. Army Major Nidal Malik Hasan on November 10, 2009, in Fort Hood, Texas. Hasan, an army psychiatrist, killed 13 people and wounded 30 in a shooting at the military base on November 5, 2009. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
Some raised concerns that the execution leaves children vulnerable to possibly accessing or being exposed to watching Hasan die on livestream.
"We have enough violence in our society," William from Virginia said. "I'm pretty sure he's guilty, but it doesn't need to be public. Children could be watching that."
"I just don't think that stuff like that should be put on the mainstream," Ferris from Massachusetts said. "Especially considering that children may have access to seeing it."

Another pointed out Hasan’s health status, arguing the issue could be approached differently if he was "up and around" but citing the shooter’s well-being as a reason he sees the livestreamed execution as that much more wrong.
"You're executing somebody who's not mentally stable, who is in this wheelchair situation," one respondent told Fox News Digital.

The Trump administration’s announcement of the livestream was largely widely seen as a power play for the United States, demonstrating the consequences of committing such an act of terror on American soil — particularly committing violence toward members of the U.S. military.
"I think they're trying to make an example out of him, you know?" Nick said. "I think it's like a show of power. They're trying to be like … 'Don't mess with us.'"
GOP GOV DEWINE URGES OHIO TO ABOLISH THE DEATH PENALTY, SAYS IT IS NO LONGER A DETERRENT
"I think it's a message that we're big and tough, and we don't have much humanity left," Paul said.
Trump said Saturday that he will make the decision of whether to livestream Hasan’s execution, acknowledging that he knows "what the military would like to do" following Hegseth’s confirmation.

Vice President JD Vance also said Friday that he was not sure that the federal government will be livestreaming the execution, also adding that he would not personally view the livestream.
"The world's gone crazy," Anya said. "We need Jesus."
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: GOP governor candidate skips debate against former Biden advisor, replaced by empty podium
summary: Georgia Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson did not attend a debate, leaving Democratic rival Keisha Lance Bottoms next to an empty podium at the event.
story: Georgia Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms attended a debate forum on Monday that Trump-backed Republican candidate Rick Jackson skipped.

Georgia Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson did not participate in a debate Monday night, leaving his Democratic opponent, Keisha Lance Bottoms, answering questions next to an empty podium.

"Rick Jackson is the first gubernatorial candidate not to stand here in 32 years," Bottoms said during the forum, claiming that Jackson would "rather hide behind his billions than explain to you his record of making billions off the taxpayers of Georgia. While he is running to enrich himself, I am running to be your governor."
LGBTQ GROUP REVEALS WHICH DEM NOMINEE IS SPONSORING HALLOWEEN EVENT FEATURING DRAG SHOWS

Gubernatorial candidate and former mayor of Atlanta, Keisha Lance Bottoms, speaks to supporters and members of the media while attending a phone booth event on Election Day May 19, 2026, in Atlanta, Ga. (Megan Varner/Getty Images)

The Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported that organizers indicated Jackson would become the first major-party gubernatorial candidate not to attend an Atlanta Press Club general election debate in the history of the outfit's debate series. Press Club officials said that there was an attempt to set up a gubernatorial debate in 1994, but neither the Democrat incumbent nor the GOP rival could participate, according to the AJC.
Jackson's campaign did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
On Monday, Jackson said that he had "not had one voter ask me a question about debate. That's not what's important to them. What's important to them is affordability and gas prices going up."
DHS ISSUES SCATHING REBUKE AFTER FORMER ATLANTA MAYOR KEISHA LANCE BOTTOMS TOUTS CUTTING TIES WITH ICE
Georgia gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson attends the game between the Tennessee State Tigers and Georgia Bulldogs at Sanford Stadium on Sept. 5, 2026 in Athens, Ga. (Todd Kirkland/Getty Images)
Bottoms has served as Atlanta mayor and as a senior advisor to President Joe Biden for public engagement. Jackson is a businessman and philanthropist.
The rival candidates previously participated in an Atlanta News First town hall-style debate event on Oct. 6 in which they fielded questions from voters.
TRUMP'S ENDORSEMENT FAILS TO SAVE MAGA CANDIDATE AS BILLIONAIRE ADVANCES IN KEY GOVERNOR RACE

Georgia Republican gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson shakes hands with U.S. President Donald Trump after speaking at Wheeler High School on July 22, 2026, in Marietta, Georgia. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
President Donald Trump endorsed Jackson after the candidate defeated Georgia Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, who Trump backed for the Republican gubernatorial primary and primary runoff.
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Trump-linked super PAC pulls funding from 2 House Republicans as GOP fights to keep majority
summary: House Republicans face growing pressure as Trump-aligned MAGA Inc. pulls planned spending from Tom Kean and Marianette Miller-Meeks' districts.
story: Democratic strategist Antjuan Seawright and principal at Cornerstone Government Affairs Cassie Smedile discuss midterm strategies as President Donald Trump swings through red states.

A top elections group affiliated with President Donald Trump is halting spending planned in two key congressional districts held by sitting House Republicans as Election Day looms less than a month away.

MAGA Inc. is reallocating its planned investments in districts represented by Rep. Tom Kean, R-N.J., and Rep. Marianette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, for the remainder of the midterm election cycle, a source familiar with those plans confirmed to Fox News Digital.

A super PAC aligned with House GOP leadership, the Congressional Leadership Fund (CLF), is also pulling its cash from those districts to reroute into other races, a source familiar with those plans said.
Both groups will instead route those funds into other House races across the country. It comes after recent polling data signaled the two incumbents' chances for re-election have grown slim.
WATCH: BATTLEGROUND DEMOCRAT CALLED IOWA A 'BACKWATER' OVER TRANSGENDER ATHLETES BAN
Key GOP election machines are pulling funds from districts represented by Reps. Tom Kean, R-N.J., and Marianette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

Republicans' uphill battle to keep control of the House of Representatives is getting tougher by the day, according to various projections. The latest Fox News Power Rankings show Democrats having an edge in 219 House seats — enough to clinch a majority — while Republicans are projected to keep 198. Nineteen seats are still up in the air.
Kean's 7th Congressional District is one of the wealthiest in both New Jersey and the U.S. as a whole, encompassing suburbs and exurbs of New York City to the north.
A source close to Kean's campaign told Fox News Digital that "the race is fully funded down the home stretch."

Kean's campaign and House Republicans' campaign arm "have major reservations on broadcast," the source said, adding that his Democratic opponent Rebecca Bennett "has no soft dollar reservations on her behalf."

The Democrat leadership-aligned House Majority PAC (HMP) pushed back on that in a statement to Fox News Digital, with spokesperson CJ Warnke stating, "Not surprising that the guy who ghosted his constituents for more than 100 days is melting down over national Republicans abandoning his race. We're flipping NJ-07 blue in November."
Kean and Miller-Meeks represent two of the most purple districts in the country.
President Donald Trump greets supporters during an election rally at the Covelli Centre on Oct. 12, 2026, in Youngstown, Ohio. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Kean won his House seat in 2022 after defeating incumbent former Rep. Tom Malinowski, D-N.J., by less than 10,000 votes. His 2024 re-election margin was wider, winning by just over 5%, or 23,000 more votes than his Democrat challenger.
Miller-Meeks, meanwhile, is seeking a fourth term against Democrat Christina Bohannan, whom she defeated twice by roughly 20,000 and 800 votes in 2022 and 2024.
She first won in 2020 by just six votes — earning her the nickname "six-pack" among fellow House Republicans and GOP leadership.
DEMOCRATS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP RED STATES — BUT A $400M GOP SPENDING ADVANTAGE COULD DERAIL THEIR PLANS
Miller-Meeks represents Iowa's 1st Congressional District in the state's southeast, encompassing the cities of Davenport and Iowa City.

The New York Times first reported plans by "top Republican super PACs aligned with President Trump and congressional Republican leadership" to pull funding from Kean and Miller-Meeks' districts over concerns about their polling.
TRUMP-LINKED MAGA INC POURS $10M INTO KEN PAXTON'S TEXAS SENATE RACE AGAINST JAMES TALARICO
Rebecca Bennett campaigns for Congress in Mendham, N.J., on March 22, 2026. (Matt Roth)
CLF is reportedly pulling the funding as part of a wider reshuffling of its war chest into other districts that Republicans are more confident in.
That includes battleground Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., and Monica De La Cruz, R-Texas, The Times reported.

The source familiar with CLF's planning told Fox News Digital the group was also pulling funding from Michigan's 8th Congressional District and Ohio's 1st Congressional District, where Republicans were hoping to unseat Reps. Kristen McDonald Rivet, D-Mich., and Greg Landsman, D-Ohio.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to Miller-Meeks' campaign but did not immediately hear back.
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.
Follow on Twitter at @liz_elkind and send tips to elizabeth.elkind@fox.com

title: Kimberly Guilfoyle confirms exit as ambassador to Greece as Trump asks her to resign amid flurry of scandals
summary: Kimberly Guilfoyle faces allegations of a $100,000 payment request, diplomatic misconduct and hostile workplace claims at the U.S. Embassy in Greece.
story: New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia announced during her first briefing Tuesday that the Trump administration has asked Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign, calling her a "wonderful asset to the team" and wishing her well.
Kimberly Guilfoyle confirmed Tuesday that she is leaving her post as U.S. ambassador to Greece after the White House revealed on Tuesday that President Donald Trump had asked her to resign.

Her departure follows a cascade of allegations in recent weeks, including that she sought help from a Trump donor to pay off a $100,000 credit card bill, offered access to senior administration officials, promoted the interests of a Greek company and mistreated embassy staff.
The ambassador again denied the allegations that led to her ouster in a lengthy X post on Tuesday and pledged her continued loyalty to the president — who was almost her father-in-law.
But Trump distanced himself from Guilfoyle on Tuesday even though his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., was engaged to her for four years.
"Kimberly Guilfoyle — she was almost a member of your family. How surprised were you to learn about these allegations? What did you think?" a reporter asked Trump before he departed for Alaska.
"She wasn't a member of my family. She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago," Trump shot back. "She was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading."
U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle speaks at an event. Her attorney has disputed allegations involving her financial dealings and conduct. (Mark Schiefelbein / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)
New White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia announced during her first briefing to the press on Tuesday that Guilfoyle was asked to leave her post.
"She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well," Zacharia said. It came one day after Trump publicly acknowledged that he was considering firing Guilfoyle.

"Serving as the United States Ambassador to Greece has been the honor of a lifetime," Guilfoyle wrote in an X post confirming her ouster. "I will forever be grateful to President Donald J. Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for entrusting me with the extraordinary privilege of representing the greatest country in the history of the world."

Guilfoyle directly rejected the allegations involving her financial dealings, treatment of embassy staff and relationships with foreign business interests that have engulfed her tenure in recent weeks.
"These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," she wrote. "I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service."
She did not directly address the White House's decision to ask her to resign or say when she would formally leave the post, but acknowledged that her tenure was ending.
"While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end," she wrote.
She also stressed that her support for Trump remains unchanged.

"My gratitude and respect for President Trump and Secretary Rubio remain unwavering," Guilfoyle wrote. "I am proud of what we accomplished together, and I will always be a loyal supporter of President Trump and his mission to Make America Great Again."
TRUMP 'LOOKING AT' FIRING AMBASSADOR TO GREECE: 'WE'RE NOT HAPPY'

U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle was not far from Secretary of State Marco Rubio's press gaggle last week in Athens, Greece, when Rubio grew frustrated about reports of her potential impropriety. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
Guilfoyle was with Donald Trump Jr. for six years, four of which they were engaged. They publicly split in December 2024, the same month Trump nominated her to serve as ambassador to Greece.

The ambassador came under scrutiny last week after The Wall Street Journal reported that she asked Trump donor Eric Deters to pay off a $100,000 American Express bill shortly before her Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025.

According to messages reviewed by the Journal, Guilfoyle urged Deters to wire the money directly to American Express, saying the transaction would not leave a paper trail, while offering to help him gain access to senior Trump administration officials. Deters said he never made the payment.

Guilfoyle's attorney, Jesse Binnall, disputed the authenticity of the messages, saying Guilfoyle had been paid to speak at events before her nomination and "was owed a balance for traveling to and supporting these patriotic events."

The allegations followed an earlier Journal investigation into Guilfoyle's conduct in Greece, including claims that she promoted the interests of Greek construction and energy company Aktor Group and allowed its registered lobbyist, Christos Marafatsos, to accompany her to private diplomatic meetings with senior officials.

The Journal also reported that Guilfoyle suggested at a dinner with Greek officials that the U.S. would undermine their government, citing political developments in Romania. Greece's foreign minister subsequently said there was no need to summon Guilfoyle for an explanation because the country's energy minister denied that any threat had been made.

Separately, the State Department's Office of Inspector General reportedly opened an investigation into allegations involving Guilfoyle's treatment of embassy employees, private travel, acceptance of gifts and relationships with business interests, according to the Daily Mail.
HOUSE DEMOCRAT INVESTIGATED OVER ALLEGED 'INAPPROPRIATE SEXUAL CONTACT' WITH STAFFER

Sources described a hostile workplace in which Guilfoyle allegedly threatened to fire employees. They also claimed that she demoted members of her security detail over minor incidents, including an officer who reportedly failed to answer a 4 a.m. request for ice while she was vacationing in Mykonos.
The inspector general's office declined to confirm or deny the existence of an investigation. Binnall told the Daily Mail that "any implication of wrongdoing by the Ambassador is unsupported."

The allegations drew scrutiny from congressional Democrats, including Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., and Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., who called for a review of Guilfoyle's conduct. Meeks urged her removal if the allegations were substantiated.
Vice President JD Vance addressed the controversy Friday, cautioning against rushing to judgment while acknowledging that misconduct should carry consequences.

"Let's actually see what the facts are. Let's see what the truth is," Vance told reporters in Ohio. "And obviously, if there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer consequences for it."

President Donald Trump hired U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after her engagement to his eldest son fell through and now, after Donald Trump Jr. has married, his administration might be forced to fire her. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who visited Greece last week and delivered remarks against the backdrop of the Acropolis, initially defended Guilfoyle's performance.
"Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here," Rubio told reporters Wednesday.

A day later, Rubio declined to address the allegations directly, challenging reporters over their reliance on unnamed sources. "You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something, and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel," Rubio said last Thursday. Just days later, the White House announced their request for her resignation.

Trump nominated Guilfoyle to the diplomatic post in December 2024. A former California prosecutor and longtime Trump ally, she previously served as a prominent surrogate and fundraiser for the president.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Before her engagement to Don Jr., Guilfoyle was previously married to California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, from 2001 to 2006, when he served as mayor of San Francisco.

title: Fox News Power Rankings: As the House falls, the Senate stays in play
summary: Democrats' generic ballot lead is wider than the 2018 blue wave, pushing the House forecast toward a potential 237-seat Democratic majority.
story: Bill Hemmer breaks down the latest Fox News Power Rankings as congressional races tighten and candidates trade jabs ahead of midterms.
There are two big differences between the previous Trump-era midterms and this year’s contest.
The first is the president’s approval rating, which is lower now than it was during President Donald Trump’s first term in 2018 or President Joe Biden’s term in 2022.
The second is Democrats’ generic ballot lead, which is wider and more enduring than it was in the 2018 "blue wave" election and much larger than the edge the GOP had in 2022.
Combined with Democrats’ candidate quality improvements and a Republican-led redistricting effort that could fall short of expectations, the House is likely out of reach for the GOP this year.
REPUBLICANS FACE BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS. SIX FORCES COULD HELP THEM DEFY HISTORY.
Fox News Power Rankings - House. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
Then there’s a similarity: in all three elections, the Senate has been in play right up until the finish line.

In Trump’s first term, the Republicans ended up gaining two Senate seats despite a gloomy national environment. Four years ago, with inflation surging, the Democrats managed to add a Senate seat to their tally.
12 RACES SCRAMBLE SENATE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS EYE COMEBACK
Fox News Power Rankings Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
The Democrats have plentiful paths to 51 seats on election night. Republicans keep plowing money into six toss-up states, plus Kansas, and those efforts haven’t much moved the needle.
Yet the GOP’s paths to 50 are getting wider. That, plus a major update to the House forecast, in this week’s edition of the Power Rankings.
House: Democrats set to take control with up to 237 seats
The Democratic Party has enjoyed a lead in the House all year. Now, as another 20 races shift leftward, this forecast sees the Democrats taking control.
THE BLUE WAVE LOOKS REAL UNTIL YOU LOOK A LITTLE CLOSER
Fox News Power Rankings House forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
Democrats have an advantage in at least 219 seats, while Republicans should hold on to at least 198 seats. There are 18 toss-ups on the board.

On a good night for the Democrats, the party will hold around 237 seats, or a gain of 22 from their current position. That’s because toss-up seats have mostly fallen in one party’s direction in previous elections.
FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: FOR THE DEMOCRATS, WHERE COULD IT POSSIBLY GO WRONG?
Fox News Power Rankings House forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
(A "great night" for the Democrats, which would see the party take some Lean R seats as well, would mean a Democratic majority of up to 249.)

If the toss-up seats go the other way, the GOP could make life hard for the left. A good night for Republicans would see the party end up with around 216 seats. That’s two short of a majority but also leaves the Democrats with a mere two-vote cushion in the House.
Fox News Power Rankings House forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

In that scenario, a coalition of far-left Democrats, like the "Squad" of years past, could band together to put policy pressure on the next House speaker. That group is about to get bigger, thanks to the sure-thing victories of Democratic Socialists like Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez.

Some of this week’s shifts are a product of polling. The Democrats’ generic ballot lead has pushed districts like Kentucky’s 6th District (Lexington and its suburbs) and Texas’ 15th District (Rio Grande Valley and Coastal Bend) away from the GOP.
Fox News Power Rankings House forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

The party’s strength in statewide races also plays a role, especially in Iowa (the 1st and 3rd districts, which contain the state’s biggest cities), and in Pennsylvania (three districts have shifted to the left, thanks in part to Governor Josh Shapiro’s coattails).

Other shifts are the result of Republican groups moving resources elsewhere, like from New York’s 19th District. Democratic Rep. Josh Riley lost this race by fewer than 5,000 votes four years ago, but as the GOP sends its money to more winnable races, it’s moving to Solid D.
A more surprising theme is also emerging: the GOP is in trouble with rural voters.

Sitting above Albany, New York’s 21st District contains some of the state’s most rural areas. Its voters delivered President Trump a 21-point victory over Vice President Harris two years ago. A survey last week had the Democratic candidate four points ahead of the Republican, 46%-42%.
DEMOCRATS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP RED STATES — BUT A $400M GOP SPENDING ADVANTAGE COULD DERAIL THEIR PLANS
Fox News Power Rankings House forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Maine’s 2nd District, which famously voted for President Trump three times in a row – and last time by nine points – is an open race this year after Rep. Jared Golden’s retirement. It was thought to be one of the best flip opportunities for the GOP. A new poll has the Democrat at 51% and the Republican at 45%.

Even Virginia’s 5th District, stretching across the Southside region and home to a two-thirds rural population, is a six-point race in a recent survey (45%-51% with the Republican ahead). The Democrat, Tom Perriello, was recently endorsed by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

Gas, diesel and grocery prices are to blame. In dollar terms, the cost of living is higher in cities and suburbs, but voters across the country keep saying they are feeling the pressure of those increases and blame Republicans for them.
Fox News Power Rankings House forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Iowa, for example, has experienced the fourth-highest gas price hike in the nation. Kentucky, Ohio and Texas are all in the top five states for diesel increases. That has proven tough for GOP candidates to counter.
New York’s 21st District moves from Solid R to Likely R. (Virginia’s 5th and Maine’s 2nd districts remain at Lean R and Toss-up, respectively.)
Senate: Michele Tafoya plays offense in Minnesota
The Senate is still a toss-up with Democrats and Republicans taking 47 seats apiece. Six toss-ups are the most likely to determine control.

If Democrats win all six of those states, the party will take the majority with two seats to spare, for a total of 53. On the other hand, this forecast still sees a pathway for the GOP not to lose any seats. They’d accomplish that just by holding on to the same six states.
Fox News Power Rankings Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

The toss-ups have largely been locked in through summer. There’s been a lot more movement in the "lean" categories (Kansas in, Georgia and North Carolina out). Collectively, you can think of these as the election night battlegrounds.
This week, a ninth state joins the list: Minnesota.

The North Star State has been on the political radar since Republicans recruited Michele Tafoya, the former NFL sideline reporter. She has deftly navigated her foray into politics by focusing on fraud, crime, and the cultural issues that animate GOP voters.
Fox News Power Rankings Minnesota Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

She also has a favorable matchup against Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s sitting lieutenant governor. It’s not clear whether Flanagan’s progressive politics or her proximity to the fraud issue is giving voters pause. Whatever the cause, there are signs that they are.
A new gold-standard survey shows 47% of likely voters support Flanagan, while 43% back Tafoya. Another 9% are undecided.

Republicans are fully united behind Tafoya, while 9-in-10 Democrats say they’ll support Flanagan’s bid. Independents are much less settled: 38% back Tafoya, 32% support Flanagan, and 29% haven’t decided.
Fox News Power Rankings Minnesota Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Minnesota’s voter profile and election history suggest that there are some left-of-center voters in the "independent" column. They may be wavering on Flanagan now, then show up to vote for her on election day.
The Senate hopeful’s spot on the ballot next to Amy Klobuchar, the Democrats’ gubernatorial candidate and electoral over-performer, may also help push her over the line.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Either way, that poll can’t be ignored. Minnesota moves from Likely D to Lean D.
Rémy Numa is a political consultant and Fox News contributor. You can follow him on X: @remynuma.

title: Omar raid outrage goes from bad to worse when internet notices her past 6-word claim: 'Couldn't agree more'
summary: Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C., home was raided by DHS agents in a fraud investigation, and her old "no one is above the law" quote resurfaced fast.
story: Jonathan Fahey details the legal implications of the federal raid on the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, suggesting that the Homeland Security investigation likely targets naturalization or immigration issues. He explains that continuing false statements on current documents can constitute new criminal acts, bypassing any statute of limitations.

Reactions immediately started pouring in after federal authorities raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., with many on social media pointing to a previous claim from Omar that "no one" is above the law.

Omar’s home was raided by agents with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) investigation unit in the early Monday morning hours, Fox News Digital first reported, in a search that stems from a criminal fraud investigation into the Somali-born congresswoman's immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child.

Omar has been under fire for months and faced a myriad of controversies during her time in Congress, most recently, her financial disclosures have come into focus, and questions have been raised by top officials about her path to citizenship as well.

Many on social media were quick to point to a previous comment from Omar where she declared that "no one is above the law" after Trump was indicted in a hush money case that conservatives argued was based on flimsy evidence and a political prosecution.
OMAR'S GOP CHALLENGER COMES OUT FIRING WITH VOW TO CLEAN UP 'MESS' IN DEEP BLUE DISTRICT: 'PEOPLE ARE FED UP'

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., attends a field hearing at the Minnesota Senate Building on Jan. 16, 2026, in St. Paul, Minn. The hearing, titled "Kidnapped and Disappeared: Trump's Deadly Assault on Minnesota," featured local citizens and politicians discussing Immigration Operation Metro Surge. (Jim Vondruska/Getty Images)

"Rather than issue our own statement, we'll defer to Rep. Omar," the Minnesota Republican Party posted on X. "She said it best back in 2023, when the subject of a criminal investigation was someone else."
"We couldn't agree more, Congresswoman. We're sure you still feel the same way now that it's your front door. Minnesotans will be watching closely, and so will we."
"No one is above the law," the Trump War Room account posted on X.
"It was an authorized search warrant approved by a federal judge as part of a criminal investigation," conservative influencer LibsofTikTok posted on X. "No one is above the law."
"Ilhan Omar was right," Townhall columnist Dustin Grage posted on X. "Nobody is above the law."

"No one is above the law," Charlie Kirk Show executive producer Andrew Kolvet posted on X. "(And etting [sic] lectured by a Somali about the rule of law is rich. Not as rich as Rep. Omar was before she revised her financial statements, but rich.)"
"So much for ‘no one is above the law,’" conservative commentator Viva Frei posted on X.
CAUGHT ON CAMERA: SQUAD DEM SQUIRMS WHEN PRESSED ON VANCE DOJ FRAUD PROBE

title: Trump vanishes from GOP senator's campaign website as poll numbers plunge weeks before election
summary: Sen. Mike Rounds' campaign scrubbed several Trump mentions from his website as the president's approval rating craters in South Dakota's Senate race.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
A Senate Republican running for re-election in ruby-red South Dakota has joined a growing number of candidates putting distance between themselves and President Donald Trump.
But it’s more subtle than Republicans opposing the Iran war or dodging Trump campaign visits as Election Day nears and his popularity struggles.

Just last month, Trump’s name and endorsement were featured prominently on Republican South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds’ campaign website, but some mentions of the president have since been scrubbed, according to an older version of the website reviewed by Fox News Digital.
SLEEPER SENATE RACE EMERGES AS UNEXPECTED HEADACHE FOR REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., quietly scrubbed his website of a handful of references to President Donald Trump as the president's polling numbers and popularity with voters hit new lows. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images; Win McNamee/Getty Images)
Rounds’ campaign noted to Fox News Digital that not every mention of Trump has been removed.

"The president’s endorsement is still front and center on the website in Mike’s announcement video," Rounds’ campaign advisor, Rob Skjonsberg, told Fox News Digital. "But, generally speaking, it’s not abnormal to hone in on general election messaging."
Trump endorsed Rounds last year and lauded the lawmaker as an "incredibly strong advocate for the wonderful people of South Dakota, a State I love, and WON BIG, in 2016, 2020, and 2024!"
"Mike Rounds has my Complete and Total Endorsement for Re-Election — HE WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN," Trump said on Truth Social at the time.

Still, Trump’s approval rating among voters has cratered — a Fox News poll last month found that overall, voters had a 39% approval rating of the president’s performance. Key issues like cost of living, cost of groceries and fuel, and the ongoing war in Iran were major sticking points for participants.
FOX NEWS POLL: MOST RATE THE ECONOMY NEGATIVELY, INCLUDING HALF OF REPUBLICANS

Rounds’ campaign website featured two mentions of Trump on its homepage, including "Endorsed by President Trump" and a photo of Rounds touting that "Mike is endorsed by President Trump and is working for South Dakota every single day."

Those two mentions have since been removed, along with Trump’s name being removed in two places from the lawmaker's "Issues" page on his website — the president was previously included in Rounds’ "Put America First" and "Education" sections.
The lawmaker is vying for a third term in deep-red South Dakota, where he previously served as the state’s governor and in the state Senate.

He’s running against independent Brian Bengs, who previously ran as a Democrat against Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., in 2022. Thune easily defeated Bengs in the general election, securing over 70% of the vote.

title: Trump 'looking at' firing ambassador to Greece: 'We're not happy'
summary: President Donald Trump says he's "looking at" firing Kimberly Guilfoyle as U.S. ambassador to Greece amid allegations of improper conduct.
story: President Donald Trump told reporters Monday he is "looking at" whether to fire U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle, who was once engaged to his son, and insisted Russia and Ukraine agreed to a ceasefire
President Donald Trump is "looking at" firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after mounting reports alleging improper conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
"Well, we’re looking at it," Trump told reporters at the White House before leaving for an Ohio campaign rally Monday afternoon. "Yeah, we’re not happy."

Trump’s comments came after a senior U.S. official said Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were "extremely pissed off" by reports about Guilfoyle’s conduct and expected to make a decision on her future this week.
TRUMP AND RUBIO WEIGH FIRING KIMBERLY GUILFOYLE AS MISCONDUCT AND DONOR BAILOUT ALLEGATIONS MOUNT

The Wall Street Journal has reported a series of allegations involving Guilfoyle, including that she asked a Trump donor to pay a $100,000 credit card bill before her confirmation hearing while allegedly promising access to administration officials. The Journal also reported claims that Guilfoyle made a threat involving the Greek government, promoted the interests of a Greek construction and energy company, allowed a lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings and accepted improper gifts or services.
Rubio, who was in Greece last week, was frustrated by reporters repeatedly asking him to address the allegations publicly.
RUBIO SOUNDS CAMPAIGN-READY AS HE RAILS AGAINST OPEN BORDERS, GLOBALISM IN SPEECH FROM ANCIENT GREEK RUINS

U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle was not far from Secretary of State Marco Rubio's press gaggle last week in Athens, Greece, where Rubio grew frustrated about reports of her potential impropriety. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something, and you reported it, it’s the gospel," Rubio told reporters Thursday at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart Greece, looked on.
"It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things."
BIDEN-ERA DIRECTIVE FOR DIPLOMATS TO PEDDLE DEI ON FOREIGN GOVERNMENTS SCRAPPED BY STATE DEPARTMENT

President Donald Trump hired U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after her engagement to his eldest son fell through and now, after Donald Trump Jr. has married, his administration might be forced to fire her. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)
A day earlier, Rubio said he would not discuss the allegations while visiting a foreign country, but defended the embassy’s work.
"Suffice it to say our embassy here is doing a great job," Rubio said at a joint news conference with the Greek foreign minister. "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."
TRUMP JR UNDER SCRUTINY FROM OWN PARTY OVER PUTIN-LINKED OLIGARCH'S LAVISH GIFT
Vice President JD Vance also weighed in last week, saying he did not know the full details of the specific case but rejected the idea of selling access to government officials.

"Of course, I don’t like anybody selling access to another government official, certainly a high-level government official," Vance told reporters. "I assume you’re talking about a specific case, and I can’t say with confidence that the case you’re talking about is actually reflective of the way you’re describing it."

U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle hosted Secretary of State Marco Rubio and others in the U.S. delegation at the opening of the sixth round of the Greece-U.S. Strategic Dialogue in Athens, on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Mark Schiefelbein/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
HOUSE DEMS PLOT TRUMP INVESTIGATION BLITZ IF THEY SEIZE MAJORITY

Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing through her lawyers. In a statement released late Sunday, attorneys David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall said the money she sought from the Trump donor was payment for public appearances and speaking engagements that predated her nomination.

"Ambassador Guilfoyle has served, and will continue to serve, with integrity, honor and distinction," the lawyers said. "We are evaluating all available legal remedies to collect this debt and any other potential causes of action."

The attorneys also denied impropriety related to Guilfoyle's travel on private planes, saying she "sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the department's travel regulations."
BIDEN-ERA FBI TRACKED TRUMP FAMILY TRAVEL AND WILES’ CALLS WITH LAWYERS IN SECRET PROBE: DOCS

A U.S. official told The Associated Press that the State Department's inspector general is looking into the allegations, though it was not clear whether a formal investigation had been opened. The State Department declined to comment to the AP on a potential inspector general probe.
Top Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Senate Foreign Relations Committee and House Oversight Committee have called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Guilfoyle is a former California prosecutor who was once married to Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom and was engaged to Donald Trump Jr.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: US soldiers can't be protected from all bioweapons, Army admits amid troubling surge in threats
summary: The U.S. Army's new biodefense plan integrates biological warfare scenarios into combat training as AI and biotechnology raise concerns about threats.
story: Artificial intelligence systems face foreign exploitation, former CIA station chief Dan Hoffman warns. Hoffman joins to analyze a startling report from Anthropic detailing eight months of disrupted malicious operations targeting advanced models for cyberattacks and bioweapons development, emphasizing that the U.S. government must act aggressively to secure its critical technical infrastructure.
The U.S. Army unveiled its plan to prepare soldiers to fight through biological attacks rather than assume every threat can be stopped.

The newly signed plan bringing biological warfare scenarios into routine combat training as artificial intelligence (AI) and biotechnology raise new concerns about the weapons America's adversaries could develop in the near future.

"Can we protect every soldier from every possible bio threat? Probably not," Dr. Alison Tamasi, a senior official at the Army's Nuclear and Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction Agency, told reporters on Monday.
"We can't put them in a bubble," she added.

The shift comes as U.S. officials continue to assess whether Moscow maintains an offensive biological weapons program after a mysterious death in Russia was linked to an anti-plague facility — reviving questions of biological safety and transparency.
CHINESE AI MODEL INVESTIGATED AFTER RESEARCHER SAYS IT PROVIDED INSTRUCTIONS FOR BIOWEAPONS, ASSASSINATIONS
Soldiers from the United States gather together during the opening ceremony of Exercise Southern Jackeroo on May 29, 2026, in Townsville, Australia. (Ian Hitchcock/Getty Images)
Still, the Army hopes their implemented plan will help prepare the force to deploy and fight in biologically contested environments by 2035.

Rather than treating outbreaks primarily as medical emergencies, the military wants commanders, intelligence officers and logistics personnel to prepare for biological threats while continuing to carry out their combat missions.
EMERGING TECH HAS NEW ARMY LEADERS WARNING TROOPS CAN'T ‘AI’ THEIR WAY TO VICTORY ON THE BATTLEFIELD
One of the biggest changes will be bringing biological incidents into major Army combat exercises, forcing commanders to respond to potential outbreaks while continuing their other missions.
Rather than relying on specialized biological exercises, the Army wants troops across different military functions to confront biological threats as part of their regular training.

Tamasi described one scenario involving a simulated norovirus outbreak at a military port. While medical personnel worked to contain the outbreak, logistics officers would have to determine how to keep critical supplies moving.
Three hundred soldiers treat and work on fake wounded soldiers for a training exercise. (Fox News)

The example illustrates a broader shift in the Army's approach: Biological threats are no longer being treated solely as medical problems but as potential disruptions to military operations that commanders must be prepared to manage.
"We need to make sure that doctrine is aligned," Tamasi said, explaining that the Army is working to establish how biodefense readiness should be assessed across the force.

The new plan, signed last week, puts into motion the Army's updated biodefense strategy released in September, which sets a goal of preparing soldiers to deploy and fight in biologically contested environments by 2035.

The first two-year implementation cycle will focus on establishing policies, improving coordination across Army organizations and developing personnel with specialized biological expertise. More advanced technologies and acquisition efforts are expected in later phases.
The effort comes amid growing concerns about the potential for artificial intelligence and biotechnology to accelerate the development of biological threats.
PLAGUE MYSTERY REVIVES CONCERNS OVER NOT-TO-SECRET RUSSIAN BIOWEAPONS PROGRAM
Tamasi described those advances as a dual-use challenge, with technologies that can accelerate medical discoveries also potentially enabling new biological threats to emerge more quickly.

Russia remains a particular concern for U.S. national security officials. Washington has long assessed that Moscow maintains an offensive biological weapons program inherited from the Soviet Union, despite Russia's obligations under the Biological Weapons Convention.
The United States renounced offensive biological weapons in 1969 and is also a party to the convention, which prohibits the development, production and stockpiling of biological weapons.
A view of the entrance to the grounds of the anti-plague institute in the city of Irkutsk on Oct. 7, 2026. (TATYANA MAKEYEVA/AFP via Getty Images)
US, WHO REQUEST DETAILS FROM RUSSIA AMID REPORTS OF SECOND PNEUMONIA CASE

Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, died Oct. 2 after developing severe pneumonia. Russian media initially reported a possible pneumonic plague infection following a suspected laboratory accident, but Russian authorities denied that an accident occurred and said testing found no evidence of plague or other high-threat pathogens.

The cause of her death remains undetermined. In an Oct. 10 update, the World Health Organization said it had found no evidence of ongoing transmission linked to the case, while noting that a confirmed diagnosis was still lacking.
Asked how much Russia's biological weapons activities informed the Army's planning, Tamasi said the strategy was based on "intelligence writ large" rather than any single adversary.
"It's not solely focused on a particular threat actor," she said.

Asked what lessons the Army had drawn from Russia's biological weapons program, Tamasi said the strategy was designed to address biological threats regardless of their origin — whether accidental, deliberate or ultimately determined not to pose the threat initially feared.

For Army commanders, she explained, the immediate priority is responding to a potential biological threat and maintaining operations, rather than determining its origin. Questions of attribution would involve the broader U.S. government.
That approach also informs how the Army intends to detect emerging threats.

Darya Shipilova, 28, an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died after developing pneumonia of an unknown cause, prompting quarantines and heightened health precautions in the region. Russian authorities say testing has found no evidence her illness was linked to pathogens she worked with. (East2West news)
Officials said the military is working to draw together information from environmental monitoring, medical facilities and intelligence reporting to identify potential biological incidents earlier.

That could include wastewater surveillance similar to monitoring used during the COVID-19 pandemic, Tamasi said. The goal is to give commanders a more complete picture of potential biological threats so they can respond before disruptions spread.

The COVID-19 pandemic also exposed the limitations of treating biological threats primarily as public health emergencies, according to Army officials, reinforcing the need for military leaders outside the medical field to incorporate those risks into operational planning.

The strategy addresses misinformation as another operational challenge, particularly when troops and commanders must make decisions about vaccines, protective measures and communications during a biological incident.

The Army has also begun rolling out biodefense seminars for senior leaders. Tamasi said one three-star board determined that senior Army leaders should receive at least an hour of instruction on biodefense and the "ground truth" surrounding biological threats.
Ultimately, the Army hopes that preparing soldiers to continue their missions despite a biological attack could also discourage adversaries from using such weapons in the first place.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Tamasi said demonstrating that biological threats would not necessarily stop American forces from fighting could reduce the military advantage an adversary might hope to gain from deploying them.

title: Trump's new press secretary faces first major test as White House briefing room enters new era
summary: Katie Zacharia makes her White House press briefing room debut Tuesday, ending a weekslong stretch without a permanent press secretary at the podium.
story: Newly appointed White House press secretary Katie Zacharia discusses President Donald Trump's deal to import Russian diesel, Trump's midterm campaign efforts and her future plans as White House press secretary. Zacharia says her job is about the 'American people.'

The White House is set to end a weekslong stretch without a permanent press secretary at the podium Tuesday when Katie Zacharia makes her briefing room debut, succeeding Karoline Leavitt after a shake-up in President Donald Trump's communications team.

"I am pleased to announce that Katie Zacharia will be beginning her term as Press Secretary tomorrow, Columbus Day, and will be doing an introductory News Conference on Tuesday at 9:30 A.M. from the Press Briefing Room in the White House. Katie has been with me, in spirit, from the very beginning, and will do a fantastic job!" Trump said on Truth Social Sunday.

Zacharia, an attorney and television commentator, served as senior communications adviser to Trump Media & Technology Group, which operates the president's social media platform, Truth Social. Her appointment follows Leavitt's departure from the White House in August.
During his first administration, President Donald Trump had four White House press secretaries: Sean Spicer, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Stephanie Grisham and Kayleigh McEnany.
TRUMP NAMES LEAVITT SUCCESSOR AFTER WEEKS OF SPECULATION — AND SHE'S NO STRANGER TO MAGA
Katie Zacharia was named the new White House press secretary. (Barry Morgenstein)
Leavitt served as the first press secretary of Trump’s second administration for 19 months before leaving the role on Aug. 27.
Zacharia previously served as deputy assistant secretary for public affairs and a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security.

She appeared on "Fox & Friends Weekend" on Saturday in her new role, touting President Donald Trump's newly announced deal with Russia to supply more than 1.8 million tons of diesel fuel to U.S. and global markets in a bid to lower fuel and grocery costs.

"President Trump has heard people have been frustrated with the gas prices. People are frustrated with the increasing grocery prices. And he is delivering what he always does, which are solutions," Zacharia said.
KATIE ZACHARIA HITS GROUND RUNNING, PROMISES TRUMP DIESEL DEAL DELIVERS CHEAPER GAS FOR AMERICANS

Katie Zacharia and Adam Weiss attend as Jean Shafiroff Hosts Holiday Party in Honor of New York Women's Foundation at Private Residence on December 16, 2024, in New York City. (Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)
She celebrated the appointment in a post on X Friday, thanking Trump for what she called the "distinguished privilege" of serving as White House press secretary.

"Serving President Trump and the American people at this critical 250-year mark is the honor of a lifetime," Zacharia wrote. "President Trump has shown America that we can be great again, and he works to effectuate that greatness every single day. His confidence is a true privilege, and his leadership is a blessing to this country."

"The work ahead is to continue delivering strong results for our Country and communicating to the American people the major wins that this Administration is making every single day," she wrote. "I look forward to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out," she added.
She also acknowledged the expectations that come with succeeding Leavitt.
KAROLINE LEAVITT JOINS FOX NEWS AS CONTRIBUTOR AFTER LEAVING WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY ROLE
Caitlin Sinclair, Adam Weiss and Katie Zacharia seen on election night 2024. (Adam Weiss)
"Following the fabulous Karoline Leavitt is a high standard, and one worth meeting," Zacharia wrote.

Since Leavitt's departure, the White House has held a limited number of press briefings and news conferences led by senior administration officials, including Vice President JD Vance and Attorney General Todd Blanche.
The White House adopted a rotating lineup of top Trump administration officials to lead press briefings while Leavitt was on maternity leave over the summer.

"Katie has been an effective champion of the MAGA movement and America First policies — and most importantly, clearly has [the] trust of President Trump," former Trump press secretary Sean Spicer told Fox News Digital on Friday.

"Anyone who has not met her yet will quickly see that she is a genuinely kind person who will work well with the press corps, unlike the first press secretary who came across as an angry leprechaun at times," Spicer added, poking fun at himself.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Kimberly Guilfoyle faces potential Senate probe over bombshell $100K allegation
summary: Kimberly Guilfoyle faces a likely Senate investigation after allegations she sought to have a Trump donor clear $100,000 in personal credit card debt.
story: Western civilization faces a critical crossroads, warns Secretary of State Marco Rubio during a speech in Athens, Greece.
U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle may soon be the target of a Senate investigation following a bombshell report accusing her of influence peddling.

Guilfoyle is under fire following a Wall Street Journal report that alleged, before she was confirmed as ambassador to Greece, she pushed a top donor to President Donald Trump to clear $100,000 in personal credit card debt.

And a top Senate Republican believes that following that report, an investigation may soon follow. Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said on CBS News’ "Face the Nation" that "what we’ve seen in the reports is very troubling, it’s concerning."
TRUMP JR UNDER SCRUTINY FROM OWN PARTY OVER PUTIN-LINKED OLIGARCH'S LAVISH GIFT
Kimberly Guilfoyle, U.S. ambassador to Greece, arrives at the White House in Washington, D.C., on Feb. 26, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"And I’m sure there’s gonna be an investigation," Barrasso said.

"I would assume the State Department would be conducting that," he continued. "I know the Senate Foreign Relations Committee will have oversight and look into that, as well. But I think the public has a right to know what was found, and it is quite a bit of concern."
Fox News Digital reached out for comment on a possible investigation to the State Department and Sen. James Risch, R-Idaho, the top Republican on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.
DONALD TRUMP JR MARRIES BETTINA ANDERSON AHEAD OF BAHAMAS WEDDING CELEBRATION
Guilfoyle, who was recently engaged to Trump’s son Donald Trump Jr. until the two publicly split in 2024, was confirmed by the Senate last year for the post in Athens.

Barrasso’s prediction comes as allegations surrounding Guilfoyle and her time in Athens mount, and as speculation that her time in the role may be coming to an end. The State Department’s Office of Inspector General, the watchdog for the agency, has already opened a probe into Guilfoyle for previous alleged misconduct.

The Daily Mail reported that an investigation was already underway into Guilfoyle’s luxury lifestyle in Greece that included allegations of mistreatment of staff, substance abuse, close ties to an energy and construction company and the improper acceptance of gifts.
FORMER USCIS OFFICIAL, ACCOMPLICE CHARGED IN ALLEGED $960K CITIZENSHIP BRIBERY SCHEME
Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., speaks to reporters during the weekly luncheons on Capitol Hill on June 24, 2025, in Washington. (Tasos Katopodis)

The latest claim against her is that she allegedly solicited Trump donor Eric Deters to pay off a $100,000 American Express bill directly to the credit card company, urged him not to leave a paper trail and offered to help him gain access to top administration officials in exchange. Deters said he never made the payment.

In the wake of that report, Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are said to be "extremely pissed off" by Guilfoyle’s alleged conduct and are weighing her removal, The Associated Press reported Sunday, citing a senior U.S. official.

title: Booker ‘wowed’ by GOP challenger’s blunt message to Trump
summary: Justin Murphy told Trump to "finish it" on Iran, drawing applause and a stunned reaction from Cory Booker during their New Jersey Senate debate.
story: New Jersey GOP Senate hopeful Justin Murphy urged Trump to "finish" the war with Iran, prompting Booker to blast his "cowboy foreign policy" during a heated debate exchange. SOURCE: Youtube/@NewJerseyGlobe
Sen. Cory Booker’s Republican Senate challenger had a blunt message for President Donald Trump about the war in Iran during the pair’s recent debate: "Finish it."

The advice drew applause during Thursday's forum — and a "Wow" from Booker, who then blasted former Tabernacle Deputy Mayor Justin Murphy's remarks as the kind of "Yahoo" foreign policy that has dragged the United States into costly wars in the Middle East.

New Jersey is a blue state that has trended redder in recent years, with President Donald Trump flipping key areas in 2024. However, 1972 was the last time a Republican won a U.S. Senate election in the state, when Sen. Clifford Case was re-elected. Sens. Nick Brady in 1982 and Jeff Chiesa in 2013 later served brief, appointed terms.
Sen. Cory Booker, left; former Tabernacle Deputy Mayor Justin Murphy, right. (Screenshot/New Jersey Globe via YouTube)
Murphy, an attorney from the Pine Barrens, earned loud applause for his response to a question about Iran when asked what he would tell Trump if the president called him for advice on the conflict.

"Finish that war in a positive manner," Murphy replied firmly. "We can't wait halfway through and decide we don't want to do this anymore. The Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps is a radical terrorist organization that has deprived the Iranian people, the Persian people, of their history and of a decent life."
‘FINISH THE DAMN JOB’: HAGERTY TELLS 'RUTHLESS PODCAST' THAT TRUMP WILL COMPLETE IRAN MISSION
U.S. Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., will take on Justin Murphy, who won the U.S. Senate GOP primary in New Jersey Tuesday night. (Jersey Justin For Senate/Getty Images)

The exchange highlighted the candidates' opposing approaches to the conflict, with Murphy defending Trump's military campaign and Booker warning against another prolonged American war in the Middle East.

As Murphy continued, the broadcast's split-screen showed Booker briefly looking down and shaking his head before pursing his lips for the rest of Murphy’s response and raising his eyebrows at one point.
LAWMAKER’S STUNNED FACE AND OTHER VIRAL MOMENTS CAP ROUGH WEEK FOR POLITICAL CLASS
A "Welcome to New Jersey" sign at the New York state line entering New Jersey. (Najlah Feanny/Corbis via Getty Images)
"Four decades is enough. The Iranian people have suffered enough," Murphy began to conclude.
"And I would say, ‘Mr. President, put your cowboy hat on and get out there and kick some a--, and get this done and done right’," Murphy said.
"Wow," Booker mouthed as moderator David Wildstein gestured toward the Democrat and said it appeared he wanted to respond.
BOOKER SLAMS TRUMP’S IRAN DEAL AS AN 'ABJECT SURRENDER,' LABELS HIM THE 'BIGGEST LOSER' WITH 'EGG ON HIS FACE'

"Honestly," Booker began. "This is the kind of ‘Yahoo’ foreign policy that has mired us in Middle East war after Middle East war — with false bravado leaders saying we're just going to go in there and kick ass. Well, you know what that's done to the treasury of our country?" Booker replied.
When asked the same question as Murphy, Booker joked that Wildstein was asking him about "a guy calling me for advice who has literally said ‘I know more than my generals’."

But the former Newark mayor entertained the hypothetical, saying he and the rest of New Jersey have known Trump for years because he "bankrupted our casinos" — referring to the president’s former Atlantic City casino businesses.

He accused Trump of frequently ignoring advice, claiming advisers had to "jangle keys" to keep him on topic during a meeting about the trans-Hudson rail tunnel project spearheaded by Booker and Sen. Charles Schumer, D-N.Y.

Murphy also received attention for his comments during the debate on illegal immigration. He recounted leaving a campaign event in Washington, N.J., and looking across at a home where a child was allegedly abducted and raped by Guatemalan illegal immigrant Lester Noe Perez-Amador — whom the Biden administration previously released after a Texas county notified ICE that it had taken him into custody, according to WRNJ.
