title: IKEA turns to driverless semis with nobody in the cab
summary: Kodiak AI plans to haul IKEA freight on Texas highways with no one in the cab, raising urgent cybersecurity and safety questions for drivers.
story: Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson spoke with Daniel Goff, vice president of external affairs at Kodiak AI, about how attitudes toward autonomous trucks have shifted over time.

You could soon be driving down a Texas highway, look over at a massive delivery truck and realize the driver's seat is completely empty. Kodiak AI plans to start hauling IKEA products between the Dallas and Houston areas later this year with nobody in the cab. The company has spent years preparing for this step, but removing the safety observer changes the equation.

What happens if something breaks while the truck is moving at highway speed? Is someone secretly driving it from a control room? How does it react to a police car or ambulance? And, yes, I wanted to know what keeps a hacker from getting anywhere near something as important as the steering or brakes. So, I took those questions directly to Kodiak founder and CEO Don Burnette to find out how the company says these driverless trucks will handle them.
PILOTLESS CARGO AIRCRAFT COULD CHANGE HOW PACKAGES MOVE
Kodiak’s self-driving semi sits outside an IKEA store as the company prepares to haul freight with nobody in the cab. (Kodiak AI)
Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist.
See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com.
Why Kodiak believes it is ready to remove the driver

"The decision to remove the driver isn't based on any single test or milestone," Burnette told CyberGuy. "It's the result of years of operating experience, rigorous validation and a clear safety case that gives us a clear, evidence-based framework for determining when the Kodiak Driver is ready to operate safely without anyone in the cab."

Kodiak calls its autonomous driving system the Kodiak Driver. The company also uses something called an Autonomy Readiness Measure, or ARM, to track its progress toward running long-haul trucks without anyone aboard.

As of the end of September, Kodiak said 96% of the claims and evidence required for its long-haul safety case were materially complete, up from 93% at the end of August. The remaining work includes engineering verification, validation and final safety assessments. Kodiak expects to complete that work before launching driverless long-haul service by the end of 2026. The company also has experience running trucks commercially with empty cabs.

Kodiak-powered trucks have been operating for Atlas Energy Solutions in the Permian Basin without anyone aboard since December 2024. Burnette says that by the end of the second quarter, 35 driverless trucks were operating there commercially and had logged more than 40,000 hours of paid driverless operations. To put things in perspective, that is the equivalent of more than 4 ½ years of nonstop driving. So, the IKEA route will take Kodiak into a different setting, but removing the driver itself will not be new territory for the company.
What changes when the IKEA driver comes out of the cab

I asked Burnette what drivers on I-45 will actually notice once the new service starts. His answer was pretty straightforward. "The biggest difference is that there won't be anyone in the cab," he said.

The driverless section will cover 219 miles, primarily along Interstate 45 between Kodiak facilities in the Dallas and Houston areas. That stretch is part of a longer 292-mile delivery route connecting IKEA's distribution center in Baytown with its store in Frisco.

Kodiak has been carrying IKEA products along the route for four years with a safety observer aboard. During that time, the companies have also been figuring out the less obvious parts of running autonomous freight, such as when trucks should leave, when they will reach the destination and how maintenance should be scheduled.

The trucks themselves have redundancy systems built into safety-critical components including braking, steering, power and computing. "From the outside, the drive itself should look pretty boring, and that's exactly what we want," Burnette said. "The Kodiak Driver is designed to be predictable, courteous, conservative and defensive." Frankly, boring is exactly what I think we all want from a giant truck with nobody sitting behind the wheel.
What happens if something breaks while the truck is moving?

This was high on my list of questions. "We've designed the Kodiak Driver around the idea that something will eventually go wrong, whether that's a mechanical issue, a damaged sensor or an unexpected situation on the road," Burnette said. "The important thing is that the truck already knows what to do when that happens."

Burnette says the Kodiak Driver continuously monitors more than 1,000 safety-critical components across the truck, its sensors, hardware and autonomy software. If the system detects a serious issue, it can switch from normal driving into what Kodiak calls a fallback maneuver. That process is designed to bring the truck to a controlled stop in a safe location.

Kodiak also puts limits around where and under what conditions the truck can operate. In the autonomous vehicle world, that is called an Operational Design Domain, or ODD. You can think of the ODD as the truck's approved operating boundaries. If the situation falls outside what the system has been designed and tested to handle, Burnette says the truck can fall back rather than continuing as though nothing has changed.
DOORDASH GETS FAA APPROVAL FOR ITS OWN DELIVERY DRONES
Kodiak plans to run driverless IKEA deliveries along a 219-mile stretch of I-45 between the Dallas and Houston areas. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)
Is a person somewhere else remotely driving the truck?

No one will be in the cab, but people will still be watching what is happening. Kodiak has a command center just south of Dallas. However, Burnette does not describe those workers as remote drivers waiting to take control. If the Kodiak Driver runs into a situation it cannot safely resolve, it can activate its fallback system and then, as Burnette puts it, "call home for help." The command center can provide guidance about what the truck should do next.

That is different from a person taking over the steering wheel from miles away. "We use redundant communications channels to ensure we remain in contact with the truck, but if connectivity is lost, the Kodiak Driver still has to be able to respond safely on its own," Burnette said.

That last part is especially important. If the cellular or communications connection goes down, the truck cannot simply sit there waiting for someone at the command center to tell it what to do. Kodiak says the vehicle still has to get itself into a safe state.
What happens when police or an ambulance show up?

Highway driving involves situations that go well beyond staying between the lane lines. Police pull vehicles over. Ambulances approach from behind. Accident scenes can suddenly change the flow of traffic. A truck with nobody in the cab still has to recognize what is happening around it and respond.

Kodiak says its autonomous system is designed to identify emergency vehicles, stopped vehicles, lane closures and accident scenes. The system can slow down or move over when appropriate. The company has also spent time working directly with first responders.

Kodiak employs a retired California Highway Patrol officer who works with law enforcement on how to interact with driverless trucks. The company also has a written First Responder Interaction Plan that explains what responders should do if they encounter one of its vehicles.

Another piece of technology comes into play if a Kodiak truck stops along the road. Kodiak has integrated HAAS Alert's Safety Cloud. That system can send digital warnings about a stopped truck to nearby motorists through compatible navigation apps and vehicle systems.
Could a hacker take over one of these driverless semis?

You knew I was going to ask this one. Once software has control of an 18-wheeler, cybersecurity becomes a major part of the conversation. I asked Burnette what keeps someone from hacking into a truck and interfering with systems like the steering or brakes. "Cybersecurity is something we take very seriously," he said.

Burnette says cybersecurity is one of six pillars in Kodiak's safety case. The company says its approach follows guidance from the National Institute of Standards and Technology and vehicle cybersecurity best practices from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. But the part that really stood out to me was how Burnette described limiting access to the truck. "First, we've minimized the number of ways into the truck," he said. "We limit data entry points to only what's necessary, and we isolate safety-critical functions like steering and braking from external communications."

That isolation is important because communication with the outside world should not provide a direct doorway into critical driving systems. Burnette says Kodiak also monitors for threats and maintains an incident response process. Burnette also addressed what happens if the truck loses connectivity. "The truck's safety doesn't depend on connectivity, and it's designed to bring itself to a safe stop if something isn't right," Burnette said. No connected vehicle comes with a promise that hackers will never target it. That is why I will be watching how these protections hold up as more driverless trucks begin traveling public highways.
AUTONOMOUS EXCAVATORS ARE DIGGING WITH EMPTY CABS
The Kodiak truck uses autonomous driving technology with backup systems for critical functions including steering and braking. (Kodiak AI)
Who is responsible if a driverless truck crashes?

With a traditional truck, investigators can look at what the person behind the wheel did before a crash. But what happens when nobody was behind the wheel? I asked Burnette who would ultimately be responsible if a driverless Kodiak truck were involved in an accident. "Responsibility for a driverless vehicle works similarly to responsibility for any vehicle: it depends on the circumstances surrounding the crash," he said.

Burnette says Kodiak trucks have more than a dozen sensors aboard. Those sensors can give the company a detailed record of what happened around the vehicle. That information could be especially useful when investigators need to reconstruct the moments leading up to a crash.
What can a human truck driver still handle that the system cannot?
I wanted to push on the limits too. Autonomous driving companies spend plenty of time telling us what their technology can do. I think it is just as useful to ask what it cannot do.

Burnette pointed back to the Operational Design Domain. "The Kodiak Driver is designed to operate under specific conditions," he said. "If the truck leaves its ODD, it will simply achieve a fallback. That's intentional." At launch, Burnette says the ODD will cover the Dallas-Houston corridor. Kodiak plans to expand the operating area during 2027 and beyond.
What does driverless trucking mean for truckers?

This may be the biggest question of all for someone who makes a living driving a truck. If a semi can travel hundreds of highway miles without a person in the cab, what happens to the person who used to sit there? "We see autonomous trucks supplementing the workload rather than eliminating the need for them," Burnette said.

Burnette also explained why Kodiak is targeting this type of work. "Our focus is on the long, repetitive highway miles that can keep drivers away from home for days or weeks at a time," Burnette told CyberGuy.

There is still a much larger question about what happens if driverless freight eventually spreads across the country. Companies could change the way they divide routes and use drivers. Some jobs could change with them. We will know much more once autonomous trucking gets beyond a limited number of routes and starts becoming part of larger freight networks.
Kurt's key takeaways

The part I keep coming back to is that there will actually be nobody in the cab. Kodiak has spent four years hauling IKEA freight on this route with a safety observer aboard. Taking that person out changes the stakes, especially when you are talking about an 18-wheeler traveling alongside the rest of us on a busy interstate. I also give Burnette credit for answering our tougher questions. What happens when something breaks? Can somebody remotely drive it? How are the steering and brakes protected from hackers? Kodiak has built systems around each of those concerns, but now comes the test that counts. Once these trucks start piling up driverless highway miles with nobody there to step in, we will get a much clearer idea of how ready this technology really is.

Would you feel comfortable driving next to an 18-wheeler with nobody behind the wheel, or would you keep your distance until driverless trucks have a much longer safety record? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Your phone can fix badly framed photos after you take them
summary: Apple Intelligence in iOS 27 adds Extend and Reframe tools to Photos, letting iPhones generate new background areas beyond your original borders.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Have you ever taken a photo you really liked, only to realize later that you stood too close, cut off part of the background or framed the subject in the wrong spot? Normally, fixing that means cropping even more of the photo. Now your phone may be able to go in the other direction.

Apple added new Extend and Reframe tools to Photos in iOS 27. Instead of simply cutting away part of an image, Apple Intelligence can generate additional areas around the original shot or change its perspective after you take it. Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel phones offer similar AI editing tools that can help rescue photos that did not come out quite the way you planned.

12 BIGGEST APPLE WWDC 2026 TAKEAWAYS YOU NEED TO KNOW
A smartphone camera makes it easy to snap photos quickly, but the framing does not always come out the way you intended. (iStock)
What is new for photos in iOS 27?
Apple added several Apple Intelligence upgrades to Photos with iOS 27. Two of the most useful are Extend and Reframe.

Extend lets you expand a photo beyond its original borders. For example, if someone's head is too close to the top of the image or you want more space around the subject, Apple Intelligence can generate additional background.

Reframe goes further. Apple says it lets you change the point of capture after taking the photo. You can move the image, zoom, rotate it and adjust its perspective while Apple Intelligence generates the additional portions needed for the new composition.

These tools go beyond traditional cropping. Cropping removes part of your image. Extend and Reframe can create parts of the image that were never captured by the camera. Because these are generative AI features, take a close look at the final result. AI-generated areas can sometimes contain strange details, especially around faces, hands, text or complicated backgrounds.
Which iPhones can use Extend and Reframe?
Extend and Reframe require Apple Intelligence and iOS 27 or later.
Apple Intelligence works on:
iPhone 15 ProiPhone 15 Pro MaxiPhone 16 models or later

Availability can also depend on your language and region. Apple says some Apple Intelligence features may have usage limits. If you have an older iPhone that can install iOS 27 but does not support Apple Intelligence, you will not get these particular editing tools.
Use Extend when you want more room around the subject or need to expand the edges of your original photo.

How to fix a badly framed photo on a Samsung Galaxy

Samsung takes a somewhat different approach. Compatible Galaxy phones use Galaxy AI Photo Assist, which includes tools for moving, removing and adding objects in a photo. For this trick, the Move tool is the one to use. It lets you reposition, rotate or resize part of the image, then uses generative AI to fill in the background created by your changes. Samsung's standard Gallery editor also lets you change the aspect ratio, rotate the picture and adjust its angle.

Google Photos has one of the closest Android alternatives to Apple's new Extend tool. It's called Auto frame. Google says Auto frame can recompose a photo that is too tightly cropped or poorly framed. It can also use AI to fill in missing areas and extend the background.
Make sure you have the latest version of the Google Photos app.

Open Google Photos .Select the photo you want to fix.Tap Edit .Tap Crop .Tap Auto frame .Let Google Photos analyze the image.Review the suggested framing or extended background.Tap Done when you're happy with the result.Tap Save .

Tap Edit .
Tap Crop .
Tap Auto frame .
Let Google Photos analyze the image.
Review the suggested framing or extended background.

Google also includes Straighten, Rotate, Perspective and Aspect ratio controls in the same Crop section if you want to make the adjustment yourself.
Google rolls out some Photos features gradually. Therefore, if you do not see Auto frame, update Google Photos and check again. Availability can also vary by device, account and region.
Google Photos' Auto frame can recompose a Pixel photo and extend the background when the original shot feels too tight. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
5 tips for getting better results with AI photo editing
AI photo editing works best when you give it a reasonably clear original image. Here are a few things to keep in mind.
AI can generate new areas around an image, but it cannot completely rescue every blurry or badly exposed shot. Start with the clearest version you have.
Instead of dramatically expanding the entire picture, try adding a little extra space around the edges. Smaller edits can look more natural.
Zoom in before saving. Check faces, hands, hair, jewelry and clothing for unexpected changes.
Generative AI can struggle with letters and numbers. Look closely at street signs, shirts, storefronts and anything else containing text.
When your phone gives you the option, save the edited version as a copy. That way, you still have the untouched photo if the AI result does not look right later.
Kurt's key takeaways

One of the frustrating things about smartphone photography is realizing you almost got the perfect shot. Maybe you stood a little too close, left the person too far to one side or tilted the camera just enough to make the composition feel wrong. iOS 27 gives supported iPhones another way to fix those mistakes with Extend and Reframe. I also like that Galaxy and Pixel owners have comparable options instead of sitting this one out. These tools will not replace taking a well-framed photo in the first place, but they can give a photo you would otherwise delete another shot.

title: Why verified social media accounts can still lead you into a scam
summary: Microsoft's X account was hijacked to promote a crypto pump-and-dump scheme, exposing its more than 13 million followers to a scam campaign.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

We have all developed little shortcuts for deciding whether something online looks legitimate. You check the account name. You recognize the company logo. Then you spot that verification badge and your guard comes down a little. That can be exactly what scammers are counting on.

Microsoft’s official X account became the latest reminder after attackers gained unauthorized access and used the account in an apparent cryptocurrency pump-and-dump scheme. The account has more than 13 million followers, giving whoever controlled it access to a huge audience and the credibility that comes with Microsoft’s name.
Here is what happened, why compromised verified accounts can be so convincing and what you should check before trusting the next surprising post that shows up in your feed.

6 CRYPTO SCAM SCRIPTS CRIMINALS USE TO STEAL YOUR MONEY
Microsoft’s name and logo carry enormous trust, which is exactly why a compromised official account can make a scam look convincing. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
How Microsoft's X account got pulled into a crypto scheme

BleepingComputer reported that Microsoft's @Microsoft account followed and reposted content from another X account that appeared to be Clippy-themed. That account was promoting a cryptocurrency called $Clippy. Microsoft tells CyberGuy that two unauthorized posts appeared during the period when its account was compromised. According to the company, the first was a quote repost of content from what appeared to be a Clippy-themed account and referenced bringing back Microsoft Office's old animated paperclip character. The second appeared to be an apology related to the earlier activity. Microsoft says neither post originated from the company.

A Microsoft spokesperson provided CyberGuy with the following statement: "We have confirmed unauthorized access to our account on X, including posts that did not originate from Microsoft. The account has been secured, the unauthorized posts have been removed, and we are continuing to investigate the circumstances."
Why a verified account can make a scam much harder to spot

If an account you have never heard of suddenly tells you Microsoft launched a Clippy cryptocurrency, you might keep scrolling. When Microsoft’s actual account appears to amplify that same message, it becomes much easier to hesitate. You may assume someone at the company approved the post. You might click a link because you recognize the account. Someone interested in crypto could move even faster because they are worried about missing an opportunity.

That is the advantage attackers get when they compromise a well-known account. They inherit trust that has already been built for them. We recently saw the same basic weakness after hackers hijacked HBO Max’s verified Reddit account. Researchers found that attackers used the compromised account to push 108 malicious ads over roughly 48 hours. Because those ads appeared under a familiar verified account, they had an extra layer of credibility.
THOUSANDS OF HACKED SITES TRICK YOU INTO INSTALLING MALWARE
Microsoft said it did not authorize or endorse the $Clippy cryptocurrency token after unauthorized access to its X account.
Microsoft has dealt with a similar account takeover before

This is also not Microsoft’s first encounter with a crypto scam involving one of its X accounts. In June 2024, scammers hijacked Microsoft India’s X account and used it to impersonate Keith Gill, better known online as Roaring Kitty. The attackers then promoted what appeared to be a GameStop cryptocurrency presale.

People who followed the link and connected their cryptocurrency wallets risked having their assets stolen through wallet-draining malware. That example shows how quickly a social media takeover can turn into something much more expensive. A post may only be the beginning. The real danger often waits behind the link.
Even the SEC’s official X account was hijacked

One of the clearest examples happened in January 2024 when attackers took over the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission’s official X account. The compromised account falsely announced that the SEC had approved spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds. According to the Justice Department, Bitcoin jumped by more than $1,000 following the false post. After the SEC regained control and corrected the announcement, Bitcoin fell by more than $2,000.

Investigators later determined that attackers gained control through a SIM swap involving the phone number associated with the SEC account. Eric Council Jr. pleaded guilty in February 2025 to conspiracy charges related to the attack and was sentenced in May 2025 to 14 months in prison. That case gives us a good example of how much influence one compromised account can have. An official-looking post can spread quickly before the real organization has time to warn everyone that something has gone wrong.
A verification badge cannot guarantee who controls the account right now

A verification badge can still be useful. It may help confirm that an account belongs to the person, company or organization it claims to represent. What it cannot tell you is whether that same organization still controls the account at the exact moment you are reading a post.

Hackers can steal credentials through phishing or take advantage of other account takeover techniques. SIM swapping has also been used to intercept password reset codes and defeat some forms of two-factor authentication. CyberGuy has covered this problem before on X, where hackers have taken over verified accounts and then changed them to impersonate cryptocurrency projects. The account may look established because it is. The person controlling it may have changed.
The Microsoft account takeover shows why even posts tied to major companies should be verified before you click, invest or connect a crypto wallet. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
7 ways to protect yourself from scams posted by trusted accounts

You do not need to assume every surprising post is the work of a hacker. Still, when an account suddenly asks you to spend money or connect something valuable, a few extra checks can save you from a painful mistake.

If a company announces a cryptocurrency, giveaway or major investment opportunity on social media, go directly to the company’s website. Look for the same announcement in its newsroom or another official channel. If the only place you can find it is one social media post, wait before acting.

If an account that normally talks about software suddenly starts pushing an obscure crypto token, treat that change as a warning sign. Scroll through its recent posts and check whether the promotion fits anything the company has announced elsewhere.

Connecting a cryptocurrency wallet can expose you to malicious approvals that allow attackers to move assets. Navigate directly to a service you already trust instead. Never enter your recovery phrase or private key into a site because a social media post tells you to.

Strong antivirus software can help warn you about phishing sites, malicious downloads and other threats that may be waiting behind a suspicious link. Security software adds another layer of protection, but it should never replace slowing down and checking where a link came from. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

Scammers love deadlines. You may be told a token is launching right now or that an offer disappears in a few minutes. That pressure is designed to get you moving before you verify what you are seeing. Give yourself time to check another source.

Even when the post comes from a legitimate account, the link inside it may lead somewhere dangerous. Look carefully at the web address before entering a password, payment information or crypto credentials. Small changes in a domain name can lead you to an entirely different site.

Use a unique password for important accounts and turn on two-factor authentication (2FA). A password manager can help you create and store strong, unique passwords so you are less likely to reuse them across accounts. An authenticator app or passkey can provide stronger protection than relying only on texted security codes. Also check your account’s active sessions periodically and sign out any devices you do not recognize.
What to do if you already clicked
What you should do next depends on how far you got before realizing something looked suspicious.

Clicked the link only: Close the page. If a file downloaded automatically or you were prompted to install something, run a security scan with strong antivirus software.Entered a password: Go directly to the real website or app and change it immediately. Update that password anywhere else you reused it, then turn on two-factor authentication (2FA). Consider using a password manager to create and store strong, unique passwords for each account.Connected a crypto wallet: Review your token approvals and revoke anything you do not recognize. Revoking suspicious approvals can help prevent additional unauthorized transfers, but it cannot recover funds that have already been stolen.Exposed a recovery phrase or private key: Treat the wallet as compromised and move any remaining assets to a new secure wallet.
Clicked the link only: Close the page. If a file downloaded automatically or you were prompted to install something, run a security scan with strong antivirus software.

Entered a password: Go directly to the real website or app and change it immediately. Update that password anywhere else you reused it, then turn on two-factor authentication (2FA). Consider using a password manager to create and store strong, unique passwords for each account.

Connected a crypto wallet: Review your token approvals and revoke anything you do not recognize. Revoking suspicious approvals can help prevent additional unauthorized transfers, but it cannot recover funds that have already been stolen.
Exposed a recovery phrase or private key: Treat the wallet as compromised and move any remaining assets to a new secure wallet.
Kurt’s key takeaways

The Microsoft attack is a good reminder of how quickly the signals we rely on can turn against us. We tell people to check the account name, look for the real profile and be cautious with impersonators. In this case, attackers briefly had control of the account people were supposed to trust. I would still use verification as one clue, but I would never let a checkmark do the thinking for me when money, passwords or a crypto wallet are involved. If a company suddenly posts something that feels out of character, verify it somewhere else before you act. Go to the company’s website, check another official channel and give yourself a minute before clicking. That extra pause can be the difference between spotting a scam and paying for one.

title: A scammer has your name, phone number and address. What can they actually do?
summary: Scammers can combine your name, phone number and address with data breach details to attempt SIM swaps, phishing and even identity theft schemes.
story: Cybercrime losses reached nearly $21 billion last year, prompting Kurt Knutsson to warn of increasingly sophisticated AI scams. He joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to break down the FBI data, highlighting that investment fraud alone cost victims $8.65 billion. Knutsson hosts a free live class to teach families how to protect their money and secure accounts.
If you've ever wondered how much damage a scammer could really do with your name, phone number and home address, the answer is probably more than you'd expect.

Those three details are generally not enough by themselves to empty your bank account, take out a major loan or completely steal your identity. However, they can give a scammer a believable starting point. From there, the goal may be to trick you into revealing the more sensitive information they still need.

That is what makes seemingly basic personal information so useful to criminals. Here's what a scammer can actually do with those details, the warning signs to watch for and the steps you can take to make yourself a harder target.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better health care . Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist .

THE SECRET LIST THAT TELLS SCAMMERS YOU'RE AN EASY TARGET

Scammers can use your name, phone number and home address to create convincing phishing attacks, impersonate trusted companies and target your financial accounts. (Photo by Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images)
Why basic personal information can help a scammer

Your name, phone number and address may already appear in public records, old directories, property records or data broker databases. As a result, people sometimes assume there is little risk if a stranger already knows them. The problem starts when those details are combined.

A scammer may add information from a data breach, social media account, people-search site or earlier phishing attempt. Suddenly, the person contacting you may know where you live, your phone number, the names of relatives or other details that make a fake story sound legitimate.

That is why a scam call can feel so convincing even when nobody has actually hacked your phone or bank account. Data brokers can also collect information such as current and previous addresses, phone numbers, approximate age and possible relatives. A scammer may use those details to learn more about you before making contact.
What can a scammer do with your name, phone number and address?
Here are some of the most common ways that information could be used.

A scammer who knows your name and address can pretend to represent your bank, utility company, delivery service or government agency. For example, hearing someone read your correct home address may make the call seem legitimate. However, knowing personal information does not prove that the caller is really from the company they claim to represent.

Once someone has your address, they can send fraudulent invoices, fake prize notices, counterfeit checks or other deceptive mail directly to you. Because the material arrives at your real address and may include your full name, it can look more credible than a random email or text.

Your phone number can also become part of a SIM-swap or account-takeover attempt. A phone number and address alone usually will not be enough to take control of your wireless account. Still, a criminal may combine those details with passwords, PINs or other information stolen elsewhere. If they successfully move your number to another SIM or device, they may then receive calls and text messages intended for you, including some verification codes.

This is where the risk can grow quickly. Perhaps one database exposes your phone number and address while another contains an old password or Social Security number. Criminals can combine pieces from multiple sources to create a much more complete profile. That information may then be used for identity theft, account takeovers or additional phishing attempts.

Personal details can also strengthen family-emergency scams. A criminal may know your relative's name, where you live or other information that helps support a fake story. With AI-generated voices making impersonation scams increasingly believable, personal details can make an already emotional call even harder to judge.

Some services still rely on personal details or knowledge-based questions during account recovery. A scammer may try information such as your address, phone number or other details to see whether they can get further into a password-reset or identity-verification process. They may still need additional information. However, every correct answer can move them one step closer.
What can't a scammer usually do with only these three details?

Knowing your name, phone number and address does not automatically give someone access to your bank account. Those details alone are also generally insufficient for opening major financial accounts or taking out loans because financial institutions typically require additional identity verification.

However, I would not treat that as a guarantee. The bigger concern is that a scammer can use the information they already have to convince you to provide what they are missing, such as a password, verification code, Social Security number, bank account information or credit card number. In other words, your basic information may be the beginning of the attack rather than the end.
HACKER CLAIMS 7.49M CUSTOMER RECORDS STOLEN FROM AMERICAN UTILITY COMPANY

Your name, phone number and address may not be enough to steal your identity, but scammers can combine those details with information exposed in data breaches. (Photo by Silas Stein/picture alliance via Getty Images)
How personal information makes a scam more believable

Suppose your phone rings and the caller immediately knows your full name and home address. Then they tell you there is suspicious activity on one of your accounts. That specificity can cause you to listen a little longer. Next, they may ask you to verify a code that just arrived by text, confirm an account number or transfer money to supposedly protect it. This is where I want you to be especially careful. A caller knowing something about you is not proof that the caller knows you. Personal information should never replace independent verification.
Warning signs that your information may be getting used
Watch for these warning signs:

Calls or texts that unexpectedly mention your full name, address or other personal detailsBills, prize notices, checks or other mail that you were not expectingA sudden loss of cellular service that you cannot explainPassword-reset messages or verification codes you did not requestFamily members receiving strange calls or messages from someone claiming to be youNew accounts, inquiries or activity you do not recognize on your credit reports or financial accountsA noticeable increase in personalized phishing attempts after a company you use reports a data breach
Calls or texts that unexpectedly mention your full name, address or other personal details
Bills, prize notices, checks or other mail that you were not expecting
A sudden loss of cellular service that you cannot explain
Password-reset messages or verification codes you did not request
Family members receiving strange calls or messages from someone claiming to be you
New accounts, inquiries or activity you do not recognize on your credit reports or financial accounts
A noticeable increase in personalized phishing attempts after a company you use reports a data breach
One unusual call does not necessarily mean someone has stolen your identity. Still, several warning signs appearing together deserve attention.
7 steps to reduce what scammers can do with your information
A few precautions can make it much harder for someone to turn basic information into a successful scam.

Search your name, phone number and address and see what comes up. You may find people-search sites and data brokers displaying information you would rather keep private. Where possible, submit opt-out requests to have those listings removed.

Ask your wireless carrier what protections it offers against SIM swaps and unauthorized number transfers. Set a strong account PIN or password and enable any available port-out or number-transfer protection.

If an unexpected caller knows your address, bank name or another personal detail, do not assume that means the call is real. Hang up and contact the company directly using a phone number or app you already trust.

Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) for important accounts. When possible, I prefer an authenticator app, passkey or physical security key over text-message verification for especially sensitive accounts. That reduces the damage a successful SIM swap could cause.
Choose a private family verification word or phrase that family members can use if someone calls claiming there is an emergency. Do not post it online or use something a stranger could easily guess.

Avoid confirming or correcting personal details during an unexpected call. If someone says, "You're still at 123 Main Street, correct?" you do not need to tell them your new address. End the call and verify the request independently.

Review bank and credit card activity for transactions you do not recognize. You should also check your credit reports for unfamiliar accounts or inquiries. If you are concerned about identity theft, a credit freeze can make it harder for someone to open new credit accounts in your name. Credit freezes are free and can be placed with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion.
How identity theft protection can add another layer of security

Personal information tends to accumulate online over time. One breach may expose an email address while another exposes an old password. Meanwhile, data brokers may already have your address, phone number and information about your relatives.

An identity theft protection service can help you watch for signs that some of this information is being misused. Depending on the service and plan, that may include identity monitoring, credit monitoring, financial account alerts, data broker removal and help recovering from identity theft.
Identity and financial monitoring: Some services can alert you to certain suspicious activity involving your identity, credit or financial accounts.
Data broker removal: Some plans include tools that can help remove your personal information from supported data broker and people-search sites.
Scam support: Certain services offer access to specialists who can help you evaluate suspicious messages, calls or websites.
Identity restoration: If identity theft occurs, some providers offer restoration specialists who can help guide you through the recovery process.

Loss coverage: Depending on the provider and plan, you may also get insurance or reimbursement for certain eligible identity theft expenses or losses. Coverage limits, exclusions and availability vary, so read the terms carefully.
No identity theft service can prevent scams or guarantee that your personal information will never circulate online. However, monitoring and alerts may help you spot suspicious activity sooner.

Even with strong security habits, identity theft can still happen. Your Social Security number, financial information or other personal data may already be exposed without you realizing it. If you are concerned, consider using an identity theft protection service as an added layer of monitoring and recovery support. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com

It is also worth checking whether your email address or other personal information has appeared in a known data breach. Free breach-checking tools can help you identify exposed accounts so you can change affected passwords, turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) and take other steps to lock them down.
What to do if you think your information is already being misused
If you notice suspicious activity, act quickly. The first priority is to stop any potential damage and determine whether someone has gained access to your accounts.

End suspicious contact. Stop responding to unexpected calls, texts or emails. Contact the company directly using an official phone number, website or app.Contact your mobile carrier. If your phone suddenly loses service or you suspect someone transferred your number, call your carrier immediately to secure your account.Secure any affected accounts. Change compromised passwords, review recent sign-ins and contact your bank or credit card company if you notice unauthorized activity.Warn your family. Let relatives know if someone may be impersonating you, especially if the scammer has mentioned family members or personal details.Report identity theft. If someone has used your identity, visit IdentityTheft.gov for a personalized recovery plan.Report scam attempts. File a report with the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov , even if you did not lose money.
End suspicious contact. Stop responding to unexpected calls, texts or emails. Contact the company directly using an official phone number, website or app.
Contact your mobile carrier. If your phone suddenly loses service or you suspect someone transferred your number, call your carrier immediately to secure your account.
Secure any affected accounts. Change compromised passwords, review recent sign-ins and contact your bank or credit card company if you notice unauthorized activity.
Warn your family. Let relatives know if someone may be impersonating you, especially if the scammer has mentioned family members or personal details.
Report identity theft. If someone has used your identity, visit IdentityTheft.gov for a personalized recovery plan.
Report scam attempts. File a report with the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov , even if you did not lose money.
Most importantly, do not let someone pressure you into making a quick decision. Scammers rely on urgency to keep you from checking whether their story is real.
SCAMMERS ARE COMING FOR YOUR MONEY. HERE’S THE ONE THING YOU MUST NEVER DO

Criminals can use basic personal information to impersonate banks, delivery services and government agencies in attempts to steal passwords and verification codes. (Photo by Silas Stein/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

Your name, phone number and address may not seem like highly sensitive information, especially when some of it can already be found online. Still, those details can give a scammer enough material to build a much more believable story. I would pay less attention to how much a caller knows about you and more attention to what they want you to do next. If they ask for money, a password, a verification code or another sensitive detail, end the conversation and verify the request yourself. You probably cannot erase every trace of your personal information from the internet. However, you can reduce what is exposed, lock down important accounts and make sure a stranger cannot use a few correct details to earn your trust.

title: 8 seriously annoying tasks you can hand off to an AI agent
summary: ChatGPT Work, Meta Muse and Gemini Spark can monitor flight prices, sort your email inbox and track important deadlines, but savvy users start small.
story: Fox News anchor and White House correspondent Aishah Hasnie reports on President Donald Trump’s executive order renaming artificial intelligence ‘Super Intelligence’ following a summit with top technology leaders on ‘Special Report.’

I have a growing list of things I would gladly never do again. Checking the same airfare every morning is on it. Digging through an overflowing inbox is right up there too. And I would be perfectly happy never having to remember when some free trial is about to start charging me. This is where AI agents are starting to get genuinely useful.

A regular chatbot waits for you to ask a question. An AI agent can potentially keep working on something after that first conversation. It might monitor a price, watch for an opening or keep tabs on a task you would otherwise have to remember yourself. OpenAI, Meta and Google are all pushing further into this kind of AI. OpenAI now has Dots and ChatGPT Work, while Meta has Muse and Google has Gemini Spark.

That all sounds very impressive. But I am less interested in having an AI run my life than I am in having it take a few irritating chores off my hands. So if you are wondering what you would actually do with one of these agents, start here.

AI AGENT HACKS GYM SYSTEM TO MOVE UP WAITLIST

AI agents can handle everyday tasks, from tracking flight prices and organizing emails to managing household reminders, while keeping users in control of important decisions. (Photo by Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
What are ChatGPT Dots, ChatGPT Work, Meta Muse and Gemini Spark?

ChatGPT Work is only one way to try an AI agent. OpenAI also offers Dots, which are more persistent. A Dot has its own cloud computer, can remember ongoing work and can keep making progress between conversations. Dots are currently rolling out to eligible ChatGPT Pro, Business Premium and Enterprise users. OpenAI says Dot usage will temporarily not count against eligible users' plan allowances during the introductory period, with longer-term usage terms still to come.

ChatGPT Work is built into ChatGPT and focuses on longer, multi-step tasks. On web and mobile, OpenAI says Work is available on eligible paid plans, including Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu, although access is still rolling out. Work can research, use connected apps and files, create finished materials and run scheduled or recurring tasks.

There are alternatives too. Meta Muse offers a free tier with usage limits, with a paid subscription available if you need more. Gemini Spark is Google's personal AI agent and is available to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in supported regions. It can manage ongoing tasks, use connected Google services and run scheduled workflows.

You do not need the most powerful or expensive agent to try the ideas in this article. Start with whichever service you already use, give it a low-risk task and see whether having AI continue the job actually saves you time.
How to get started with an AI agent in ChatGPT

If you have never used an AI agent, the first step is simply knowing where to find one. We will use ChatGPT Work as an example. OpenAI is rolling the feature out to eligible accounts, so what you see can vary depending on your plan and device. Before you get started, I recommend checking a few privacy settings so you have more control over what ChatGPT does with your information.
You can stop new ChatGPT conversations from being used to train OpenAI's models. Here's how:

Go to ChatGPT.com and sign in. If you do not have an account yet, choose the option to sign up and create one.Click your profile icon.Select Settings.Click Data Controls.Turn off Improve the model for everyone.
Go to ChatGPT.com and sign in. If you do not have an account yet, choose the option to sign up and create one.
Click your profile icon.

Turn off Improve the model for everyone.
Your conversations can still appear in your chat history, but new chats will not be used to train OpenAI's models.
Open Settings.Select Personalization.Find Memory.Turn off Enable memory if you do not want ChatGPT using remembered information to personalize future conversations.
Open Settings.
Select Personalization.
Find Memory.
Turn off Enable memory if you do not want ChatGPT using remembered information to personalize future conversations.

You can also use Temporary Chat for conversations you do not want saved in your history or used for model training. OpenAI may still retain these chats for up to 30 days for safety purposes. Finally, review your connected apps under Settings > Plugins. Remove any connections you no longer need. Keep in mind that turning off model training does not prevent ChatGPT from processing information you provide to complete a task.
Once you've reviewed those settings, you're ready to give an AI agent its first task. Here's how to get started:

Look near the top of the screen for Chat and Work .Click Work .Start a new chat .In the message box, describe the task you want the agent to handle.Add any useful files or information the task requires. If the job needs access to a supported app, ChatGPT may give you the option to connect it.Be specific about what the agent can and cannot do. For example, you can tell it to research or draft something without sending, booking or buying anything.Send your request and follow along as the agent works. Look near the top of the screen for Chat and Work .

Send your request and follow along as the agent works. Review its results before approving anything important.

You do not need to start by connecting your entire digital life. In fact, I would not. Try a simple task first, such as researching several products within a budget or comparing options for an upcoming trip. That lets you see how the agent works before you give it access to email, calendars or other personal information. Once you are comfortable with the basics, the eight ideas below show where an AI agent can start saving you some real time.
MALICIOUS BROWSER EXTENSIONS CAN HIJACK AI ASSISTANTS
ChatGPT Work, OpenAI Dots, Meta Muse and Google Gemini Spark offer ways to automate time-consuming tasks using artificial intelligence. (Photo by Celine Frohnapfel/picture alliance via Getty Images)
1) Have AI prepare you for the day

I do not need another app demanding my attention first thing in the morning. What I would like is something that looks at the information I already have and tells me what I need to know. An AI agent with access to your calendar and other approved information could review what is coming up, flag a meeting you need to prepare for and surface something time-sensitive you might have missed. The key is asking for a briefing instead of another information dump.

Prompt to try:"Review my calendar and relevant messages for today. Tell me what I need to prepare for, flag anything time-sensitive and point out any scheduling conflicts. Do not send messages or change my calendar without asking me first."
That last sentence would absolutely stay in my prompt. I want AI to tell me that my afternoon looks impossible. I do not want it quietly deciding which meeting gets moved.
2) Stop checking the same price over and over

You find a flight. It costs too much. So you check again tomorrow. Then you check again the next day. I have done this with airfare, hotels and products I was not in a hurry to buy. It gets old fast. This is almost a perfect AI agent task because there is very little value in you personally opening the same page 12 times. Give the agent the item and the price you are hoping to hit. Then let it tell you when something changes.

Prompt to try:"Track the price of [item, flight or hotel]. Let me know if the total price drops below $___ or if you find a comparable option that costs less. Show me the details before taking any action."

You can even use this after a purchase. If the retailer offers price adjustments or you are still inside the return window, have the agent keep watching. I like this type of task because the AI does the watching while I keep control of the wallet.
3) Let AI sort the email you do not want to sort

There are days when opening my inbox feels like volunteering for another job. Some emails need an answer. Others are simply FYIs. Then you have the message you meant to answer two days ago sitting underneath six newsletters and a shipping notification. An AI agent connected to your inbox can help with that first pass. It can summarize what arrived, identify the messages that appear to need attention and prepare a reply for you to review.

Prompt to try:"Review my unread email from the last 24 hours. Show me what needs my attention today and summarize the rest. Draft responses where appropriate. Do not send, delete or archive anything without my approval."

I would absolutely keep that approval requirement in place. Let AI write the first draft. Let AI tell you what looks urgent. But before something goes out under my name, I want to see it. That goes double if the recipient is my boss, my doctor or anybody who might interpret an AI hallucination as something I actually meant to say.
4) Make AI remember all the little deadlines you forget

Life is full of deadlines that are incredibly easy to miss because they do not feel urgent until suddenly they are. A subscription renews Friday. A rebate expires next week. Your insurance paperwork is due. Somewhere in your inbox there is a form you completely forgot existed. That is the kind of mental clutter I would love to hand off. An agent could keep track of deadlines you give it and remind you before something needs your attention.

Prompt to try:"Keep track of the deadlines, renewals and appointments I give you. Tell me what is coming up this week and alert me early when I need to do something. Never renew, cancel or submit anything without my approval."
I would keep the agent in reminder mode when money is involved. Tell me the bill is due. Tell me the trial expires tomorrow. Then get out of the way and let me decide what happens next.
5) Let AI figure out what’s for dinner

I don't know about you, but deciding what to make for dinner every night gets old fast. You open the refrigerator, stare at what's inside and somehow still can't think of anything to eat. Why not hand that job to AI? Tell an AI agent what foods you like, what ingredients you already have and how much time you want to spend cooking. It can put together a weekly dinner plan, suggest simple recipes and even help you use up food before it goes bad.
Prompt to try:

"Every Sunday, prepare a dinner plan for the coming week with five easy meals. Use my food preferences and any ingredients I've told you I have. Keep each meal under 30 minutes. Include simple recipes and a grocery list of anything else I'll need. Don't order groceries without my approval."

You can schedule this as a weekly task so the agent prepares fresh dinner ideas without you having to ask each time. Just update it with what's in your refrigerator and pantry before it creates the next plan. That means fewer nights staring into the refrigerator wondering what to cook.
6) Put somebody else in charge of the household to-do list

Every home seems to have a list that nobody actually wrote down. The air filter needs replacing. The dog is running out of food. There is something in the garage you promised to fix about four months ago. Then, at exactly the wrong moment, somebody remembers it. An AI agent could become the place where all those loose ends go. Every time something pops into your head, give it to the agent and let the agent keep track of what is coming due.

Prompt to try:"Keep a household task list based on the things I give you. Remind me when something needs attention and help me keep track of what is still unfinished. Ask me before adding anything to my calendar, ordering something or contacting anyone."

This is one of those uses that sounds almost too simple for AI. That may be exactly why I like it. If it remembers that I need a new refrigerator filter before the old one stops working, we are making progress.
7) Let AI remember who owes you an answer

This one drives me crazy. You send an email. You request a refund. You call somebody about a bill. They tell you they will get back to you. Then life happens. Two weeks later, you suddenly think, "Wait, did anybody ever answer me?" An AI agent could keep track of those loose ends for you. Tell it what you are waiting on and when you expect a response. If nothing arrives, have it remind you. Better yet, let it prepare the follow-up so you do not have to stare at a blank email trying to remember what happened in the first place.
Prompt to try:"Keep track of the requests I am waiting on. If I have not received a response by the deadline I give you, remind me and draft a polite follow-up. Do not send it without my approval."

That could work for a contractor estimate, a disputed charge or a return you are still waiting to hear about. I like this because the agent becomes responsible for remembering that the conversation never actually ended.
8) Have AI watch for the opening you keep missing

Sometimes the issue is not the price. It is getting your hands on the thing at all. Maybe the restaurant you want is booked Saturday night. Your doctor has no opening for three weeks. The product you want keeps selling out. You could keep checking. Or you could make the AI check.

Prompt to try:"Check [restaurant, appointment, event or product] for availability. Let me know when an opening appears that meets these conditions: ___. Do not book, buy or confirm anything without asking me first."

This will depend on the AI agent you are using and whether the website allows that kind of automated access. But the idea is exactly where agents become useful. I do not want to ask AI whether the table is available right now. I want it to tell me Friday afternoon when somebody cancels and suddenly it is.
CyberGuy pro tip: Make your AI agent earn its permissions

Here is the part I would pay close attention to. An AI agent becomes more useful as you give it more access. That can include your email, calendar and other accounts. More access also means there is more that can go wrong. So I would make the agent earn those permissions.

Start by letting it read something. See what it does with the information. If that goes well, maybe allow it to organize information or prepare drafts. Only then would I consider letting it perform a limited action, and even then I would keep approval turned on whenever something important could happen.
Think about email. Let the agent summarize messages first. Then maybe let it draft replies. Sending those replies is another level entirely.

The same thinking applies to shopping and your calendar. OpenAI says Dots can follow rules that determine which actions they can perform on their own and when they need your input. Meta says Muse asks for approval before certain critical actions, including purchases and sending emails. I would use those controls.

And I would never paste passwords, PINs or two-factor authentication codes into a chat window because an AI agent asks for them. If the service offers a secure way to connect an account, use that instead. Give AI what it needs to complete the task. Do not automatically give it everything it asks for.
Do you actually need an AI agent?
Here is an easy way to figure that out. Ask yourself whether the job ends when AI answers you. If you ask ChatGPT to help plan dinner tonight, you probably do not need an agent.
But suppose you say, "Keep watching the price of this flight and tell me when it drops below $300." Now the useful part of the job happens after you leave.

The same goes for appointments. Asking what appointments you have tomorrow can be a normal AI request. Asking AI to alert you when an earlier doctor's appointment becomes available requires something that keeps checking.
Agents make the most sense when the task has an unfinished part. That is where I see the real appeal.
What I still would not hand over to AI

There are some areas where convenience would not persuade me to give up control. I would not give an AI agent unrestricted access to move money or make major purchases. I also would not let one make medical decisions for me or handle a legal decision without a human involved.

Be careful with connected accounts too. If you connect an agent to your inbox or cloud storage for a particular task, check what it can see. Once you no longer need that connection, consider removing it. AI agents may get much better at taking action on our behalf. That does not mean every action should be theirs to take.
IDENTITY RESTORATION: WHAT TO DO AFTER IDENTITY THEFT

AI agents can monitor prices, check appointment availability and draft email responses without requiring users to repeatedly check for updates. (Photo Illustration by Stanislav Kogiku/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

I think AI agents get a lot more appealing when you forget the hype for a minute and ask one simple question: What am I tired of doing myself? For some people, that could be checking a price every morning. Others may want help remembering follow-ups or keeping track of household chores that always seem to surface at the worst possible time. Those are the kinds of tasks I would hand over first.

I become much more cautious when AI moves from watching and reminding to actually doing something in my name. I am happy to let an agent tell me that a restaurant table opened up. Before it books dinner for me, though, I want to know exactly what it is about to do. That is where I see the sweet spot with AI agents. Let them handle the annoying part while you stay in charge of anything that could cost you money, expose your information or create a mess you have to clean up later.
What is the one annoying task you would happily hand over to an AI agent tomorrow, and what is one thing you would never trust it to do for you? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: 16-year-old allegedly led ransomware gang behind hundreds of attacks
summary: Operation KillSwitch dismantled KillSec's ransomware infrastructure, but investigators say a 16-year-old allegedly ran the entire cybercrime operation.
story: Following the arrest of an alleged leader in the Netherlands, a top FBI cyber official released an unusual public address urging the remaining cybercriminals to turn themselves in "while the choice is still yours."

When you picture the person running an international ransomware operation, a 16-year-old probably does not come to mind. Yet investigators say a teenager was the suspected main operator behind KillSec, a cybercrime group linked to around 1,000 suspected attacks worldwide. About 500 of those attacks have so far been identified as successful.

Now, an international law enforcement operation has taken KillSec's leak site and key servers offline. Authorities also secured at least 110 terabytes of stolen data that could have been exposed or used to pressure victims. The takedown offers a remarkable look at how accessible cybercrime has become. More importantly, it shows how attackers continue to find their way into poorly protected systems and turn stolen files into leverage. What investigators uncovered about KillSec shows how the group operated, how AI reportedly played a role and what you can do to make ransomware attacks harder to pull off.

FBI STRIKES BACK AT HACKING GROUP WITH OVERSEAS ARREST OF ALLEGED LEADER
Guardia Civil, Mossos d’Esquadra and FBI personnel took part in the coordinated international investigation targeting KillSec. (Europol)
Police take down KillSec ransomware operation

The crackdown, known as Operation KillSwitch, took place on Sept. 30. Authorities from the United States and several European countries participated in the investigation. Europol and Eurojust also helped coordinate the effort.

Police carried out eight searches in Greece, Romania, Spain and the United Kingdom. Three suspects were provisionally arrested. Investigators also took control of five central servers connected with KillSec's operation. One of the biggest moves involved KillSec's dark web leak site. The group allegedly used the site to name victims and threaten to publish stolen files unless they paid. Authorities have now taken control of that infrastructure.
A 16-year-old is suspected of running the operation

Perhaps the most startling part of this case involves the age of the suspected operator. Investigators identified a 16-year-old as KillSec's suspected administrator and main operator. Another suspected member, described as a developer, turned 18 in August and was reportedly still a minor when some of the alleged crimes occurred.

Investigators also identified people suspected of serving as a negotiator and an affiliate. Authorities say the investigation remains ongoing. Age aside, the alleged operation was anything but small. KillSec has been active since around 2024. According to Europol, the group exploited software vulnerabilities and poorly secured access points to break into organizations. Attackers then copied sensitive internal files to systems they controlled.
How KillSec allegedly pressured its victims

Once attackers had the files, the pressure began. KillSec allegedly listed organizations on its dark web site and threatened to publish their stolen data if they refused to pay. In some cases, the stolen files were reportedly made available after victims declined to hand over a ransom.

Europol says the group received substantial ransom payments from some attacks. That strategy shows how ransomware has changed over the years. Criminals do not always need to lock every file on a computer to create leverage. Stolen information itself can become the threat. If an attacker gets employee records, customer information or confidential business documents, the victim can face serious consequences even when backups work perfectly.
KillSec reportedly used AI to support its attacks

Investigators also uncovered another detail that caught my attention. Europol says members of KillSec used artificial intelligence to help build and maintain ransomware infrastructure and identify potential victims.

That does not mean AI carried out the entire attack by itself. However, it shows how cybercriminals can use the same technology everyone else is experimenting with to speed up parts of their work. A teenager may no longer need to build every piece of an attack from scratch. Tools, stolen credentials, vulnerable systems and AI assistance can lower some of the barriers that once required deeper technical expertise. That should make all of us pay closer attention to basic security habits.
FBI'S FIRST CYBER FUGITIVE ON TEN MOST WANTED LIST RETURNS TO US AFTER CAPTURE IN VENEZUELA
Operation KillSwitch brought together international law enforcement agencies to seize KillSec’s servers, leak site and stolen data. (Felix Zahn/Photothek via Getty Images)
What happens to KillSec now?
The investigation remains active. Authorities are examining computers, servers and other seized evidence. Investigators are also following cryptocurrency and other alleged criminal proceeds.

That evidence could uncover additional attacks, victims or people connected with the operation. Europol also cautions that the current number of successful attacks may change as investigators continue reviewing what they seized.

For now, KillSec's core infrastructure has taken a significant hit. However, ransomware groups have a long history of disappearing, reorganizing and resurfacing under different names. That makes prevention especially important even after a major takedown.
Why this ransomware takedown should get your attention

KillSec appears to have focused mainly on organizations rather than individual home computer users. Still, the methods behind the attacks offer lessons that apply to everyone. Europol says the group exploited software vulnerabilities and poorly secured access points. Those are the same types of weaknesses security experts have warned about for years.

An old router, forgotten account or unpatched computer can give attackers an opening. A compromised password can do the same. Once criminals gain access, they can steal information before anyone realizes something has gone wrong. So, while you probably cannot stop an international ransomware gang yourself, you can make your devices and accounts harder to break into.
7 ways to reduce your ransomware risk
A few simple security habits can close some of the openings attackers commonly look for.

Do not keep putting off updates on your computer, phone, browser and other connected devices. Security updates often fix vulnerabilities attackers already know how to exploit. CISA recommends regularly patching operating systems and software, especially on devices exposed to the internet. Turn on automatic updates when that option is available.

Using the same password across several accounts gives an attacker more opportunities if one login is exposed. Create a different password for each important account. A password manager can help generate and store strong credentials without forcing you to remember every one. You should also check whether passwords you already use have appeared in known data leaks. Your iPhone or Android phone may already have tools that can flag compromised passwords.
HACKER CLAIMS 7.49M CUSTOMER RECORDS STOLEN FROM AMERICAN UTILITY COMPANY
Law enforcement collected laptops, phones and storage devices as evidence during the Operation KillSwitch takedown. (Europol)

A stolen password becomes much less useful when your account requires another form of verification. Enable two-factor (2FA) or multifactor authentication on your email, financial accounts, cloud storage and other important services. When available, consider phishing-resistant options such as passkeys or security keys instead of relying only on text-message codes.

Ransomware becomes far more painful when your only copy of a photo, document or financial record lives on the compromised device. Back up important files regularly. Consider keeping one copy in the cloud and another on an external drive. If you use an external drive, disconnect it when the backup finishes. Some ransomware can also target drives that remain connected to an infected computer.

A convincing email, fake update warning or malicious attachment can provide an attacker with a way into your computer. Avoid opening files you were not expecting. Instead of clicking an urgent update prompt from a webpage or email, open the app itself and check for updates there. If something feels unusual, stop before entering a password or running a downloaded file.

Strong antivirus software can help detect ransomware, malicious downloads and other threats before they spread. Keep the protection updated and run a full scan if your computer suddenly behaves differently, redirects your browser or shows unfamiliar programs. Security software will never replace safe habits. However, it can provide another opportunity to catch a threat before the damage grows. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com.

If you see a ransom message or suddenly lose access to important files, disconnect the affected device from your network. Avoid plugging backup drives into the compromised computer until you know the device is clean. The FBI says it does not support paying ransomware demands because payment does not guarantee that your information will be restored. The agency also encourages victims to report ransomware incidents. You can file a report with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.gov or contact your local FBI field office. The FBI specifically directs ransomware victims to use those channels. One more thing: type IC3.gov directly into your browser. The FBI has warned that scammers have created fake IC3 websites, including lookalike pages that may appear in sponsored search results.
Kurt's key takeaways

The age of KillSec's suspected operator is going to grab the headlines, and I understand why. Sixteen is incredibly young to be accused of running an operation connected with this many attacks. What stays with me, though, is how familiar the alleged entry points sound. Vulnerable software and poorly protected access can still give criminals exactly the opening they need. That is why I keep coming back to the basics. Update your devices. Protect important accounts with more than a password. Keep a backup that an attacker cannot easily reach. You may never know which security step stopped an attack. That is far better than discovering which one you skipped after your files are already gone.

If a 16-year-old can allegedly help run a ransomware operation tied to hundreds of successful attacks, do you think powerful hacking tools and AI are making cybercrime too easy to enter at a young age? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

summary: The Fox News Artificial Intelligence newsletter covers where voters will decide on AI data center ballot measures and Jeff Bezos' tech vision.

America’s multibillion tech boom comes into focus as 7 key states put it to a midterm testJeff Bezos reveals his vision for America's next frontier — from AI to the moonAmerica’s new blue-collar job boom is one nobody saw coming — and it’s just getting started
America’s multibillion tech boom comes into focus as 7 key states put it to a midterm test
Jeff Bezos reveals his vision for America's next frontier — from AI to the moon

PEOPLE DECIDE: The rapid buildout of data centers powering America’s artificial intelligence boom is heading to the ballot box this November, as voters across the country weigh measures that could shape where and how the massive facilities are built. Voters will decide 34 data center-related ballot measures across seven states — California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Nevada, Ohio and Wisconsin.

NEXT GIANT LEAP: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos laid out a sweeping vision for America’s future Wednesday, telling Fox News the U.S. must beat China to the moon, artificial intelligence could help families get by with less work and data centers could one day operate in space.

TRUST ISSUES: As artificial intelligence rapidly evolves to make financial scams hyperrealistic, cybersecurity experts warn that the best defense isn't sophisticated detection software. It's good old-fashioned human skepticism.

'OUR CITY': A Memphis City Council meeting descended into chaos Tuesday night after lawmakers postponed a vote on a proposed yearlong moratorium on new data centers, as protesters chanted inside City Hall, police cleared the chamber and a fight broke out in the lobby.
FAMILY NIGHTMARE: A California mother and Navy veteran was having breakfast with her husband when a caller who cloned her daughter's voice claimed to have kidnapped her.

MIND GAMES: A top official at the Department of War discussed how artificial intelligence is playing a role in war readiness strategy, and said foreign adversaries are carrying out "psyop" operations to fuel the anti-data center and anti-artificial intelligence movement across the U.S.

METAL MANIA: Investors have long prized gold as a hedge against inflation and economic uncertainty, but one of the world’s fastest-growing industries is now fueling a new source of demand for the precious metal. The buildout of artificial intelligence is driving investment in advanced semiconductors, servers and the sprawling data centers needed to power the technology. That expansion also requires a range of materials used in high-performance electronics, including gold.

WIRED FOR WORK: Inside a sprawling Texas data center campus, blinking tower lights and rows of neatly organized cables power the technology Americans use every day. Keeping it all running, however, takes an army of electricians, mechanics, technicians and construction workers — and the industry says it needs more of them.

TOMORROW'S TRADE-OFF: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview on Sunday that the benefits of artificial intelligence are enough to justify accepting some risks and suggesting that the public should continue to have broad access to the emerging technology.

CAN'T SAY: During a Monday New York City Council hearing, representatives from OpenAI, Google, Meta and Anthropic were asked to assure under oath whether AI agents will always comply with safety guardrails to prevent catastrophic harm.
FACE TIME: Chick-fil-A is bucking a growing fast-food industry trend, with CEO Andrew Cathy saying the chicken chain does not plan to use artificial intelligence to take customers' drive-thru orders.

POWERING UP: President Donald Trump announced Sunday the creation of a new federal "Super Intelligence Force" tasked with coordinating the government’s efforts to keep the United States at the forefront of rapidly developing artificial intelligence technology.

FAST TRACK: Workers in the U.S. who use artificial intelligence regularly in their job are seeing benefits like working more quickly or creatively, though a new study finds that those gains aren't evenly distributed across the workforce.
NEW TO CAMPUS: OpenAI on Wednesday announced that it's adding a college planner tool to its ChatGPT for Teens along with new study features on the platform.
