title: Anti-scam settings on iPhone, Pixel and Galaxy you should check
summary: Apple's Impersonation Risk Detection in iOS 27 can flag suspicious activity inside apps, but the setting is off by default and must be enabled.
story: From voice cloning to fake arrests, cyber expert Morgan Wright breaks down how scammers use high-tech tools to exploit basic human fears.

Scammers have become very good at getting us to do the dirty work for them. Someone may pose as your bank, claim your account was hacked or tell you to move money before something terrible happens. The call or message might sound convincing enough that you willingly follow the instructions.

That's one reason a new iOS 27 setting caught my attention. Apple calls it Impersonation Risk Detection, and it can help supported apps recognize signs that you may be acting under the influence of a scammer.

If you use Android, keep reading. Google Pixel and Samsung Galaxy phones have their own built-in scam protections, and some of them go after the problem from a different direction. I would check these settings no matter which of these phones is in your pocket.
Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist.
See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com
SCAMMERS ARE BUYING GOOGLE ADS TO STEAL BANK LOGINS
An iPhone running iOS 27 can use Impersonation Risk Detection to help supported apps spot signs of a possible scam. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What Impersonation Risk Detection does on iPhone

Apple introduced Impersonation Risk Detection with iOS 27. The feature is designed to help with active social engineering scams, where someone pressures or guides you into doing something yourself. That last part is important. Traditional security can help block malware or stop an unauthorized login. However, those defenses can have a harder time helping when you are the legitimate account holder and a scammer has convinced you to send money or change sensitive account information.

When you perform certain sensitive actions inside a supported third-party app, that app can ask Apple for a risk assessment. Apple says examples may include making a payment or changing critical security information such as a password.
The app then receives one of three risk levels:

Unknown: No evidence of suspicious activity was detected. Apple warns that this does not confirm the action is safe.Medium: Some signs of suspicious activity were detected.High: Significant signs of suspicious activity were detected.
Unknown: No evidence of suspicious activity was detected. Apple warns that this does not confirm the action is safe.
Medium: Some signs of suspicious activity were detected.
High: Significant signs of suspicious activity were detected.

From there, the app decides how to respond. It might ask you to verify your identity, delay an action or display a warning before letting you continue. That could give you one more opportunity to stop when a scammer is rushing you through a payment or account change.
How Apple's anti-scam feature decides something looks suspicious

Impersonation Risk Detection looks at signals related to how you are using your device. Apple says those signals can include interaction patterns, timing, context and basic sensor data. Apple's privacy documentation gives some additional examples. Your iPhone may consider whether you are sharing your screen as well as the approximate number of recent phone calls or emails you have received. It can combine that assessment with certain Apple Account information, including recent App Store downloads and purchases.

The goal is to look for unusual behavior that could suggest someone is guiding or pressuring you. However, there is an important limitation. This feature works only with third-party apps that support Apple's Impersonation Risk Detection system. Turning it on does not give every app on your iPhone automatic scam detection.
What Apple can see when you use Impersonation Risk Detection

Apple says it never analyzes the content of your Photos, Messages or Mail for this feature. The underlying device information used to create the assessment also stays protected from both Apple and the requesting app. There is still some information sharing you should understand before turning it on. Your iPhone creates an on-device assessment and sends that assessment, rather than the underlying device data, to Apple.

Apple can then combine it with certain Apple Account activity to generate the final risk signals. Apple also learns the category of activity you were attempting, such as signing in or making a payment. Apple says it does not learn which app requested the signals or the content of what you were doing inside the app. The requesting app receives the resulting risk level. It does not receive the underlying information Apple used to produce it.
Why the iPhone anti-scam setting is off by default

Apple requires you to choose whether supported apps can request Impersonation Risk Detection signals. As a result, Share with App Developers starts out turned off. That means simply updating your iPhone to iOS 27 does not activate the protection. You need to go into Settings and enable it yourself.

One warning from Apple really stands out. If somebody on the phone tells you to disable Impersonation Risk Detection, Apple says you might be dealing with a scammer. I would treat a request like that as a major red flag. Hang up and contact the company using a number or app you already trust.
Here's how to check the setting on an iPhone running iOS 27:
Open Settings.Tap Privacy & Security.Scroll down and tap Impersonation Risk Detection.Turn on Share with App Developers.If prompted, sign in to the App Store with your Apple Account.
Open Settings.
Tap Privacy & Security.
Scroll down and tap Impersonation Risk Detection.
Turn on Share with App Developers.
If prompted, sign in to the App Store with your Apple Account.

Apple says changes to this setting may take up to 24 hours to take effect. After you turn it on, you can return to Settings > Privacy & Security > Impersonation Risk Detection to see which apps have recently requested a risk assessment. You can also review why each app requested access and turn off access for individual apps.
Samsung Galaxy phones have built-in scam and spam protection

Samsung Galaxy phones also include tools designed to identify suspicious callers, although the exact features you see can vary by model, carrier and software version. On many Galaxy phones, Caller ID and spam protection is the main setting to check. Samsung uses technology from Hiya to identify suspected spam, scam and potential fraud calls, including numbers that aren't saved in your contacts.

Samsung also offers a separate real-time Scam detection feature on some compatible Galaxy phones running One UI 8.5 or higher. Samsung says that feature can analyze calls for scam patterns and alert you with a tone or vibration. However, that option does not appear on every Galaxy phone, even when the device is running current software. Samsung began rolling out One UI 9 in September 2026, starting with the Galaxy S26 series after its debut on Samsung's newest foldables. Feature availability can still depend on your model, carrier and region.
MAKE UNKNOWN CALLERS EXPLAIN WHY THEY'RE CALLING
Some smartphones can use Caller ID and spam protection to identify and block suspected spam and scam calls. (Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images)
On a Samsung Galaxy, the exact options can vary by model, carrier and software version. To check the protection available on your phone:

Open the Samsung Phone app.Tap the three vertical dots in the upper-right corner.Tap Settings.Tap Caller ID and spam protection.Make sure the main switch at the top is turned on.Turn on Block spam and scam calls.Choose either Block all spam and scam calls or Only block high-risk scam calls.
Open the Samsung Phone app.
Tap the three vertical dots in the upper-right corner.
Tap Settings.
Tap Caller ID and spam protection.
Make sure the main switch at the top is turned on.
Turn on Block spam and scam calls.
Choose either Block all spam and scam calls or Only block high-risk scam calls.

Samsung uses call-identification technology from Hiya to help identify suspected spam and scam callers, including numbers that aren't saved in your contacts. On compatible Galaxy phones, you may also see Call screening in the Phone app's settings. That feature can handle certain incoming calls before you answer. Samsung documents Call screening for compatible phones running One UI 8.5 or higher.
Pixel owners have Scam Detection for calls
Google takes a different approach on Pixel phones. Its Scam Detection feature can analyze a phone conversation in real time and warn you when the call shows patterns commonly associated with fraud.

In the U.S., Google currently supports call Scam Detection on eligible Pixel 6 and later devices, with some model-specific exceptions. Pixel 9 and newer models use Gemini Nano on the device for scam detection during calls.
Google says the feature works on the device. However, the company also warns that it cannot detect every scam, so a call that receives no warning should never automatically be considered safe.
To check it:
Open the Phone app.Tap the menu in the upper-right corner.Tap Settings.Tap Scam Detection.Turn on Scam Detection.
Open the Phone app.
Tap the menu in the upper-right corner.
Tap Settings.
Tap Scam Detection.
Turn on Scam Detection.

Call Scam Detection requires you to opt in. If Google detects patterns associated with a scam during an eligible call, your Pixel can warn you while the conversation is still happening. That's useful because many scams become more convincing once a criminal gets you talking. The scammer can adjust the story based on what you say and keep applying pressure.

Pixel owners have another protection worth checking. Scam Detection for chat messages can analyze new message notifications from supported apps and warn you when something looks suspicious. Google says this feature is available in the U.S. and several other countries. In the U.S., Scam Detection can also work with Gboard in select messaging apps and warn you as you begin responding to a suspicious message. Google expanded that capability with its September 2026 Pixel update. Unlike call Scam Detection, message Scam Detection is turned on by default.
Open Settings.Tap Security & privacy.Tap More security & privacy.Tap Scam Detection.Make sure Message scams is turned on.
Open Settings.
Tap Security & privacy.
Tap More security & privacy.
Tap Scam Detection.
Make sure Message scams is turned on.

Google says the feature runs in a secure, isolated environment. Your message content stays private and is not sent to Google unless you choose to share a message after receiving an alert. Google's September 2026 Pixel update is rolling out to supported Pixel devices running Android 17, so I would also make sure your Pixel has the latest available system update installed.
SCAMMERS KNOW THE BEST TIME TO TEXT YOU
Pixel phones can use Scam Detection during calls to warn you when a conversation shows signs of a likely scam. (Halfpoint/Getty Images)
Apple, Pixel and Galaxy approach scam detection differently

These features aren't interchangeable, which is actually helpful. Apple's Impersonation Risk Detection focuses on signs that you may be getting manipulated while performing sensitive actions inside supported apps. Pixel can watch for scam patterns during calls and suspicious messages. Samsung can analyze supported calls for scam patterns.

A scam may also move between several channels. Someone could text you first, get you on the phone and eventually convince you to open a legitimate banking app. Having protections at different points in that process gives your phone more opportunities to warn you before money or account information changes hands.
What to do when your phone warns you about a possible scam
Treat a scam warning as a reason to stop and verify what is happening. Don't keep following the caller's instructions while trying to decide whether the warning is right.
Hang up if you're on a suspicious call. Then contact the bank, government agency or company directly using its official app, website or a phone number you already trust.
The same goes for payment alerts. Open your financial institution's official app yourself and check the account. Don't use a phone number or link supplied by the person who contacted you.
Also remember the reverse. No warning does not prove that a call, message or transaction is legitimate. Apple and Google both make clear that these systems can miss scams.
Don't rely on your phone to catch every scam

I like these features, but I would use them as another layer rather than my only protection. Scammers constantly change their scripts. They can spoof caller ID, impersonate companies you know and use personal information to make a fake story sound believable.
If someone unexpectedly asks for a password, verification code or payment, slow down. A demand to transfer money to a "safe account" should also send up an immediate warning sign.

Strong antivirus software can help protect against malicious links, phishing sites and malware that may appear alongside these scams. A password manager can also help by generating unique passwords and making it harder to reuse the same credentials across accounts. The phone can warn you. You still get the final say.
Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

What I find most interesting about these scam protections is how close they're getting to the moment when someone might actually lose money. For years, we've relied heavily on spam filters and caller warnings to keep criminals away. Now our phones are starting to look for what happens after the conversation begins. Apple's approach in iOS 27 could be especially useful when a scammer has already convinced you to open a legitimate app and take action yourself. Pixel can warn about suspicious calls and messages, while some compatible Galaxy phones can detect scam patterns during calls.

Would you trust your phone enough to stop a payment after it warned you that you might be getting scammed, or would you still need to see more proof before changing course? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: What strangers can learn from your political donation
summary: Federal Election Commission records can expose your name, address, employer and donation history once contributions exceed the $200 threshold.
story: Fox News hosts Bill Hemmer, Dana Perino and Shannon Bream, alongside guests Trey Gowdy and Karl Rove, analyze pivotal Supreme Court decisions. The court upheld transgender sports bans, allowing states to block participation by biological males. It also ruled on campaign finance limits, striking down restrictions on party spending. Additionally, the Court upheld birthright citizenship, rejecting challenges to the 14th Amendment.

Search your name in the Federal Election Commission's contribution database or on a campaign finance site such as OpenSecrets.org. If you have given enough to trigger federal disclosure requirements, you may be surprised by how much information can be connected to your donation. Depending on the record, that can include your name, mailing address, employer, occupation, donation amount and the political committee that received your money.

This is not a data breach. It is part of federal campaign finance disclosure law. And once information about you is public, it can potentially be combined with personal details found elsewhere online. Here's what your political donation can reveal, how that information can be used and what you can do to reduce the rest of your exposure.
Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist.
See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com.
DEM FUNDRAISING GIANT MAKES DAMNING ADMISSION AS GOP PROBES FOREIGN DONATION ALLEGATIONS
A simple online search can show how easily public records and people-search profiles connect information about you. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What's actually in your political donation record

Federal campaigns generally must itemize an individual's contributions once that person's contributions exceed $200 in the aggregate during the applicable election cycle. For PACs and party committees, the reporting period can be based on the calendar year.
An itemized federal contribution can include:
Your full nameYour mailing addressYour employerYour occupationThe date of the contributionThe amount you contributedThe candidate or committee receiving the contribution
Your full name
Your mailing address
Your employer
Your occupation
The date of the contribution
The amount you contributed
The candidate or committee receiving the contribution

One contribution may not seem revealing on its own. The privacy concern grows when those details can be connected with information already available through people-search sites, public records and data brokers.

Pay particular attention to your employer and occupation. A people-search profile may already include addresses and relatives, while a campaign finance record can add another verified detail about where you work or what you do. Want to see how much of your personal information is already exposed online? Use the free data exposure scanner at CyberGuy.com to check.
How public donation information can add to your online profile

A campaign finance record alone provides only part of the picture. Other public sources and people-search sites may reveal much more. Sites such as Spokeo, Whitepages and BeenVerified can contain address histories, possible relatives, phone numbers, email addresses and property information. When information from several sources lines up, someone researching you may be able to build a much more detailed profile. Here is how those pieces can connect.

Names are rarely unique. An address, employer or occupation can help distinguish you from another person with the same name. That makes publicly available information useful for confirming that someone has found the right person.

Once someone has your name and location, people-search services may make it easier to identify possible relatives. Your political donation record does not normally list your family members. However, information found elsewhere can connect your identity with a spouse, adult child, parent or other relative. That can create opportunities for impersonation scams and highly personalized phishing attempts.
HOW HURRICANE CHARITY SCAMS TARGET YOU BEFORE STORMS HIT
Political donations can create public records that reveal more personal information than many donors realize. (Graeme Sloan for The Washington Post/Getty Images)

Knowing where you work gives a scammer another detail that can make an email, text or phone call feel legitimate. A phishing message that mentions your actual employer or professional role can be more convincing than a generic message because it contains information you recognize. That is why limiting the amount of personal information available across the web can reduce what criminals have to work with.

Scammers frequently imitate legitimate organizations, charities and fundraising groups. The FTC warns that fraudulent fundraisers may use familiar-sounding names, pressure people to act quickly or falsely claim someone donated before. There is also an important legal protection around federal campaign finance data. Information copied or obtained from FEC reports about individual contributors cannot legally be sold or used to solicit political or charitable contributions or for commercial purposes. Criminals do not always follow the law, of course. Still, you should be suspicious of any unexpected fundraising request that seems unusually familiar with your personal history.
What if you donated through ActBlue or WinRed?

Using an online fundraising platform does not automatically make a federal contribution private. For earmarked federal contributions exceeding $200, reporting requirements can include the contributor's name, mailing address, employer, occupation, date and amount.

State campaign finance rules are different. Disclosure thresholds and the information made public vary by state, so a contribution that is not itemized under federal rules could still be subject to separate state reporting requirements.
What data removal services can and cannot remove

This is an important limitation to understand. A data removal service generally cannot erase legally required government records such as federal campaign finance filings. That means an FEC filing is not something a removal service can simply delete. What these services can address is the personal information surrounding that public record.

Your campaign finance record might identify your name, mailing address, employer and occupation. Meanwhile, data brokers may have phone numbers, email addresses, relatives, previous addresses and other personal information. Removing those additional profiles can make it harder for someone to connect separate pieces of information about you into one detailed profile.

Some data removal services automatically send opt-out requests to data brokers and continue checking for information that may reappear. Others also offer custom removal requests for websites where your personal information is exposed. However, legal and technical restrictions still apply, especially when the information comes from government records or other sources that are required to remain public.

You can also submit removal requests yourself. The process takes more time, but reducing the amount of personal information spread across people-search sites and data brokers can make it harder for strangers or scammers to build a detailed profile about you. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.
What to do right now
Here are several steps I would take to see what information about you is already exposed.

Start by searching your name through the FEC's campaign finance records and OpenSecrets.org. Look closely at what information is associated with your contributions. Do not assume every result belongs to you, especially if you have a common name.
THE SECRET LIST THAT TELLS SCAMMERS YOU'RE AN EASY TARGET
Scammers can use personal details found online to make phishing messages and fraudulent requests feel more convincing. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

For federal candidate committees, individual contributions generally become itemized once your aggregate contributions exceed $200 during an election cycle. PAC and party committee reporting rules can use a calendar-year threshold instead. Also remember that some committees voluntarily disclose contributions below the amount they are required to itemize.

State disclosure laws vary significantly. Your state may use a different reporting threshold or disclose different information than the federal system, so check the campaign finance database maintained by your state election authority.

Do not assume a message is legitimate because it mentions a candidate, organization or contribution you recognize. Instead of clicking a link in an unexpected email or text, visit the organization's official website independently. Also be wary of anyone pressuring you to donate immediately or asking you to pay through gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency.

You may not be able to remove a legally required campaign finance filing, but you can reduce the additional information available about you through data brokers and people-search sites. You can submit opt-out requests yourself or use a data removal service to handle many of those requests for you. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

I think the surprising part here is how much information can become connected to something as simple as making a political contribution. Federal disclosure rules can make your name, mailing address, employer, occupation and contribution history publicly available once you cross the reporting threshold. You cannot erase a legally required FEC filing with a data removal service, but you can reduce the other information surrounding it. I would search my own name, see what is visible and then work on removing the people-search and data broker profiles that make it easier for strangers or scammers to fill in the rest of the picture.
How much personal information do you think should become public when someone makes a political contribution? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: The best defense against high-tech AI scams is low-tech skepticism, expert warns
summary: Cybersecurity expert Morgan Wright says human skepticism remains the strongest defense against AI-driven phishing scams and voice cloning fraud schemes.
story: From voice cloning to fake arrests, cyber expert Morgan Wright breaks down how scammers use high-tech tools to exploit basic human fears.
As artificial intelligence rapidly evolves to make financial scams hyperrealistic, cybersecurity experts warn that the best defense isn't sophisticated detection software.
It's good old-fashioned human skepticism.

While adversarial states like China and Russia leverage AI on a global scale, average Americans are most frequently targeted by cybercriminals looking to exploit personal vulnerabilities for a quick payout, according to cybersecurity expert Morgan Wright.

"Let's go back to around 1860, when Edgar Allan Poe wrote, ‘Believe nothing that you hear and only one half that you see,’" Wright told Fox News Digital. "That advice is as good now as it was 160 years ago."
AI VOICE SCAMS CAN CLONE YOUR FAMILY’S VOICE

Cybercriminals are using artificial intelligence to refine their scams, targeting everyday Americans with voice cloning and tech that removes language barriers to make it easy to swindle unsuspecting people, experts say. (Getty Images)

AI technology has allowed bad actors to automate and scale personalized fraud schemes against everyday citizens. Generative tools eliminate language barriers, draft convincing phishing texts and generate hyperrealistic voice and video clones.

By capturing just a few seconds of audio — often scraped from social media — fraudsters can convincingly replicate the voice of a family member. Wright pointed to the case of Deborah Del Mastro, a California mother who lost thousands of dollars after scammers used AI to clone her daughter’s voice to stage a terrifying kidnapping hoax.
THE FAMILY GROUP CHAT IS A GOLDMINE FOR SCAMMERS
"It's my daughter's voice," Del Mastro recalled during an interview on The CyberGuy Report podcast. "And she's having a panic attack."
Convinced her daughter was in immediate danger, Del Mastro transferred more than $5,000 to the scammers before realizing she had been swindled.
FRAUD EXPERT WARNS AI IS HELPING CRIMINALS OUTPACE THE GOVERNMENT: 'DON'T HAVE THE RIGHT TOOLS'

"When you can fool a mother, that's how good these things are getting," Wright said of the voice-cloning technology. "What they do is use manipulation, influence and deceit. The more urgent I can make it sound, the more you're going to lower your guard and take action."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE U.S. NEWS

An illustration created on June 9, 2023, shows a smartphone recording in front of a voice-clicking screen in Los Angeles. Experts say artificial intelligence's biggest peril is its ability to blur the boundaries between reality and fiction, handing cybercriminals a cheap and effective technology to exploit.  (Chris Delmas/AFP via Getty Images)

Wright, who has trained federal, state and local law enforcement in behavioral analysis, interviewing and interrogation — including teams at the FBI and the National Security Agency — emphasized that every scam relies on basic psychological triggers.
His primary advice for anyone on the receiving end of a suspicious call or message is to pause before reacting.
"We're not storming the beaches at Normandy; you're not going to get arrested," Wright said. "No law enforcement agency sends you an unsolicited text saying you're about to get arrested."
While AI platforms roll out updated security features, scammers continuously find ways around them, making software-based detection a constant moving target.

The OpenAI logo is displayed on a smartphone screen in Creteil, France, Oct. 1, 2026, as OpenAI begins rolling out Dots in ChatGPT, its new system of autonomous AI agents. (Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"We hear about all the different models from xAI, Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini. They change models constantly," Wright said.
"So, when the model changes, how effective is [detection software]? We don't know because this stuff is moving so fast. What you see today will be drastically different tomorrow."
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Your phone says it's updated. Check other settings, too
summary: iPhone, Google Pixel and Samsung Galaxy each handle security updates differently, and one screen saying "up to date" may not tell the whole story.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Most of us have done it. A software update pops up when we're busy, so we swipe it away and figure we'll deal with it later. Then later turns into tomorrow, and suddenly that update has been sitting there much longer than we planned. There's another wrinkle. Even when your phone appears to be running the latest software, there may be another security update or protection worth checking.

Apple, Google and Samsung all have ways to get security fixes onto your phone between larger software releases. However, they handle those protections differently. If you use an iPhone running iOS 27, a Google Pixel running Android 17 or a Samsung Galaxy running the latest software available for your model, there are a few places I would check right now.
Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist.
See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com
TURN ON LOST-PHONE SETTINGS BEFORE YOU NEED THEM
Keeping your phone’s software current can help close security holes before attackers have a chance to exploit them. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Your iPhone can get security fixes between full updates

Apple has a feature called Background Security Improvements that can deliver certain security protections without waiting for another complete iOS update. Apple says these lightweight releases can protect Safari, WebKit and other system libraries. That gives Apple another way to address certain vulnerabilities between larger software releases. iOS 27 is Apple's latest public iPhone software, so make sure your compatible iPhone is running it before checking the security setting below.
Open SettingsTap GeneralTap Software UpdateInstall any available update
Open Settings
Tap General
Tap Software Update
Install any available update
If your iPhone says iOS 27 and no newer update appears, you're current at the time you check.
Once your iPhone is updated:
Open SettingsTap Privacy & SecurityTap Background Security ImprovementsTurn on Automatically Install
Open Settings
Tap Privacy & Security
Tap Background Security Improvements
Turn on Automatically Install

Your iPhone can then automatically install eligible Background Security Improvements as Apple releases them. These smaller protections do not replace regular iOS updates. You should still install full updates because they can contain additional security patches, bug fixes and broader changes throughout the operating system.
HOW TO FIND COMPROMISED PASSWORDS ON IPHONE AND ANDROID
On iPhone, Background Security Improvements can install certain protections automatically between full iOS updates. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Samsung Galaxy phones have their own update process

Samsung Galaxy phones run Android, but Samsung adds its One UI software on top. Because of that, Galaxy owners often see different menus than Pixel owners. As of today, One UI 9 is Samsung's latest interface. Samsung began its U.S. rollout on Sept. 16 with the Galaxy S26 Ultra, S26+ and S26 after One UI 9 debuted on its newest foldable phones. However, you should not assume that every Galaxy phone eligible for One UI 9 has received it yet. Samsung rolls updates out by device, carrier and region. Whether your Galaxy has One UI 9 already or is still waiting for it, you can check directly from Settings.
On a current Galaxy phone:
Open SettingsScroll down and tap Software updateTap Check for updates
Open Settings
Scroll down and tap Software update
Tap Check for updates

Depending on your Galaxy model or carrier, Samsung says you may instead see Download and install, System updates or Check for software updates. If an update appears, follow the on-screen instructions to install it. You can also check which version your phone is running by going to:
SettingsAbout phoneSoftware information
Settings
About phone
Software information
That screen shows details about the software currently installed on your Galaxy.
Galaxy phones also use Google's underlying system services, so there is one more update worth checking.
Open SettingsTap About phoneTap Software informationTap Google Play system updateFollow the prompts if an update is available
Open Settings
Tap About phone
Tap Software information
Tap Google Play system update
Follow the prompts if an update is available
If you have a Samsung Galaxy, you may be running the latest Samsung software available for your phone and still have a separate Google Play system update waiting to install.
Samsung Galaxy phones can have a separate Google Play system update waiting even when Samsung’s own software looks current. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Google Pixel uses a different security update system

Pixel owners will not find Apple's Background Security Improvements setting. Google handles the job differently. As of today, supported Pixel phones are running Android 17. Google began rolling out its September 2026 Pixel software update on Sept. 15, while the October 2026 Android Security Bulletin was published Oct. 5. Pixel phones receive regular Android software updates that can include security fixes. They also receive Google Play system updates, which let Google update certain parts of Android separately from a complete operating system release. That means Pixel owners should check two areas rather than assuming one update screen tells the whole story.
On a Pixel running Android 17:
Open SettingsTap SystemTap Software updateCheck your update statusFollow the on-screen instructions if an update is available
Open Settings
Tap System
Tap Software update
Check your update status
Follow the on-screen instructions if an update is available

Google says supported Pixel devices running Android 17 are receiving the September 2026 software update in phases. Your exact availability can depend on the device and carrier. Pixel phones can also install downloaded Android updates in the background. However, you may need to restart the phone before the update becomes active.
You should check this separately:
Open SettingsTap About phoneTap Android versionCheck Android security updateCheck Google Play system update
Open Settings
Tap About phone
Tap Android version
Check Android security update
Check Google Play system update

If an update is available, follow the prompts to install it. The Google Play system update can be easy to overlook because the name sounds like an update for the Play Store. It actually helps Google update underlying parts of Android and its system services.
Pixel owners should check both the Android security update and Google Play system update to make sure every layer is current. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Don't assume automatic updates mean you're fully current

I'm a fan of automatic updates because they remove one more thing you have to remember. Still, I wouldn't turn them on and completely forget about them. An update might need your phone to restart before the protection becomes active. Your device may also be waiting for Wi-Fi, sufficient battery power or the next stage of a phased rollout. That's why I like checking the update screens every so often. If you see an update waiting, finish it. A downloaded security fix cannot fully protect you if your phone still needs a restart before activating it.
Older phones may eventually stop getting security fixes

Your phone can keep working long after the manufacturer stops supporting it. That's where things can get tricky. If a phone no longer receives security updates, newly discovered vulnerabilities may remain unpatched. That can leave an otherwise usable device exposed to security problems that newer phones have already fixed. Apple supports iPhones with software and security updates for years, but older models eventually stop receiving the newest iOS releases. If you're wondering whether your current iPhone has reached that point, check out our guide on whether it's time to upgrade to a new iPhone at CyberGuy.com.

Google currently provides seven years of operating system and security updates for Pixel 8 and newer phones, measured from when each device first became available in the U.S. Samsung also provides extended software support for many newer Galaxy devices, although the support period depends on the model. If your iPhone, Pixel or Samsung Galaxy no longer receives security updates, that should become part of the decision about when it's time to replace it. If you're thinking about upgrading your Pixel or Samsung Galaxy, take a look at our Top Android phones of 2026 for our current picks at cyberguy.com .
Keep your phone protected beyond software updates

Updates close known security holes, but criminals have plenty of other ways to go after your phone. Phishing texts can trick you into handing over passwords. Fake websites can imitate Apple, Google or a financial institution. Malicious apps can also create problems if you install software from an untrusted source.

That's why I would combine current software with a strong device passcode, biometric protection and the theft-protection features available on your phone. I would also use a password manager to create and store strong, unique passwords for your accounts. Strong antivirus software can add another layer by helping detect malicious links, risky downloads and other threats before they cause trouble. I like security protections that can do some of the work for me. Still, seeing "up to date" on one screen does not always mean you've checked every security layer your phone uses. On my iPhone, I'd look at Background Security Improvements and Software Update. If you're carrying a Pixel, check both the Android update and Google Play system update. Galaxy owners should check Samsung's software update and Google's system update too. Then finish the job when your phone asks for a restart. That extra minute could be what finally activates the protection you thought was already there.

title: AI voice scam traps mom in 5-hour kidnapping nightmare
summary: Deborah Del Mastro heard what sounded like her daughter's terrified voice on the phone, launching a five-hour virtual kidnapping scam ordeal.
story: California woman Deborah Del Mastro said she was having breakfast when a caller using a suspected AI voice clone claimed to have kidnapped her daughter. (The CyberGuy Report Podcast)

I want you to think about the voice of someone you love. You know how that person sounds when they're laughing, and you also know the voice you would hear if they were terrified. So what would you do if your phone rang, and you heard that voice begging you for help? That's what happened to Deborah Del Mastro.

I recently sat down with Deborah on "The CyberGuy Report" podcast to hear her tell this story in her own words. Even after everything she has been through, you can hear how deeply the experience still affects her. Months after the scam, she also told a U.S. Senate committee that she remained "completely traumatized."

The California mother and Navy veteran was having breakfast with her husband when a local number appeared on her phone. The man on the other end claimed a Mexican drug cartel had taken her 37-year-old daughter Sarah. Then Deborah heard the voice that made the threat feel terrifyingly real. "It's my daughter's voice," she told me. "And she's having a panic attack."

For the next five and a half hours, the caller threatened Deborah and her family, sent her and her husband from place to place and demanded thousands of dollars. What Deborah didn't know was that the story unfolding on the phone was very different from what was actually happening to Sarah.
Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist.
See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com
THE FAMILY GROUP CHAT IS A GOLDMINE FOR SCAMMERS
Deborah Del Mastro, left, and her daughter Sarah, whose voice Deborah says sounded exactly like the one she heard during the kidnapping scam. (Deborah Del Mastro)
The phone call that changed everything

The call started strangely enough. "I get a local phone call, my area code," Deborah told me. When she answered, the man asked, "Who is this?" Deborah turned the question back on him, and he replied that he was "someone you need to talk to."

Then he asked whether Deborah's daughter was prone to panic attacks. That question immediately got her attention. Deborah could hear commotion in the background before the caller put someone else on the line. She heard Sarah. The voice was crying and struggling to breathe. "I'm so sorry, Mom. I'm so scared," Deborah remembers hearing. "It was exactly her voice," she told me.

There was another reason Deborah believed she was hearing her daughter. Sarah had recently gone through a breakup, and Deborah had heard her daughter sobbing like that only days earlier. The sound on the phone matched something painfully familiar, which made the call even more convincing.
Then came the threat of a Mexican drug cartel

The man told Deborah that Sarah had witnessed something she was never supposed to see in a parking lot. He claimed ties to a Mexican drug cartel and said Sarah had her phone out when she saw what happened. According to Deborah, his boss had ordered him to take her.

Then he told Deborah what they wanted. "They were going to sell her for $20,000 unless I could come up with the money," Deborah told me. The threat became even darker. She said the caller repeatedly talked about selling Sarah and suggested she could "pay her way in other ways," leaving Deborah terrified that the criminals could sexually traffic her daughter. At that point, she believed violent criminals had Sarah.
The scammer made sure Deborah stayed on the phone

One of his first instructions was to bring a phone charger. "He tells me that I better charge my phone or bring a phone charger because if my phone dies before we're finished, I'll never see her again," Deborah recalled. That told me a lot about how carefully this scam was run. The caller needed control. He demanded that Deborah keep the phone connected so he could hear what was happening around her. He wanted to know when she moved, what she was doing and who she was talking to.

At one point, Deborah muted the call so she could speak privately with her husband. The caller noticed and began screaming. He warned her against trying "funny business." Deborah told me, "He wants to keep my phone open right here so he can hear everything." That control continued for five and a half hours.
YOUR FAMILY COULD BE ONE PHONE CALL FROM A BANK SCAM
Deborah Del Mastro with her daughter Sarah, whose safety became the only thing on Deborah's mind during the five-and-a-half-hour ordeal. (Deborah Del Mastro)
'Bargaining with the devil'

The caller initially wanted $20,000. Deborah didn't have it. "We just don't have that," she remembers telling him. So she started negotiating for what she believed was her daughter's life. "Now I'm bargaining with the devil," she told me. Deborah said she had roughly $2,000 in savings. The caller instructed her to go to a nearby Walmart and use MoneyGram to wire money to Mexico. She went, keeping the phone where he could hear everything happening around her.

The man warned that people were watching her in the parking lot and claimed undercover police officers were nearby. He also gave Deborah a story to use if anyone questioned the transfer. The caller told her to say she was helping a relative with medical expenses. "Be discreet," she remembers him telling her. That detail bothers me because scammers often go beyond demanding money. They prepare victims to get around the very people who might recognize that something is wrong.
Nobody stopped her

Deborah moved from location to location sending money. When I asked whether anyone challenged her or asked whether she was OK, her answer was immediate. "No. No. Not at all." By then, the scammer had already given her a cover story. He had also spent hours convincing Deborah that talking to someone could get Sarah killed.

In the end, Deborah sent $5,400 through four separate transactions using MoneyGram and Western Union. She said the transfers took all the accessible money she and her husband had. Later, she put it to me another way: "We were held hostage for 5.5 hours." Deborah and her husband could physically move, but emotionally, the caller had them exactly where he wanted them.
Deborah heard Sarah a second time

Several hours into the call, Deborah kept asking to speak with her daughter again. Eventually, the caller agreed, but even that conversation came with instructions. He told Deborah exactly what she could say: "This nightmare is nearly over. We're going to come get you as soon as we can."
Then Sarah's voice responded. "I'm so sorry, Mom. I love you." I asked Deborah again whether it really sounded like her daughter. "It was her voice," she said. "It was absolutely her voice."
Immediately afterward, another man came onto the phone. Deborah described him as an "enforcer" whose threats sounded even harsher. Soon, the scammers demanded more money.
A mother was already thinking about her daughter's life afterward

There's something Deborah later said that gives you an idea of where her mind had gone during those hours. While her husband drove and the caller listened over the phone, Deborah spent much of the trip sitting silently. Instead of wondering whether this could be a scam, her mind went to Sarah and whether she would survive it.

Deborah was already trying to figure out how her daughter would get through life after an experience like this. Paying the ransom was only part of what was running through her mind. She believed something terrible had already happened to her child and started thinking about how she would help Sarah recover afterward. That shows you how completely real this had become to her.
The caller finally says Sarah has been released

Eventually, the man told Deborah the ordeal was over. He claimed they had released Sarah outside a Walmart where Deborah and her husband were waiting. "Go get her," Deborah remembers him saying. Then he hung up.

Deborah could see the front entrance, so she got out of the car and looked for her daughter. Sarah wasn't there. For a moment, Deborah thought the criminals still had her even after taking every dollar she could reach. She frantically looked around before finally calling Sarah herself. Her daughter answered. "Hi, Mom. What's going on?" Sarah was at work.
Deborah and Sarah, whose close relationship made the fake emergency call especially convincing when Deborah heard what sounded like Sarah crying for help. (Deborah Del Mastro)
'I'd never been so relieved to be scammed in my life'

For more than five hours, Deborah believed people were holding her daughter and might kill her or sell her. Then Sarah simply answered her phone from work. "I'd never been so relieved to be scammed in my life," Deborah told me.

She believes she screamed in the parking lot before the tears came. Deborah told Sarah she loved her, and after work, Sarah came to her parents' home. Her mother hugged her and sobbed. The family then went to the local police department to report what had happened. Losing the money hurt, but Sarah was alive.
Sarah immediately suspected an AI voice clone

When Deborah explained what had happened, Sarah had an immediate reaction. "Mom, that was probably an AI clone of my voice," Deborah remembers her saying. Both of Deborah's adult children work in IT, so they already knew this kind of technology existed. Deborah didn't. "I didn't know," she recalls.

Deborah firmly believes she heard an artificial intelligence-generated version of Sarah's voice. We do know the technology exists, and federal authorities have warned about criminals using it. The FTC says scammers can take a short clip of someone's real voice, including audio posted online, and use voice-cloning technology to make a call sound like that person.
How virtual kidnapping scams work
The underlying scam has been around much longer than today's AI tools. The FBI calls it "virtual kidnapping." Criminals claim they have taken someone you love even though no kidnapping occurred.

One classic warning sign closely matches Deborah's experience. The FBI says virtual kidnappers often work hard to keep victims on the phone so they can't check where their loved one actually is. The agency has also warned about ransom demands involving wire transfers to Mexico.

More recently, the FBI warned that criminals are using altered media in virtual kidnapping schemes. AI can make an old scam much more convincing. Deborah put it perfectly: "It is an old scam with new technology."
She's a Navy veteran who usually runs toward a crisis

One reaction Deborah still encounters is the question some people ask after a scam: Why didn't you hang up? Why didn't you know? Why didn't you tell someone? She understands those questions, but she also knows what was happening inside that call.

As a Navy veteran, Deborah describes herself as someone who stays calm in a crisis. "I always say I am the person that runs to the fire, not away from it." Yet the voice on the phone convinced her completely that Sarah was in danger.

That's something I want people to remember before judging anyone who falls for one of these calls. You can know about scams and handle pressure well. Then someone puts the terrified voice of your child in your ear. Criminals understand exactly what kind of emotional reaction they're trying to trigger.
The financial damage hit hard too

The $5,400 represented every readily available dollar Deborah and her husband could access. She says they are seniors living on Social Security along with income from other work, so the loss hit them hard. The following morning, Deborah went to Facebook and told her community what had happened. She also warned that criminals now had "high-tech capability."

Friends began sending money, but Deborah initially resisted because she didn't want to profit from what happened. Eventually, they convinced her to create a fundraiser on GoFundMe limited to replacing what the couple had lost. Her community raised the money back. That support couldn't erase the five-and-a-half-hour ordeal, but it meant a great deal to Deborah. Her community had shown up for her before, and they showed up again.
7 ways to protect your family from an AI voice kidnapping scam

You don't have to become an expert at detecting synthetic audio. In fact, I wouldn't build your family's defense around your ability to recognize a fake voice. A better approach is to decide now how your family will verify an emergency.

If someone claims your child, spouse or another relative has been kidnapped or injured, contact that person directly at the number you already have saved. If they don't answer, try someone who should know where they are. The FTC specifically recommends verifying the story through a phone number you know belongs to your loved one.
Choose a word or phrase that someone couldn't easily discover through social media. The FBI recommends establishing a family code word for situations like virtual kidnapping scams.

Deborah also recommends a safe word now, although her experience shows why you need more than one way to verify an emergency. "There was no way I could have done any of that in this particular situation," she told me. The caller controlled when she could speak with Sarah, so don't make a safe word your family's only verification method.

After the scam, Deborah and Sarah began using a location-sharing app so each could see where the other was. Apple and Google also offer built-in location-sharing options. If you want to set this up on your phone, see our guide on how to share your whereabouts in any situation using your cell phone.

Location sharing comes with its own privacy considerations, so only share your location with people you trust. An agreed-upon way to check someone's whereabouts can give your family another verification tool during an emergency.

Secrecy played a major role in Deborah's ordeal. The caller told her not to speak to anyone, listened during the transactions and gave her a fake explanation to use if someone asked questions. The FTC says urgency and secrecy are common characteristics of family emergency scams. If someone claims a loved one's survival depends on keeping you from contacting anyone else, treat that as a major warning.
Scammers like payment methods that move money quickly and make recovery difficult. The FTC specifically warns about emergency scammers demanding wire transfers, cryptocurrency and gift cards.

If you've already sent money, contact the bank or transfer company immediately and ask whether it can stop or recall the transaction. Then report what happened to local police and the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov.

Your name, relatives, phone numbers and other family connections can appear across people-search sites and data broker databases. That information can make a fake emergency more believable. I've tried manually removing my own information from these sites before, and keeping up with it can turn into a job because the information often returns.

A data removal service can help automate some of that work by requesting removal of your information from people-search sites and data broker databases. You can also learn more in our CyberGuy guide on removing your personal information from the web. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

This may be the most useful conversation you have with your family this week. Tell them that a familiar voice can be faked. Agree that nobody sends emergency money until someone verifies the situation another way. A few minutes spent setting that expectation today could become extremely important when someone tries to scare you tomorrow.
Kurt's key takeaways

I've talked with a lot of scam victims over the years, and Deborah's story hit me hard. This wasn't some robotic impersonation that immediately made her suspicious. The voice sounded like her daughter having the kind of panic attack Deborah had heard before. For more than five hours, this guy kept her terrified and focused on one thing: getting Sarah home alive.

What stays with me most is where Deborah's mind went during that ordeal. Sitting in the car, she was already wondering how she would help Sarah recover from whatever these supposed kidnappers had done to her. That's a parent's mind at work. The money came later. Sarah came first.

I don't think the answer is expecting people to become experts at spotting fake audio. As the technology improves, a convincing voice could fool any of us. Instead, build another way to verify an emergency before one happens. Have a safe word, call your loved one directly and check with someone who may be physically near them. If your family feels comfortable using location sharing, set that up ahead of time.

Most importantly, talk about this with the people you love. Deborah had no idea this kind of voice scam was possible before that phone rang. Now she's sharing what happened because she doesn't want another parent sitting in a parking lot wondering whether their child is coming home. Watch or listen to my full conversation with Deborah on The CyberGuy Report podcast at CyberGuy.com.

If you heard what sounded exactly like your child or spouse crying and begging you not to hang up, would you remember to verify the call before sending money? What does your family have in place right now? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Lawyers for Charlie Kirk's accused assassin Tyler Robinson want cameras banned after report on taxpayer burden
summary: Tyler Robinson's defense lawyers argue that cameras at the upcoming hearing could threaten his right to a fair trial in the Charlie Kirk case.
story: A trial is ordered for Charlie Kirk's alleged killer after Utah District Court Judge Tony Graf rules that the prosecution can proceed with the case. Tyler Robinson pleads not guilty to all seven counts, including aggravated murder, which carries a potential death penalty.

Lawyers for accused Charlie Kirk assassin Tyler Robinson are again asking a Utah judge to block cameras from the courtroom, this time ahead of a hearing where a trial date could be set — as they warn that scrutiny over the cost of his defense may be creating a risk to his right to a fair trial.

The hearing is not expected to include witness testimony, but Robinson's lawyers argue that ongoing coverage of Kirk's murder could have an "incremental adverse effect" that outweighs the benefit of video coverage to the public's understanding of court proceedings.

"Only a few weeks ago, the media reported on costs associated with the defense," his lawyers wrote Monday in an opposition filing from local media to send a camera to cover the Oct. 23 hearing. "Against that backdrop, statements by defense counsel at the upcoming proceeding concerning the time and resources necessary to prepare this case are likely to be examined and disseminated in real time through social media and other media channels and viewed through the lens of cost, rather than in the context of Mr. Robinson’s constitutional rights to the effective assistance of counsel, a fair trial, due process of law, and a reliable penalty determination."

Tyler Robinson, left, accused in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, points with defense attorney Kathryn Nester during a hearing in 4th District Court in Provo on Friday, Jan. 16, 2026. (Bethany Baker/The Salt Lake Tribune via Pool)

title: NYPD detective who survived stabbing attack makes first public remarks since leaving hospital
summary: NYPD Detective Jose Mercedes speaks out after two illegal immigrants from the Dominican Republic allegedly stabbed him seven times in the Bronx.
story: NYPD Detective Jose Mercedes holds a news conference at the Detectives' Endowment Association headquarters to speak publicly for the first time after surviving an attempted robbery in the Bronx where he was stabbed seven times.

The NYPD detective who survived a robbery in which two illegal immigrants allegedly stabbed him 10 times in the Bronx thanked his colleagues, paramedics and others involved in saving his life after her fought of the attackers, speaking publicly for the first time since checking out of Jacobi Medical Center.

"I want to thank the 52 [precinct] NYPD officers that responded and just gave me my aid and helped me in this difficult time that I was going through where I, I almost died," he told reporters. "And then the NYPD, [Emergency Services Unit]. They just demonstrated their calmness and their professionalism…in rendering aid to me and applying tourniquets to both of my arms and then inspecting my body for further injuries."

Jose Mercedes, a 33-year-old detective with 10 years on the job, was off-duty and cleaning the trunk of his personal vehicle when two men attacked him from behind, the NYPD said previously. Despite his injuries, he chased after them before they sped away on an e-bike.
NYPD DETECTIVE RELEASED FROM HOSPITAL AFTER BEING STABBED MULTIPLE TIMES IN BRONX

NYPD Detective Jose Mercedes speaks outside the Detectives Endowment Association headquarters after surviving a robbery in which two illegal immigrants allegedly stabbed him 10 times and stole a gold necklace that he said was a gift from his mother. (Fox News)
Mercedes said he was on vacation, not working, when he went through a "very scary time."

The suspects, identified as D’Angelo Caraballo, 25, and Sneider Mejia, 24, allegedly fled to Massachusetts, where they were later arrested in a basement hideout. They are being held without bail and are expected to face attempted murder charges once extradited to New York.
Mercedes said he told his attackers that he was a police officer and "they didn't care."
"I told them in English, I told them in Spanish that I was a police officer," he said. "They didn't care."

Dangelo Rafael Jean Caraballo, 25, left, and Sneider Mejia Bautista, 24, both Dominican citizens living illegally in the United States, are accused of stabbing off-duty NYPD Detective Jose Mercedes. (Department of Homeland Security; NYPD)
Both are illegal immigrants from the Dominican Republic with criminal records, Fox News Digital reported previously.
Mercedes, who is also of Dominican descent, was asked if he was concerned that people would use his case to push a deportation agenda.
"I dedicate my life to investigating crime, and I think that it's very important to keep our community safe for all of us," he said.
SEND US A TIP

"These perpetrators, they're illegal, their prior crimes, I'm calling out they need to do 25 years to life," said Scott Munro, the president of the Detectives Endowment Association. "They stabbed an NYPD detective. They didn't know at first. He told them over and over, I'm a police officer. I'm a New York City detective. And he continued to get stabbed."
Mercedes had chased his attackers for multiple blocks before they got away, Munro said. Then a group of good Samaritans helped him.
Caraballo had been arrested in December 2024 and released before Immigration and Customs Enforcement could lodge a detainer request.
DHS DEMANDS NEW YORK SANCTUARY POLITICIANS HONOR DETAINER FOR MAN CONVICTED OF RAPING CORPSE ON SUBWAY
Detective Jose Mercedes was wheeled out of Jacobi Medical Center in Morris Park on Monday before standing up in front of a group of clapping officers. (NYPD)

title: 911 operators questioned whether Christa Pike failed execution call was prank, audio reveals
summary: 911 audio reveals dispatchers initially dismissed Christa Pike's failed execution as a prank call, delaying the ambulance response to Riverbend Prison.
story: 911 dispatch audio obtained by the Associated Press shows emergency responders first trying to determine if a 911 call describing Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike's failed execution was a prank. Credit: The Associated Press.

911 dispatch recordings show a series of miscommunications led to delayed emergency response in the immediate aftermath of the Tennessee Department of Correction’s failed execution of death row inmate Christa Pike.
An initial 911 call came through to dispatchers around 8:40 p.m. on Sept. 30, roughly an hour after Pike’s planned execution began, according to documents and audio recordings obtained by Fox News.
During the call, the unidentified caller informed operators of a failed execution but was unable to provide the operators with a code that would verify the legitimacy of the call.
Following that call, operators sought to determine the authenticity of the audio shows.
TENNESSEE DEATH ROW INMATE SURVIVES 2 LETHAL INJECTION DOSES IN FAILED EXECUTION ATTEMPT

Convicted killer Christa Gail Pike listens to proceedings on April 2008 in Knox County Criminal Court in a bid for a new trial in the 1995 killing of fellow Job Corps student Colleen Slemmer. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
"So we have a medical call for service at the Riverbend Prison," a dispatcher says in the Fox News-obtained audio.
The dispatcher explains to another operator that the caller said, "They carried out the execution, the subject didn’t pass away, and they need an ambulance because she’s not breathing normally."
DEATH ROW INMATE UNCONSCIOUS ON VENTILATOR AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION FOR TEEN’S KILLING: ATTORNEYS

"We are trying to find out if that is an actual thing that is happening, and we need to send an ambulance, and/or if you need police assistance, or if this is someone that is just basically prank calling or like swatting us," the operator can be heard saying.
In another snippet of internal dispatcher audio, an operator can be heard calling off the emergency response.
Emergency vehicles arrive at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution after the execution of Christa Pike was halted Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn. (AP Photo/George Walker IV)
TENNESSEE PRISON CHIEF RESIGNS AFTER FAILED EXECUTION AS FORMER US ATTORNEY TAPPED TO LEAD INDEPENDENT REVIEW

"Per supervisors here at the DEC [Department of Emergency Communications], we have been informed it is a false call," a dispatcher can be heard saying at approximately 9:03 p.m. "There is no medical assistance needed at Riverbend Prison."
An additional correspondence between an operator and what appeared to be somebody working at Riverbend Prison displayed further confusion.
CHRISTA PIKE'S FIRST WORDS REVEALED AFTER SHE UNEXPECTEDLY WOKE UP WHILE LAWYERS THOUGHT SHE WAS 'BRAIN DEAD'
"We got a call about a failed execution at your guys’ facility, and we’re just calling to verify," a dispatcher said.
"Um … who called you?" the prison employee responded.
"Is there like a sergeant I could speak with, or a supervisor?" the dispatcher asked.
"Who called you? Do you know?" the employee said.
"No, we don’t exactly know," the dispatcher replied.
"I’m being told nobody from our facility called you, so there’s not really anything to speak of at the moment," the employee said.
CHRISTA PIKE NOW CONSCIOUS AND TALKING AFTER SURVIVING 2 DOSES OF LETHAL INJECTION DRUG

An execution gurney is shown alongside a Tennessee Department of Correction booking photo of death row inmate Christa Pike, whose attorneys filed an emergency motion seeking to preserve evidence after the state's failed execution attempt. (Greg Smith/CORBIS/Corbis via Getty Images ; Tennessee Department of Correction via AP)
Pike’s attorney Kelly Gleason also called 911 to report the botched execution, audio recordings prove.

"What’s going on is my client, Christa Gail Pike, is undergoing a state execution. She has completed the stages of the protocol and last we knew from the attorney who is present, she is still alive and breathing and needs immediate life-saving care," Gleason can be heard saying during a phone call timestamped at approximately 9:08 p.m.
CHRISTA PIKE'S ATTORNEY SAYS SHE'S 'UP AND WALKING' MORE THAN A WEEK AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION

Around the same time as Gleason’s call, Riverbend Prison’s Central Control told emergency responders that they "would have been the ones to call in" but that they "did not make that call," according to the audio.

But also around that time, a first responder can be heard on a separate recording saying: "Somebody is outside the gate at the prison telling us that it’s real and demanding us to go in. They say they are some sort of state official. I need somebody to get out to the gate and talk to those people."
At that point, Central Control cleared the way for first responders to enter the prison at 9:11 p.m.
Media witnesses leave Riverbend Maximum Security Institution after the execution of Christa Pike was halted Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn. (AP Photo/George Walker IV)
Pike was in an ambulance and being transferred to a hospital by 9:34 p.m., the Associated Press reported.

Pike was convicted of first degree murder and conspiracy to commit first degree murder in 1996 for the 1995 torture and murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. She was sentenced to death and had been on death row for over 30 years when she arrived at her scheduled execution by lethal injection on Sept. 30.

Prison execution authorities administered a single dose of pentobarbital, a central nervous system depressant used in Tennessee execution protocol. When Pike remained conscious after the initial dose, authorities administered a second dose per state protocol.
When the second dose did not kill Pike, Tennessee’s single-drug execution protocol prevented authorities from administering a third dose.
Christa Gail Pike is seen during her trial for the murder of Colleen A. Slemmer on March 18, 1996, in Knox County Criminal Court. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
Pike was taken to a hospital where she was placed on a ventilator and remained unconscious for six days, waking up on Oct. 6, according to her attorneys.
Pike was taken back to the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center women’s prison on Oct. 10 where she is continuing to receive medical care, her attorneys said in a statement.
Following the failed execution, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has paused all state executions pending a further review.

title: FBI operation targets scam compounds in Africa with arrests, account takedowns
summary: Operation Blackout's latest raids across Ghana and Nigeria netted 28 arrests, freed trafficked workers and saw Meta remove 3.7 million accounts.
story: Feds seize $52 million in cryptocurrency during a massive global crackdown on alleged Chinese-run scam networks based in Madagascar. U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro joins Lawrence Jones to analyze the major operation that shut down 13 scam compounds and led to 400 arrests.

The FBI's expanded global efforts to disrupt and dismantle sprawling scam compounds that prey on Americans netted multiple arrests in Africa last week, as well as millions of dollars in potentially freezable funds and the takedown of social media accounts tied to fraud, officials said.

Operation Blackout is the FBI’s global campaign to identify and dismantle foreign scam compounds through overseas raids, asset seizures and the disruption of web domains and infrastructure linked to scam networks.
Authorities also worked to rescue trafficked workers and return stolen money to victims.

"Thanks to a brilliant partnership with the Department of Justice, across multiple African countries, we arrested 28 alleged criminal actors, seized over 350 devices, identified at least $11 million in potentially freezable funds, freed over 100 trafficked workers, and identified over 100 potential scam victims here at home," FBI Director Kash Patel exclusively told Fox News Digital.
FIRST ON FOX: FBI TARGETS GHANA SCAM COMPOUND LINKED TO NEARLY $10M IN LOSSES, MORE THAN 130 DETAINED

The operation also identified more than $11 million in potentially freezable funds, helped take down 3.7 million social media accounts and identified more than 120 trafficked workers for repatriation. (Silas Stein/picture alliance via Getty Images)
"This is what happens when law enforcement executes with precision across the inter-agency," Patel added. "We are demolishing criminal scam centers across the globe and truly saving lives."

In a series of initiatives stemming from the larger FBI operation, authorities conducted law enforcement raids and seizures last week as part of a "Joint Disruption Week" based out of London that resulted in 28 arrests across Ghana and Nigeria.
GLOBAL PARTNERS ARE JOINING THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AND THIS FBI TO TAKE DOWN SCAM EMPIRES FOR GOOD
In addition to the arrests, authorities identified more than 100 scam victims with losses so far exceeding $10 million.
The more than 120 trafficked workers identified are slated to be repatriated, the FBI said.
Additionally, more than 3.7 million Facebook and Instagram accounts allegedly linked to fraudulent activity were taken down in partnership with Meta.
FBI WRAPS UP CYBERCRIME OPERATION TARGETING GLOBAL NETWORKS PREYING ON AMERICANS

"Scams are a global threat that demand a global response," Chris Sonderby, vice president and deputy general counsel for Meta, said in a news release from the tech giant regarding last week's operations. "Working with the U.K. National Crime Agency, the FBI, DOJ and the Homeland Security Task Force, we took the fight to scam centers across West Africa.

"As part of the disruption, we removed more than 3.7 million accounts, Pages and Groups targeting people in the U.S., U.K., and beyond, and shared leads on over 30 suspected scam centers resulting in dozens of arrests, the rescue of trafficking victims and cryptocurrency seizures," Sonderby added.
The FBI’s Operation Blackout led to 28 arrests across Ghana and Nigeria as authorities targeted scam compounds preying on Americans. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
GLOBAL TASK FORCE DISMANTLES 'PIG-BUTCHERING' CRYPTO FRAUD RINGS PREYING ON AMERICANS

In Ghana, 117 victims are pending repatriation to Nigeria, and 19 suspects were arrested and detained. In Nigeria, local authorities will prosecute nine individuals arrested for violations of Nigerian law, the FBI said.
The Ghana and Nigeria operations follow a warning from Patel that international scam networks were expanding beyond Southeast Asia and the Middle East into Africa.

"That’s why you’re seeing the migration of these scam compounds to central and sub-Saharan Africa, which is where we are already pre-positioned to take them off," Patel told Fox News Digital in September.

The FBI-led initiative targets transnational cybercrime groups operating massive scam centers where trafficked workers are forced to carry out fraud schemes from thousands of miles away against unsuspecting Americans.
AMERICANS LOST OVER $20 BILLION TO ONE TYPE OF CRIME. HERE’S HOW WE CAN FIGHT IT
In total, Operation Blackout has resulted in roughly $17 billion being seized, hundreds of alleged scammers arrested and thousands of trafficked workers freed.
Furthermore, more than 10,000 Americans were warned about being targeted for potential fraud before losing their money, preventing an estimated $670 million in financial losses, according to the FBI.
Many of the victims are senior citizens, Patel previously told Fox News Digital. Criminal networks have begun a geographic shift in an effort to broaden their scams, Patel has said.
BURMA APPROVES DEATH PENALTY FOR SCAMMERS MONTHS AFTER FBI'S $8 BILLION CRYPTO CRACKDOWN

In September, a Justice Department Scam Center Strike Force team helped authorities in Madagascar take down 13 scam centers operated by Chinese organized crime syndicates and process more than 3,200 electronic devices, Fox News Digital previously reported.
Criminal networks have now begun using artificial intelligence to further their scams, experts said.
The technology gives scammers the ability to use voice cloning and send flawless emails and messages to potential victims, eliminating the language barriers that once made scams easy to spot.

"AI gives scam fighters powerful new tools," said Jack Stubbs, the lead scams investigator at OpenAI. "At OpenAI, we’re using AI to disrupt scam operations and help people spot scams. By sharing insights responsibly with industry and law enforcement partners, we can identify scam networks across platforms and build stronger collective defenses."
Fox News Digital's Brittany Miller and Ashley J. DiMella contributed to this report.
