title: Woman, 87, dies after being carried from home of 70 years on stretcher during eviction in Spain
summary: Maricarmen Abascal's eviction from her Madrid apartment of 70 years sparked massive protests, and her death has deepened Spain's housing crisis.
story: Fox News contributor Jason Chaffetz discusses the Democratic Socialists of America platform and draws parallels between its policies and Spain's ongoing migration crisis.

The death of an 87-year-old woman who was evicted from her longtime home has intensified a political crisis in Spain, where nationwide protests over soaring housing costs have helped force an early election.

María del Carmen Abascal, known as "Maricarmen," died Wednesday after being hospitalized following her eviction from a Madrid apartment where she had lived for seven decades, according to The Associated Press.
Her death came just days after Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election for Nov. 29 after his government's failure to pass emergency housing measures through Parliament.
The controversy has put renewed pressure on Sánchez's Socialist Party as Spain grapples with widespread frustration over rising rents and housing affordability.
SPANISH OPPOSITION LEADER CALLS PRIME MINISTER A ‘TRAITOR’ OVER CEUTA MIGRANT CRISIS
People rally in downtown Madrid, Spain, to honor the memory of Maria del Carmen Abascal, 87, whose eviction from her home sparked nationwide protests Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. (AP Photo/Manu Fernandez)

At the center of the uproar was Abascal's Sept. 23 eviction, which drew national attention after images showed the elderly woman, who used a wheelchair, being carried from her apartment on a stretcher.
Police had cordoned off the street and removed demonstrators who attempted to stop the eviction.
The images sparked demonstrations in Madrid and other Spanish cities, turning Abascal into a symbol of the country's housing crisis.
The real estate company responsible for her eviction had sought to lease the apartment at a substantially higher price, according to the AP.
ANGRY LOCALS BLOCK FAMOUS BEACH AS MASS TOURISM PROTESTS ESCALATE AT VACATION HOT SPOT

A view of the door of the home from which Maria del Carmen Abascal, 87, was evicted, sparking nationwide protests, with a sign reading "Rest in peace, Maricarmen," in Madrid, Spain, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026 (AP Photo/Manu Fernandez)
Facing mounting public pressure, the company eventually agreed to allow Abascal to return to her home. She died before she could move back.
Her cause of death has not been disclosed.
After news of her death, demonstrators gathered outside Spain's Parliament and in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square, where some observed a minute of silence.
Protesters also chanted, "Maricarmen lives, the fight goes on!"
TENS OF THOUSANDS FLOOD STREETS TO PROTEST SPAIN BORDER CRISIS

A woman places flowers in Madrid, Spain, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, near the entrance to the building where Maria del Carmen Abascal, 87, was evicted from her home, sparking nationwide protests. (AP Photo/Manu Fernandez)
Sánchez offered condolences in a statement on X.
"All my love to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," he wrote. "A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today. Rest in peace."
Conservative opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo also expressed condolences and urged political leaders not to use the woman's death for political gain.
"No campaign, no party, no use for political advantage," he wrote. "When faced with the death of a person, we must only show respect."
Abascal's eviction and death have become a rallying point for housing activists demanding changes to Spain's rental policies as the country prepares for its November election.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Cornell bans fraternity parties for the rest of the academic year amid investigation into alleged sexual assault
summary: Cornell University said Tuesday it is suspending all “parties and social events” at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year amid.
story: Cornell University said Tuesday it is suspending all “parties and social events” at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year amid an uproar over a former student’s allegation that she was sexually assaulted by members of the campus Chi Phi chapter nearly two years ago.
Cornell suspends fraternity events through end of year

Michael I. Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, also announced that the Ivy League institution would bring on “experienced, trauma-informed criminal investigators” to review allegations of sexual assault on campus.

“These are first steps toward systemic change on our campus,” Kotlikoff said in a statement posted on Cornell’s website. “We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe’s experiences, and those of other survivors.”

The former student, identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe, alleges she was sexually assaulted and plied with drugs Oct. 19-20, 2024. She filed a civil lawsuit last month against multiple parties, including the university, the fraternity, her sorority, Tri Delta, and seven former Chi Phi members.

Attorneys for four of the men have said their clients deny sexually assaulting Jane Doe or coercing her with drugs. The three other men have not responded to requests for comment. None of the seven have been criminally charged. The fraternity and sorority previously declined to discuss the pending litigation.

Jane Doe’s lawsuit put renewed scrutiny on the Cornell University Police Department’s handling of the 2024 probe and the local district attorney office’s decision not to bring criminal charges against the accused. Cornell and Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten have each defended their investigations, with the prosecutor saying that his office was not provided with all the materials from the campus police investigation.
Add to Google
Add to Google

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has appointed state Attorney General Letitia James to oversee the case going forward. Cornell separately tasked former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates with an independent review of how the school responds to sexual harassment, assault and misconduct on campus.

“I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community,” Kotlikoff said in Tuesday’s announcement. “It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action.”
Tuesday’s announcement outlined other changes in response to the Jane Doe case, including additional staff members at the Cornell Office of Civil Rights.
In response to a request for comment, Jane Doe’s lawyer said his client’s “goal in filing her lawsuit was not solely for herself.”

“She wanted to achieve her aim of improving Cornell and its response to abuse claims. While the steps announced today are helpful to achieve this goal, they are too late to protect Ms. Doe,” said the lawyer, Thomas Giuffra. “However, these steps will hopefully go a long way to help ensure that there are no more Jane Does.”

title: Trump attacks Rep. Ilhan Omar and Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed at Ohio rally
summary: The crowd chanted “deport” at several points as Trump denigrated Omar, who was born in Somalia and immigrated to the U.S., and El-Sayed, who was born in Michigan.
story: Chants of “deport” rang out Monday night as President Donald Trump criticized Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, at a rally for Republican candidates in Youngstown, Ohio.

“I don’t know what they’re doing with it, but I can tell you this: She’s a disaster,” Trump said of Omar, whose home in Washington, D.C., was searched hours earlier by federal agents, two people familiar with the investigation told NBC News.

A Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement that Homeland Security Investigations “executed a judicially authorized search warrant” as “part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation.” The statement did not specify that the investigation was related to Omar, nor did it provide more information about the search.

“She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other, and she comes into our country and she says, ‘I have a constitutional right,’” Trump said. “She’s telling us about the Constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet.”

Trump then spoke of Somali gang activity in Minnesota and what the FBI has described as a recently thwarted shooting at the state’s Mall of America, alleged to have been plotted by an American-born U.S. citizen of Somali descent, The Associated Press reported. That’s when the first wave of “deport” chants began.
Add to Google
Add to Google
Omar, who was born in the war-torn country of Somalia, immigrated to the U.S. as a child decades ago. El-Sayed was born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrants.
“For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns,” Omar wrote earlier Monday on X. “This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”
Speaking to reporters Monday afternoon, Trump said he had “nothing to do” with the search of Omar’s home.
At the rally, he segued from his attack on Omar and people of Somali descent in Minnesota to an attack on El-Sayed.
“These people are crazy,” Trump said. “You look at the guy running in Michigan. He’s a jihadist.”

Trump went on to praise El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, before he again referred to El-Sayed as a “jihadist” and proclaimed that “Somalia bandits, Third World gangsters, jihadist sympathizers do not belong in Ohio.”
He added: “They don’t belong in America. Better get them the hell out of here.”
For Subscribers
More chants of “deport” then erupted from the audience at Youngstown’s Covelli Centre.
For Subscribers

A spokesperson for El-Sayed’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday night. Last week, after Trump referred to him on social media by his middle name, Mohamed, El-Sayed condemned it as a tactic meant to raise fears about his religion.

“They point to my name and they point to my faith, trying to distract us from the challenges that we have,” El-Sayed, who is Muslim, told supporters at an event Thursday in Grand Rapids, Michigan. “My name did not raise your gas prices. My faith is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.”

Trump’s remarks Monday continued his leading role in ratcheting up rhetoric around Muslims and immigrants. Days after El-Sayed won Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, Trump warned that the U.S. could become a “jihadist-run country.” And Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., accused El-Sayed of sympathizing with Osama bin Laden as he was campaigning with Rogers last week in Michigan.

Trump was in Ohio’s Mahoning Valley — a once reliably Democratic region that has become increasingly Republican since his rise in politics — to campaign for Sen. Jon Husted and Vivek Ramaswamy, the state’s GOP nominee for governor.

It was his second visit to Ohio in less than 10 days. His last trip, to the Dayton area, included remarks about nearby Springfield. During a 2024 presidential debate, Trump repeated the unsubstantiated and racially charged claim that Haitian immigrants in the city were eating pets.
Trump mentioned Springfield again Monday in Youngstown, immediately after his attacks on Omar and El-Sayed.

“All of a sudden, they dropped 35,000 people in from Haiti, and it didn’t work out too well,” he said before he defiantly repeated his past falsehoods. “Remember during the debate I said some of the things they were doing? I was right.”

title: Duane Davis gets 40 years to life for Tupac Shakur’s murder
summary: The man convicted of orchestrating rapper Tupac Shakur’s killing in 1996 has been sentenced to 40 years to life in prison.
story: The man convicted of orchestrating rapper Tupac Shakur’s killing in 1996 has been sentenced to 40 years to life in prison. The sentence includes a 20-year mandatory enhancement for profiting off the murder, Judge Carli Kierny told the court.

“You don’t get to take a man from his family,” she said to Duane “Keffe D” Davis. “You don’t get to take his very life, his whole life, and just walk away from it, especially when that man is Tupac Shakur.”

Davis, 63, was found guilty in August of first-degree murder with use of a deadly weapon. Much of the two-week trial hinged on Davis’ own accounts of the killing in media and in a memoir, which prosecutors said was precipitated by a scuffle between Davis’ nephew and Shakur on the night of his death.

“He would have been the promise of our parents. I believe when you take away someone like that, you deserve the maximum sentence,” Shakur’s younger sister Sekyiwa Shakur said during her victim statement Tuesday.
She said her brother was “born an icon” and was raised to be a human rights activist and a protector for his family and friends.
“He was a father figure to me,” Sekyiwa Shakur aded. “It wasn’t just me in everybody in our immediate family, our extended family, and as we got older, our community as a whole.”

It took jurors less than three hours to convict him. On Tuesday, Davis appeared in court shackled in handcuffs and wearing a navy blue prison uniform. When asked if he wanted to address the court, including Shakur’s family, Davis declined.
“I’m good,” he said.
Pointing to five other convictions and Davis’ public boasting, Clark County Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal asked for the maximum possible sentence.

“Whatever your decision is, ultimately, in my mind, he deserves the maximum possible sentence because he’s earned through his actions, his behavior, who he is as he stands here today,” Palal told the judge. “He 100% deserves the maximum possible sentence.”
Davis remains the only person convicted in Shakur’s murder. He was not accused of firing the fatal shots, but prosecutors argued he provided the gun and helped orchestrate the attack.
His role in Shakur’s assassination in Las Vegas had been at the center of a nearly 30-year mystery that riveted rap fans, true-crime experts and conspiracy theorists.

Investigators at the time pointed to an East Coast-West Coast record label rivalry that they said prompted a bloody feud between Shakur’s entourage and Davis’ henchmen. They blamed Shakur, his friends and other associates for stymying their investigation, and failed to connect the dots between known gang leaders, prosecutors said.

The case went cold for decades until 2019 when Davis released his memoir “Compton Street Legend.” In it, Davis recounted his involvement in Shakur’s assassination and described himself as a “shotcaller” for the South Side Crips. Their rivals, Mob Piru, was associated with Shakur’s record label and its co-founder, Marion “Suge” Knight.

During the trial over the summer, Palal argued that Davis “went hunting” for Shakur and Knight after they were spotted at a Las Vegas hotel beating up Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, known as the “prince” of Compton in California because of his ties to Davis.
Knight was in the car with Shakur and was also shot that night. He survived his injuries, but Shakur died six days later.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

His death sparked a gang war hundreds of miles away in Compton, and was followed by the killing six months later of New York-based rapper Christopher Wallace, also known as Notorious B.I.G. or Biggie.
No one was ever charged or convicted in Wallace’s death.

title: Diesel futures jump, signaling higher prices to come despite Trump’s Russia deal
summary: Diesel futures traded sharply higher Tuesday, as doubts mounted that the Trump administration’s recent maneuvers to lower prices would make much of an impact.
story: Diesel futures traded sharply higher Tuesday, as doubts mounted about the likely impacts of the Trump administration’s latest efforts to push prices down.
U.S. diesel futures were up 5% by midday to their highest level in weeks.
In Europe, diesel futures rose by about 3.8%, while gas futures spiked to levels not seen all year.
A move higher in futures markets typically signals that prices will climb in the coming days.
Already, the average nationwide price of diesel is up 70% since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. The cost of unleaded gas has risen by more than 45% over that period.

Crude oil prices, meanwhile, were mixed. Brent traded around $106 per barrel, while U.S. crude oil neared $95 per barrel. Both of those key energy benchmarks have risen around 70% since the start of the year.
Gas and diesel prices are rising especially fast in parts of the country where President Donald Trump and Republicans can least afford to anger voters ahead of November’s midterm elections.
“Absolutely stunning price spikes in wholesale diesel today,” Gulf Oil adviser Tom Kloza wrote Tuesday on X. “US retail diesel price record of $6.53/gal could be topped by the midterms.”
“Up 18cts/gal Gulf Coast and East Coast; but up 28cts/gal in Southern California and 25-30cts/gal in Great Plains and Great Lakes,” he wrote.
Patrick De Haan, the head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, wrote on X that “$6/gal diesel may be here to stay for now.”
“Truckers and farmers not going to see any relief anytime soon,” he wrote.

The broad spike higher in diesel futures came just days after Trump announced a controversial deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to increase diesel supplies in the United States by buying previously sanctioned Russian reserves.
When Trump announced the deal, he said it would result in millions of metric tons of additional diesel for the world.
For Subscribers
While that may sound like a lot, analysts have since crunched the numbers and determined that, at best, the diesel in question would amount to less than two weeks’ worth of U.S. demand.
For Subscribers
Tuesday’s higher diesel futures are evidence of the market “clearly not believing that Russian oil is on the way,” Kloza said.
The deal with Putin also required that the Trump administration suspend long-standing sanctions on Russian energy purchases.
The sanctions were put in place after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, and the decision to lift them until April has drawn widespread backlash both at home and abroad.
Add to Google
Add to Google
Trump has also applied pressure to European allies in an effort to get them to release more of their diesel reserves.

The president’s Oct. 2 announcement that Europe had bowed to the pressure and would release fuel temporarily cooled prices for a few days. But a lack of additional details about that release gradually erased any price relief.

A subsequent statement from the International Energy Agency confirmed what traders had suspected: Europe would not be releasing any new diesel reserves, merely continuing to fulfill a pledge it made in March as part of a multinational effort to cap rising fuel prices.
Trump also signed an executive order this month that sought to ease restrictions on an off-road formulation of diesel that is dyed red and not subject to federal gas taxes.
But industry groups quickly warned truckers to avoid using “red dye” diesel without more information about how the taxes would work.
As of Tuesday, it was unclear whether Trump’s red dye diesel order had any impact on domestic prices or supply.

title: Romance scammers are getting harder to catch. The consequences are costly.
summary: For people looking for love online, a match with a scammer could cost them their life savings.
story: For people looking for love online, a match with a scammer could cost them their life savings.

A congressional investigation, which began in September 2025 and lasted about a year, found that Tinder’s scam detection systems struggled for years to keep fraudulent accounts off the dating app. Parent company Match Group has since moved to address the shortcomings with new verification requirements and upgraded detection technology.
Romance scams have become a leading form of financial fraud in the U.S., costing Americans nearly $1.5 billion in reported losses last year, according to the Federal Trade Commission.

“There’s a lot of stigma to being a victim to scams,” Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., who launched the investigation alongside Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in an interview last week. “People should understand that really sophisticated people who are doing all the right things are still getting scammed because of the level of technology and resources that these criminal enterprises now do.”
I fell prey because of my personality and because I was lonely. And I was very ashamed of what happened.
-Sue nuss, who spoke to Congress’ Joint Economic Committee about her experience turning to Tinder in search of companionship.

Scammers today can realistically pose as representatives from familiar organizations like the local YMCA or a bank, and the accessibility of AI tools makes it easier than ever to research family members and mimic their voices. But romance scams, Hassan said, can be particularly emotionally devastating.

That was the case for Pennsylvania resident Sue Nuss, who told Congress’ Joint Economic Committee about her experience turning to Tinder in search of companionship after she lost her husband. There, she met a man who claimed to be from New Jersey.
Nuss told NBC News that, over a month and a half, he won her trust with words that made her feel like he really “sees” and “understands” her.

The committee’s report, published Tuesday, stated that the man duped Nuss with a series of “fabricated” crises: job problems on an oil rig, an arrest in Mexico, his mom’s stroke and even her funeral — all excuses to ask Nuss, 77, for money. When the scammers behind the profile tried to trick her into believing the man she was dating had died, she said, she realized it was all a scam.

“I have always been a very giving person my entire life, and I’ve always been a caregiver,” Nuss told NBC News last week. “And I fell prey. I was very vulnerable. I fell prey because of my personality and because I was lonely. And I was very ashamed of what happened.”
Days after what she thought was a budding online relationship fell apart, Nuss’ scammer showed back up on Tinder with the same profile, she said in an interview.

Soon, another group approached her claiming they could recover what she had lost. Then, through an elaborate cryptocurrency scheme, that group managed to scam even more money from Nuss. She believes both scammer groups were connected, the report stated. It added that, in total, she lost more than $700,000.

“I struggle. Some days are really bad days and some days are good days. I do get therapy. I’m starting a very special therapy next week called EMDR because it’s a trauma,” Nuss said. “I don’t trust my decisions now.”

Congress last month passed the Romance Scam Prevention Act, which would require online dating service providers to notify and warn any users who get messaged by potential scammers. The bill awaits President Donald Trump’s signature.

This summer, Hassan also introduced legislation with Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., to create a central reporting portal for victims of scams, an initiative that she said could give the federal government the tools to detect patterns in scams to shut them down more effectively.
Scammers stole more than $1 trillion globally in one year, according to a 2024 report from the Global Anti-Scam Alliance.

“Enterprises that run scams are now costing the global economy more than the illicit drug trade does,” Hassan said. “This is really important for individuals. It’s really important for our economy. And so, the more people speak up about the need to change the way the federal government handles scams, the faster it’s going to happen.”
For Subscribers

The Joint Economic Committee’s investigation sought to combat the prevalence of romance scams on platforms owned by Match Group, the biggest online dating company in the world, with a portfolio that includes Tinder, Hinge, Match and Plenty of Fish.

It found that during the third quarter of 2025, nearly 1.5 million scammers or other bad actors on Tinder and Hinge matched with someone. Nearly 500,000 of those accounts then exchanged contact information with other users.

Internal documents shared voluntarily with the committee noted that most of Tinder’s machine-learning detection scam models hadn’t been updated in years, and Match Group staff members found that scammers could quickly circumvent the company’s patchwork detection rules. Excessive false positives also overwhelmed the human moderators trying to detect dangerous accounts.
For Subscribers
The committee wrote that it welcomes the changes Match Group has made to address those concerns.

Match Group deployed new detection models throughout the latter half of 2025 and the first half of 2026 to better catch bad actors, according to the committee’s report. This year, it introduced 169 automated rules and “improved” 108 others aimed at targeting and removing inauthentic actors.

One of its key rollouts is a mandatory biometric face check for all new users on Tinder and Hinge, meant to prevent users from making multiple accounts and ensure banned users can’t make new accounts.

Yoel Roth, Match Group’s senior vice president of trust and safety, told NBC News the company is “grateful the Committee recognized our significant advancements to protect our users against romance scams.”

“That said, the report mischaracterizes both the historical scale of our investment and the work already completed. Alongside our engagement with the Committee over the past year, we’ve made the largest safety advancements in Match Group’s history,” Roth wrote in a statement. “Trust and Safety is a foundational priority, and we intend to continue leading the industry in building tools that promote authentic, safe connections.”

Much of that safety work, including the face checks, was already underway before the committee’s investigation, according to Match Group. It reports having seen a roughly 60% reduction in exposure to bad actors in every market since the face checks began.
Hassan similarly said those measures have “already been successful in dramatically reducing the number of matches that their customers have with a scammer.”

“They need to do more, though, because there are still gaps in their systems,” she added. “And they are going to need to stay vigilant in new ways, because the criminals are always changing their technology and their tactics, too.”

title: Bryan Cranston mourns ‘Breaking Bad’ co-star RJ Mitte: ‘My sweet son’
summary: Emmy winning actor Bryan Cranston on Monday lamented the death of “Breaking Bad” co-star RJ Mitte, calling the late actor and disability advocate “my sweet son.”
story: Emmy winning actor Bryan Cranston on Monday lamented the death of “Breaking Bad” co-star RJ Mitte, calling the late actor and disability advocate “my sweet son.”
Cranston, 70, said he was in “deep despair” over Mitte’s death by suicide and wondered if he’d still be alive today had they only met up for lunch in recent days.

“It is especially devastating to hear that he took his own life. Why? We were texting each other just a few weeks ago — figuring out when we could meet for lunch,” Cranston said in a statement on Monday night.
“I don’t know if that lunch would have changed his future … But I do know that I loved him, and thoroughly enjoyed being with him throughout the years on the series.”
The 34-year-old Mitte, who played the son of Cranston’s lead character Walter White in the hit AMC series “Breaking Bad,” died Monday in Brownsville, Texas.

“I’m in deep despair as I write this tonight. RJ Mitte, my sweet son on Breaking Bad has died,” Cranston said. “I met him when he was only 14 years old when he was cast as Walter White Jr., a part he played with such joy and enthusiasm.”
Mitte had cerebral palsy and Cranston said that challenge never slowed down his late co-star.
“He met the demanding shooting schedule head on with great determination,” according to Cranston.
“He parlayed his experience on the show to be a vocal advocate for performers with disabilities, and was the head of a philanthropic organization with a focus on helping the disabled community.”
“Breaking Bad” ran for 62 episodes between 2008 and 2013, as one of the era’s most critically acclaimed shows.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Cranston won six of his seven Emmys for work on “Breaking Bad,” playing a high school chemistry teacher-turned-meth kingpin Walter White.
Cranston was in all 62 episodes of “Bad” and Mitte’s Walter White Jr. appeared 56 times.
“That kid was pretty raw when we started shooting the pilot in February of 2007, but little by little we watched him grow into a really fine actor,” Cranston wrote.
“All that promise and potential now is such a loss.”

If you or someone you know is in crisis, call 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. You can also call the network, previously known as the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, at 800-273-8255, text HOME to 741741 or visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources for additional resources.

title: Duane Davis gets 40 years to life for Tupac Shakur’s murder
summary: The man convicted of orchestrating rapper Tupac Shakur’s killing in 1996 has been sentenced to 40 years to life in prison.
story: The man convicted of orchestrating rapper Tupac Shakur’s killing in 1996 has been sentenced to 40 years to life in prison. The sentence includes a 20-year mandatory enhancement for profiting off the murder, Judge Carli Kierny told the court.

“You don’t get to take a man from his family,” she said to Duane “Keffe D” Davis. “You don’t get to take his very life, his whole life, and just walk away from it, especially when that man is Tupac Shakur.”

Davis, 63, was found guilty in August of first-degree murder with use of a deadly weapon. Much of the two-week trial hinged on Davis’ own accounts of the killing in media and in a memoir, which prosecutors said was precipitated by a scuffle between Davis’ nephew and Shakur on the night of his death.

“He would have been the promise of our parents. I believe when you take away someone like that, you deserve the maximum sentence,” Shakur’s younger sister Sekyiwa Shakur said during her victim statement Tuesday.
She said her brother was “born an icon” and was raised to be a human rights activist and a protector for his family and friends.
“He was a father figure to me,” Sekyiwa Shakur aded. “It wasn’t just me in everybody in our immediate family, our extended family, and as we got older, our community as a whole.”

It took jurors less than three hours to convict him. On Tuesday, Davis appeared in court shackled in handcuffs and wearing a navy blue prison uniform. When asked if he wanted to address the court, including Shakur’s family, Davis declined.
“I’m good,” he said.
Pointing to five other convictions and Davis’ public boasting, Clark County Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal asked for the maximum possible sentence.

“Whatever your decision is, ultimately, in my mind, he deserves the maximum possible sentence because he’s earned through his actions, his behavior, who he is as he stands here today,” Palal told the judge. “He 100% deserves the maximum possible sentence.”
Davis remains the only person convicted in Shakur’s murder. He was not accused of firing the fatal shots, but prosecutors argued he provided the gun and helped orchestrate the attack.
His role in Shakur’s assassination in Las Vegas had been at the center of a nearly 30-year mystery that riveted rap fans, true-crime experts and conspiracy theorists.

Investigators at the time pointed to an East Coast-West Coast record label rivalry that they said prompted a bloody feud between Shakur’s entourage and Davis’ henchmen. They blamed Shakur, his friends and other associates for stymying their investigation, and failed to connect the dots between known gang leaders, prosecutors said.

The case went cold for decades until 2019 when Davis released his memoir “Compton Street Legend.” In it, Davis recounted his involvement in Shakur’s assassination and described himself as a “shotcaller” for the South Side Crips. Their rivals, Mob Piru, was associated with Shakur’s record label and its co-founder, Marion “Suge” Knight.

During the trial over the summer, Palal argued that Davis “went hunting” for Shakur and Knight after they were spotted at a Las Vegas hotel beating up Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, known as the “prince” of Compton in California because of his ties to Davis.
Knight was in the car with Shakur and was also shot that night. He survived his injuries, but Shakur died six days later.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

His death sparked a gang war hundreds of miles away in Compton, and was followed by the killing six months later of New York-based rapper Christopher Wallace, also known as Notorious B.I.G. or Biggie.
No one was ever charged or convicted in Wallace’s death.

title: Clavicular’s accuser drops sexual assault claims from civil lawsuit amid MA criminal rape case
summary: A woman who accused “looksmaxxing” influencer Clavicular of raping her at his family’s Cape Cod home last May has refiled her civil lawsuit and dropped the sexual assault allegations against him, a move her lawyer said was intended to avoid interfering with a pending Massachusetts criminal case in connection with the encounter.
story: A woman who accused “looksmaxxing” influencer Clavicular of raping her at his family’s Cape Cod home last May has refiled her civil lawsuit and dropped the sexual assault allegations against him, a move her lawyer said was intended to avoid interfering with a pending Massachusetts criminal case in connection with the encounter.

Clavicular, 20, whose real name is Braden Peters, was charged last month with rape, drugging someone for sexual intercourse, and procuring liquor for someone under 21 years old. He has denied the allegations detailed in the Sept. 8 criminal complaint filed in Orleans District Court in Barnstable County, Massachusetts.

Aleksandra Vasilevna Mendoza, an 18-year-old influencer known online as Alorah or Alorah Ziva, alleged that in May 2025, while she was in Massachusetts, Peters called her an Uber to his family’s Cape Cod house. Once there, she said he got her drunk on vodka while they livestreamed on Twitch and then raped her, according to a criminal complaint from the Chatham Police Department.

The charges come months after Mendoza filed her original civil lawsuit against Peters in Miami, accusing him of sexual assault in connection with the events of May 2025. The civil lawsuit also separately alleged he injected her face with a non-FDA-approved fat-dissolving substance during a November livestream in Florida.
A source familiar with the matter previously confirmed to NBC News that the charges against Peters stem from Mendoza’s allegations.

On Thursday, Mendoza filed a second amended civil complaint in Miami-Dade County, Florida, removing the sexual assault allegations against him and scaling back the details of the alleged assault. The civil complaint also details allegations that Peters falsely represented himself as qualified to perform cosmetic injections during a November 2025 encounter, concealed their risks, and misled Mendoza about what was being injected into her face.

“In light of Mr. Peters’ recent posts and other conduct, this matter is more appropriate for the criminal justice system,” Mendoza’s lawyer, Drew Moss, said in a statement, noting that the sexual assault claim was dropped “due to the pending criminal charges in Massachusetts.” “Ms. Mendoza does not want her civil case to interfere with that process.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Mendoza’s earlier civil complaint alleged that Peters had sex with her after getting her so intoxicated that she was unable to consent. It also alleged that Mendoza woke up to find Peters having sex with her without her consent.
Peters’ arraignment in the Massachusetts criminal case, previously scheduled for Oct. 14, was canceled, according to the case docket. The next hearing date appears to be on Oct. 22.

The second civil complaint, however, no longer includes those explicit allegations of nonconsensual sex, instead stating that Peters “had sex with Mendoza multiple times while she was intoxicated.” It also does not include the original claim that Peters had sex with her while she was asleep.
Moss did not respond to additional questions about the decision or why an attorney originally on the civil case filed a motion to withdraw on Friday.

Peters’ spokesperson declined to comment on Mendoza’s latest civil complaint. The influencer has previously denied the criminal allegations and defended himself in a series of posts on X shortly after the charges were reported. The posts include a video of Mendoza calling Peters “super nice.”

Mendoza’s amended civil complaint still accuses Peters of battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress, fraudulent misrepresentation, fraudulent concealment, and unauthorized publication of name and likeness.

The amended complaint also alleges that in November 2025, Peters invited Mendoza and her friends to his place in Delray Beach, Florida, for a streaming session on Kick after they ran into each other at a networking event in Miami.

Mendoza alleged that during the livestream, Peters injected her with a syringe of Aqualyx, a fat-dissolving compound he did not reveal was not approved by the Food and Drug Administration, which he said would reduce fat in her face, without her consent, according to the amended civil complaint.
The amended civil complaint also provides more detail about the November 2025 incident, including that Peters allegedly knew Mendoza was a minor when he gave her the injection.

It also includes screenshots of livestream viewers’ comments warning Peters that Mendoza was 17 at the time. According to the civil complaint, Peters allegedly responded to comments about her age, defended their two-year age difference, and proceeded with the injections.

If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse, & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at rainn.org/get-help.

title: Anthropic says its A.I. model submitted a false cold case tip to Philadelphia police
summary: Artificial intelligence research company Anthropic says one of its models generated a bogus tip about an unsolved murder and submitted it to Philadelphia police.
story: Artificial intelligence research company Anthropic says one of its models generated a bogus tip about an unsolved murder and submitted it to Philadelphia police, warning that the incident raises concerns about high tech “behaviors” that “could do far more harm as models become more powerful.”
The A.I. model reached out to PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com on July 18 and made a “false homicide tip,” the Philadelphia Police Department said Tuesday in a statement.

The tip, though, was flagged as spam by the agency and was never forwarded to investigators, police said. The department emphasized that all tips have to go through human vetting before ever getting an a detective’s desk.
“The department’s regular investigative process for crime tips requires human review and vetting before any tips are disseminated for investigative follow-up,” the department said.

“Regardless of who submits information or how it reaches the department, a tip is a lead to assess — not an established fact. Investigators evaluate its credibility and seek corroborating evidence,” the statement said. “An automated submission does not bypass that process.”
Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 4.5 “had been tasked with generating and performing example tasks on randomly selected webpages,” according to a company statement.
And in one run on July 18, Claude “landed on a page referencing an unsolved homicide” and came to a page that “contained a tip form run by a police department,” Anthropic said.
For Subscribers

Claude filled out an online form with: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.”
For Subscribers
While Anthropic insisted no harm was done, the company said it takes these kind of unintended model actions seriously.
While this case “had minimal impact, we do not want to diminish the findings, because the same behaviors could do far more harm as models become more powerful,” the company said.
The disclosure from Anthropic shows just one example of many recent actions taken by AI agents from various companies that weren’t predicted or intended by their human operators.
Anthropic, the San Francisco-based A.I. titan, is a private company that has taken initial steps that could lead to one of the biggest initial public offerings in Wall Street history.

title: Cornell bans fraternity parties for the rest of the academic year amid investigation into alleged sexual assault
summary: Cornell University said Tuesday it is suspending all “parties and social events” at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year amid.
story: Cornell University said Tuesday it is suspending all “parties and social events” at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year amid an uproar over a former student’s allegation that she was sexually assaulted by members of the campus Chi Phi chapter nearly two years ago.
Cornell suspends fraternity events through end of year

Michael I. Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, also announced that the Ivy League institution would bring on “experienced, trauma-informed criminal investigators” to review allegations of sexual assault on campus.

“These are first steps toward systemic change on our campus,” Kotlikoff said in a statement posted on Cornell’s website. “We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe’s experiences, and those of other survivors.”

The former student, identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe, alleges she was sexually assaulted and plied with drugs Oct. 19-20, 2024. She filed a civil lawsuit last month against multiple parties, including the university, the fraternity, her sorority, Tri Delta, and seven former Chi Phi members.

Attorneys for four of the men have said their clients deny sexually assaulting Jane Doe or coercing her with drugs. The three other men have not responded to requests for comment. None of the seven have been criminally charged. The fraternity and sorority previously declined to discuss the pending litigation.

Jane Doe’s lawsuit put renewed scrutiny on the Cornell University Police Department’s handling of the 2024 probe and the local district attorney office’s decision not to bring criminal charges against the accused. Cornell and Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten have each defended their investigations, with the prosecutor saying that his office was not provided with all the materials from the campus police investigation.
Add to Google
Add to Google

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has appointed state Attorney General Letitia James to oversee the case going forward. Cornell separately tasked former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates with an independent review of how the school responds to sexual harassment, assault and misconduct on campus.

“I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community,” Kotlikoff said in Tuesday’s announcement. “It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action.”
Tuesday’s announcement outlined other changes in response to the Jane Doe case, including additional staff members at the Cornell Office of Civil Rights.
In response to a request for comment, Jane Doe’s lawyer said his client’s “goal in filing her lawsuit was not solely for herself.”

“She wanted to achieve her aim of improving Cornell and its response to abuse claims. While the steps announced today are helpful to achieve this goal, they are too late to protect Ms. Doe,” said the lawyer, Thomas Giuffra. “However, these steps will hopefully go a long way to help ensure that there are no more Jane Does.”

title: Judge extends order blocking Trump administration from clearing trees at DC golf course
summary: The judge presiding over a court fight over President Donald Trump’s plans for a public golf course in D.C. temporarily barred the removal of trees at the site.
story: The judge presiding over a court fight involving President Donald Trump’s plans to redo a public golf course in D.C. issued an order Tuesday temporarily barring the administration from knocking down any more trees at the site.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes handed down the order a day after an emergency hearing where she accused the government of engaging in deception to knock down more than 400 trees at the East Potomac Golf Links over the holiday weekend.
“The Court ORDERS that Defendants may not fell any further trees on the East Potomac Golf Course through Monday, October 26,” the judge wrote in a directive posted on the docket.

Reyes is overseeing a lawsuit filed by a preservation group and two Washington, D.C., residents challenging Trump’s golf-course renovation. Earlier this year, she denied  the plaintiffs’ request for a restraining order in the case after administration lawyers assured her they would give her and the plaintiffs ample notice of any large scale work being done on the course.

On Friday, attorneys for the Justice Department said in court papers filed shortly before 5 p.m. that the National Park Service would be removing roughly 500 trees from the course over the three-day holiday weekend. That work started Saturday morning, a park official testified in court Monday, and 430 trees were knocked down.

The official, Superintendent of National Mall and Memorial Parks Kevin Griess, said workers had identified about 300 more trees that still need to be cut down, but they weren’t able to work on Sunday because of bad weather.
Reyes told lawyers for the Justice Department at the hearing that she was “furious” with the government.
“I was hearing from everyone on plaintiffs’ side this was going to happen. I said repeatedly, ‘No, I trust the government.’ I trusted you all not to do precisely what you have done,” the judge said.
“What has happened has cost the government all of its credibility,” Reyes added.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The administration argued in a filing Friday the work was for “maintenance activities” that were unrelated to Trump’s plans to transform the 100-year-old course into championship-style greens. It said they were implementing recommendations from a 2019 “Cultural Landscape Report” aimed at restoring the course closer to its original design.

The plaintiffs in the case, which include the D.C. Preservation League, scoffed at the argument in court papers, and said there would have been no mad scramble to implement a years-old plan — and noted that Trump’s plan for the site would “require massive tree-clearing.”

“Defendants would have this Court believe that this unprecedented operation is merely the sudden and purely coincidental fulfillment of recommendations posited in a Cultural Landscape Report seven years ago and is totally unrelated to the ongoing implementation of the Washington National plan,” they wrote.
“Even if Defendants were entitled to the benefit of the doubt, they are not entitled to a suspension of disbelief.”

Reyes has demanded to know how the decision to chop down the trees came together. She initially ordered a follow-up hearing with testimony from a top official of the Interior Department on Tuesday, but issued an order in the morning delaying the hearing until Monday the 19th. She also directed NPS Acting Director Jessica Bowron to appear as well.

Reyes, a Biden-appointed judge, had made clear at hearing last month that she’d been hoping to avoid issuing a restraining order in the case. “I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees. I am a judge,” she said then.

title: Why advanced U.S. weapons aren’t stopping Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia
summary: Saudi Arabia has one of the world’s most expensive and sophisticated arsenals, filled with American warplanes, missile defenses and other cutting-edge technology.
story: Saudi Arabia has one of the world’s most expensive and sophisticated arsenals, filled with American warplanes, missile defenses and other cutting-edge technology.

But in recent days it has appeared helpless in the face of barrages of missiles and drones fired by the Houthi rebel group from neighboring Yemen. The attacks have struck Saudi airports, killed at least 14 people and forced schoolchildren and businesspeople to stay indoors and work from home.

The Iran-backed Houthis, once seen as little more than a ragtag militia, have grown into a formidable fighting force. They have inflicted damage on the region’s top oil producer, threatened critical supply routes in the Red Sea and now risk reigniting a full-scale war on the Arabian Peninsula that displaced millions and killed tens of thousands.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The Houthis are attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports government forces in Yemen the rebels seek to overthrow. As Saudi Arabia investigates how its air defenses failed to stop the Houthis’ attacks, it must also consider how to respond and what the rebels might do next.
Here’s what we know and don’t know about the Saudi and Houthi conflict:
Vast arsenal

Saudi Arabia is the world’s top purchaser of American weapons, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. It says the Saudis received 12% of all U.S. arms exports from 2021-2025.

Over the years, the Saudis have purchased American F-15 warplanes, Patriot air defense systems, as well as advanced radars and offensive missile systems, according to the think tank, which tracks global arms transfers.
Saudi Arabia’s annual budget for 2026 listed $83 billion for military expenditures. Earlier this year, it struck a $9 billion deal with Washington for 730 Patriot missiles.
Huge area to defend
The Houthis have been able to exploit Saudi Arabia’s large size.

Vulnerable energy, civilian and military assets are scattered across the country’s sparsely populated territory roughly three times the size of Texas. Its border with Yemen stretches more than 800 miles through rugged desert areas.

“Expecting a country the size of Saudi Arabia to intercept every missile is simply unrealistic. No defense can guarantee complete protection,” Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst, said in a post online Monday.
Add to Google
Add to Google
At the same time, regional officials say that Saudi Arabia is running low on interceptors and has reached out to allies for help.
Saudi Arabia recently struck a joint defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey. But so far, the two countries appear to be largely staying on the sidelines or limiting their support.
President Donald Trump said this week he is evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes on the Houthis. But he has not yet announced a decision.
Battle-tested

Like their patron Iran, the Houthis have deployed asymmetric warfare for the 21st century by capitalizing on their strengths — primarily drones and missiles. For the Houthis, success on the battlefield doesn’t require toppling Saudi Arabia; disrupting the Saudi economy and sowing fear within its society may be enough to give the Houthis leverage in any possible negotiations to end the fighting.
The Houthis have a large arsenal capable of striking targets well over 1,000 miles away. Some warheads change direction during flight and pose an extra challenge to air defenses.

The group has fired hundreds of drones and missiles at Israel since its war in Gaza erupted in October 2023. While most were intercepted, a handful managed to land, in one case killing an Israeli man. Another strike hit an Israeli airport last year.

title: Diesel futures jump, signaling higher prices to come despite Trump’s Russia deal
summary: Diesel futures traded sharply higher Tuesday, as doubts mounted that the Trump administration’s recent maneuvers to lower prices would make much of an impact.
story: Diesel futures traded sharply higher Tuesday, as doubts mounted about the likely impacts of the Trump administration’s latest efforts to push prices down.
U.S. diesel futures were up 5% by midday to their highest level in weeks.
In Europe, diesel futures rose by about 3.8%, while gas futures spiked to levels not seen all year.
A move higher in futures markets typically signals that prices will climb in the coming days.
Already, the average nationwide price of diesel is up 70% since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. The cost of unleaded gas has risen by more than 45% over that period.

Crude oil prices, meanwhile, were mixed. Brent traded around $106 per barrel, while U.S. crude oil neared $95 per barrel. Both of those key energy benchmarks have risen around 70% since the start of the year.
Gas and diesel prices are rising especially fast in parts of the country where President Donald Trump and Republicans can least afford to anger voters ahead of November’s midterm elections.
“Absolutely stunning price spikes in wholesale diesel today,” Gulf Oil adviser Tom Kloza wrote Tuesday on X. “US retail diesel price record of $6.53/gal could be topped by the midterms.”
“Up 18cts/gal Gulf Coast and East Coast; but up 28cts/gal in Southern California and 25-30cts/gal in Great Plains and Great Lakes,” he wrote.
Patrick De Haan, the head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, wrote on X that “$6/gal diesel may be here to stay for now.”
“Truckers and farmers not going to see any relief anytime soon,” he wrote.

The broad spike higher in diesel futures came just days after Trump announced a controversial deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to increase diesel supplies in the United States by buying previously sanctioned Russian reserves.
When Trump announced the deal, he said it would result in millions of metric tons of additional diesel for the world.
For Subscribers
While that may sound like a lot, analysts have since crunched the numbers and determined that, at best, the diesel in question would amount to less than two weeks’ worth of U.S. demand.
For Subscribers
Tuesday’s higher diesel futures are evidence of the market “clearly not believing that Russian oil is on the way,” Kloza said.
The deal with Putin also required that the Trump administration suspend long-standing sanctions on Russian energy purchases.
The sanctions were put in place after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, and the decision to lift them until April has drawn widespread backlash both at home and abroad.
Add to Google
Add to Google
Trump has also applied pressure to European allies in an effort to get them to release more of their diesel reserves.

The president’s Oct. 2 announcement that Europe had bowed to the pressure and would release fuel temporarily cooled prices for a few days. But a lack of additional details about that release gradually erased any price relief.

A subsequent statement from the International Energy Agency confirmed what traders had suspected: Europe would not be releasing any new diesel reserves, merely continuing to fulfill a pledge it made in March as part of a multinational effort to cap rising fuel prices.
Trump also signed an executive order this month that sought to ease restrictions on an off-road formulation of diesel that is dyed red and not subject to federal gas taxes.
But industry groups quickly warned truckers to avoid using “red dye” diesel without more information about how the taxes would work.
As of Tuesday, it was unclear whether Trump’s red dye diesel order had any impact on domestic prices or supply.

title: Britain faces ‘new era’ of security threats from Iran and Russia, MI5 says
summary: Britain’s MI5 boss Ken McCallum warned of a range of threats posed by Russia, Iran, China, AI and terrorist groups.
story: LONDON — Iran is escalating its campaign of threats on British soil, expanding attacks beyond dissidents abroad and Jewish sites to now focusing on harder military targets, the country’s domestic intelligence chief said Tuesday.

MI5 Director General Ken McCallum was speaking less than two weeks after the United States rushed to withdraw its bombers from a key air base in England, with American officials saying there had been reports of a possible Iranian drone attack.

Giving a wide-ranging “annual threat update” at MI5’s Thames House headquarters in London, McCallum warned that Britain and Europe had “entered a new era of national security,” which he likened to the shift that came after the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001.
Add to Google
Add to Google

His speech comes at a moment of tumult not just for the Middle East and Ukraine, which continue to be ravaged by war, but also the rest of Europe, which has suffered so-called hybrid aggression from Moscow and Tehran including sabotage, arson and cyberattacks. European governments are now openly telling people to stockpile food and prepare for more of their taxes to be spent on defense, warning that Russia may launch a direct attack on their soil.
MI5 is now devoting more resources than it had during the Cold War to countering threats from countries such as Russia, Iran, China and others, McCallum said.
“Russia remains aggressor No. 1, as Putin’s Kremlin continues to lash out at the U.K. and its allies,” he added.

But another arch belligerent is Iran, whose leaders have been “attempting to expand their hybrid campaign” of “using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations and Israeli sites,” the spy chief said.

“Much of this aggression has been aimed at British Jewish communities, with whom I want to express solidarity,” he said. But this year has seen a shift of “Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites.”
Over the past year, intelligence operations have led to more than 50 Iran-linked arrests in Britain, he said.

McCallum made reference to the incident last month at RAF Fairford, the military base in rural England from where the U.S. had been launching bombers involved in the assault against Iran. He declined to give details, citing ongoing investigations and operations, but said the case was “not unique.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Details are hazy, but in the early hours of Sept. 27, a member of the public called the police after spotting three vans in a country lane near the base. Seven men in their 20s, one of them a dual British-Iranian national, have been arrested and released on bail. Authorities said they found only gasoline in the vehicles.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told lawmakers in Parliament on Monday that the incident “is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed” by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the powerful political, military and economic group that holds huge sway in the country.
A week after the incident, Washington hastily withdrew its bombers from the base because, according to two U.S. officials, of reports of a possible drone attack against the site.

On Tuesday, McCallum downplayed fears that Iran could mount such a complex attack, saying it has so far been hiring unsophisticated criminals for operations in the United Kingdom. But he warned that could change.

On Russia, McCallum said its military and intelligence services “are once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare,” being careful not to trigger NATO’s Article 5 threshold, in which other countries would be expected to defend their allies.
“We see them scrambling to pay criminals to do their bidding,” he said. “The whole aim of hybrid tactics is to try to intimidate us.”

Within the U.K.’s “multifaceted relationship with China” — Beijing is a major trading partner to London — MI5 has been focused on efforts by the Chinese government “to conduct espionage, coercion or democratic interference.”
On Al Qaeda and the Islamic State terrorist group, or ISIS, MI5 still has to respond “to attempts to carry out mass casualty attacks,” he said.
But perhaps the gravest warning came when it came to artificial intelligence, which he said in the future could be used by terrorist groups and other actors to create new “bioweapons.”
And “beyond misuse of AI by human adversaries sit the potential risks posed by AI itself,” he said.

“Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are. Is capable of out-thinking us. This is genuinely novel. And deserves the serious attention it is getting, including in MI5.”

title: Research crew searching for Amelia Earhart plane arrives on remote island in South Pacific
summary: An expedition has reached a remote island in the South Pacific where it believes Amelia Earhart’s lost plane may have landed when the famed female pilot disappeared nearly 90 years ago.
story: An expedition has reached a remote island in the South Pacific where it believes Amelia Earhart’s lost plane may have landed when the famed female pilot disappeared nearly 90 years ago.

A group of researchers with the Archaeological Legacy Institute and Purdue University arrived Tuesday at the island of Nikumaroro, the university announced in a press release. The crewmembers will then hike their way toward a lagoon where an anomaly was spotted on satellite images.

Earhart mysteriously vanished in the summer of 1937 while flying around the world, hoping to be the first woman to accomplish such a feat. But on the morning of July 2, 1937, the U.S. Coast Guard ship lost contact with Earhart and her navigator as they attempted to fly to Howland Island.

The last transmissions from the two-person crew was Earhart reporting unexpected cloudy weather before she told the Coast Guard crew that she could not find them and that her plane was running out of a fuel.
She and her navigator, Fred Noonan, were never heard from again.

title: Former ‘SNL’ star Ego Nwodim mocks Shane Gillis monologue about women’s gym outfits
summary: Former “Saturday Night Live” cast member Ego Nwodim appeared to respond to Shane Gillis’ controversial monologue from his latest hosting stint Saturday, during which he said that women who wear short shorts to the gym are dressing like “whores.”
story: Former “Saturday Night Live” cast member Ego Nwodim appeared to respond to Shane Gillis’ controversial monologue from his latest hosting stint Saturday, during which he said that women who wear short shorts to the gym are dressing like “whores.”
“Whore reporting for duty,” Nwodim captioned an Instagram story Monday that featured a photo of her in the gym wearing black leggings, a black long-sleeved shirt and a black baseball hat.
She then posted a photo of her post-workout meal, writing, “Getting my 30 grams of protein in after heauxing,” with “heauxing” being slang for “whoring.”

Gillis’ monologue garnered backlash online in the days since, with people calling the raunchy comedian “tone deaf” for making a comment about women’s bodies, especially as the country reckons with the scandal over an alleged sexual assault at Cornell University.

In the seven-minute, stand-up-style monologue, Gillis claimed he “didn’t know women just dress like whores now” at the gym. He went on to describe the “neon, artificial-vape-colored” shorts that women are wearing to work out and the fact that men are not allowed to look at women in those shorts.

Actor Dan Levy also joined the conversation Sunday night. In a selfie video posted to Instagram, he said, “Women wearing short shorts at the gym does not make them whores. It makes the men calling them whores misogynists. There’s a difference there.”
He went on to call women “superior human beings to men” and called on the male population to more often support their female counterparts.

Saturday was Gillis’ third time hosting the late-night sketch comedy show. He was hired, and then quickly fired, from the cast in 2019 after clips of racist jokes he had previously made on his podcast surfaced online.
Nwodim was on “SNL” from 2018 to 2025 and became a mainstay in the cast with recurring characters such as Miss Eggy and Lisa from Temecula.

title: Bryan Cranston mourns ‘Breaking Bad’ co-star RJ Mitte: ‘My sweet son’
summary: Emmy winning actor Bryan Cranston on Monday lamented the death of “Breaking Bad” co-star RJ Mitte, calling the late actor and disability advocate “my sweet son.”
story: Emmy winning actor Bryan Cranston on Monday lamented the death of “Breaking Bad” co-star RJ Mitte, calling the late actor and disability advocate “my sweet son.”
Cranston, 70, said he was in “deep despair” over Mitte’s death by suicide and wondered if he’d still be alive today had they only met up for lunch in recent days.

“It is especially devastating to hear that he took his own life. Why? We were texting each other just a few weeks ago — figuring out when we could meet for lunch,” Cranston said in a statement on Monday night.
“I don’t know if that lunch would have changed his future … But I do know that I loved him, and thoroughly enjoyed being with him throughout the years on the series.”
The 34-year-old Mitte, who played the son of Cranston’s lead character Walter White in the hit AMC series “Breaking Bad,” died Monday in Brownsville, Texas.

“I’m in deep despair as I write this tonight. RJ Mitte, my sweet son on Breaking Bad has died,” Cranston said. “I met him when he was only 14 years old when he was cast as Walter White Jr., a part he played with such joy and enthusiasm.”
Mitte had cerebral palsy and Cranston said that challenge never slowed down his late co-star.
“He met the demanding shooting schedule head on with great determination,” according to Cranston.
“He parlayed his experience on the show to be a vocal advocate for performers with disabilities, and was the head of a philanthropic organization with a focus on helping the disabled community.”
“Breaking Bad” ran for 62 episodes between 2008 and 2013, as one of the era’s most critically acclaimed shows.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Cranston won six of his seven Emmys for work on “Breaking Bad,” playing a high school chemistry teacher-turned-meth kingpin Walter White.
Cranston was in all 62 episodes of “Bad” and Mitte’s Walter White Jr. appeared 56 times.
“That kid was pretty raw when we started shooting the pilot in February of 2007, but little by little we watched him grow into a really fine actor,” Cranston wrote.
“All that promise and potential now is such a loss.”

If you or someone you know is in crisis, call 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. You can also call the network, previously known as the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, at 800-273-8255, text HOME to 741741 or visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources for additional resources.

title: Trump’s new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, keeps first briefing short
summary: President Donald Trump’s new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, held an unusually short first briefing with the media Tuesday, concluding after less than 15 minutes and calling on just three reporters, all from conservative outlets.
story: President Donald Trump’s new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, held an unusually short first briefing with the media Tuesday, concluding after less than 15 minutes and calling on just three reporters, all from conservative outlets.
The press secretary spent more than half of that time reading remarks before taking questions from Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail.
In response to the Daily Mail, she also revealed that the administration has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, to resign following allegations of misconduct.

Zacharia spent most of her remarks touting the president’s policies and framed her new position as a job to “amplify” the president, something she said she’d done as a conservative commentator. She referred to those appearances, telling reporters that she hopes to “take that into an official capacity.”

Now, Zacharia said, she hopes to “only build on, only amplify and only multiply, to the extent possible, all of the wins” that Trump is “making for Americans, for Americans to understand how much has changed in this brief period of time, what he’s been able to accomplish.”
“My goal is to be able to communicate that in complete tandem with the president, as he is his own best spokesperson and will absolutely be leading the way with that,” she added.
Asked by Fox News whether the U.S. has stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, she said she would “have to get back to you on that.”

Zacharia is stepping into the role as the top White House spokesperson in the final weeks before the midterm elections, as the president is embarking on a series of campaign trips to shore up his base. She said Trump would continue his midterm “blitz,” pointing to future stops in Kentucky, Georgia and Florida.

At the same time, voters are souring on the president’s performance, which Trump has chalked up to a public relations issue. Last month, an NBC News poll found that 41% of registered voters approved of the president’s performance, a second-term low.

The same poll found that voters largely disapprove of the president’s handling of the economy. The administration hasn’t shown a path to ending the Iran war, which has raised fuel prices and contributed to inflation. And in recent days, some Republican candidates in battleground races have been breaking with the president on his handling of tariffs and the war.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Trump said during a recent rally in Oklahoma that the administration is “not doing a good job of public relations.” At a separate event, he said that the administration was “doing an extremely poor job of promotion,” despite doing an “extremely great job of running the country.”

Zacharia painted a rosy picture of the president’s popularity, describing the Ohio venue of his rally Monday as “overflowing with enthusiasm.” Attendance of the president’s rallies is at “record highs as enthusiastic, hardworking Americans are lining up and packing arenas to support President Trump and Republicans,” she said.
NBC News has reported that the president has been speaking in smaller venues that are not filled.

Zacharia also expressed her views on the shifting media landscape and discussed balancing her family life in response to other questions. She said she wanted to “expand” on the new media seat “to the extent possible,” referring to predecessor Karoline Leavitt’s decision to include a seat in the briefing room for nontraditional media. Breitbart held the seat Tuesday.

Leavitt said in August that she was departing the administration to spend more time with her family. Asked about balancing the job with her own family in California, Zacharia said her husband and four children are moving to the Washington area.
“I adore my family. I love them. They are my priority,” she said. “I love being with my kids. The idea of not spending evenings with my kids is completely unacceptable.”
She then accidentally referred to her husband as “my president” before correcting herself and saying he would be in Washington for the week.
The president announced Friday that he was tapping Zacharia to fill the position. She had served as a senior communications adviser for Trump Media & Technology Group.
Zacharia has said multiple times that she is a lawyer and that she practiced in China.

After the press conference, as Trump prepared to depart the White House, a reporter asked Zacharia what state she passed the bar exam in. Zacharia said that she “moved to China.” Her LinkedIn says she worked at Zhong Lun Law Firm from 2011 to 2013. Her LinkedIn also states that she was “general counsel” for Fix California, which was founded by Trump ally Ric Grenell.
Asked whether she had passed the bar exam, which is required in the U.S. to practice law, a White House official did not directly respond to the question.

“She moved to China with her husband after graduating Pepperdine Caruso School of Law because of his job at an American private equity firm,” the official said. “In China, she worked on international transaction law until they moved back to the states.”
Asked for further clarification, the official said, “She practiced international transactional law, with all the appropriate credentials.”
In a Fox News interview over the weekend, Zacharia said she was looking forward to “working for President Trump,” adding, “This job is not about me.”
“This job is about him and how he wants to communicate to the American people,” she said Saturday.

title: Romance scammers are getting harder to catch. The consequences are costly.
summary: For people looking for love online, a match with a scammer could cost them their life savings.
story: For people looking for love online, a match with a scammer could cost them their life savings.

A congressional investigation, which began in September 2025 and lasted about a year, found that Tinder’s scam detection systems struggled for years to keep fraudulent accounts off the dating app. Parent company Match Group has since moved to address the shortcomings with new verification requirements and upgraded detection technology.
Romance scams have become a leading form of financial fraud in the U.S., costing Americans nearly $1.5 billion in reported losses last year, according to the Federal Trade Commission.

“There’s a lot of stigma to being a victim to scams,” Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., who launched the investigation alongside Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in an interview last week. “People should understand that really sophisticated people who are doing all the right things are still getting scammed because of the level of technology and resources that these criminal enterprises now do.”
I fell prey because of my personality and because I was lonely. And I was very ashamed of what happened.
-Sue nuss, who spoke to Congress’ Joint Economic Committee about her experience turning to Tinder in search of companionship.

Scammers today can realistically pose as representatives from familiar organizations like the local YMCA or a bank, and the accessibility of AI tools makes it easier than ever to research family members and mimic their voices. But romance scams, Hassan said, can be particularly emotionally devastating.

That was the case for Pennsylvania resident Sue Nuss, who told Congress’ Joint Economic Committee about her experience turning to Tinder in search of companionship after she lost her husband. There, she met a man who claimed to be from New Jersey.
Nuss told NBC News that, over a month and a half, he won her trust with words that made her feel like he really “sees” and “understands” her.

The committee’s report, published Tuesday, stated that the man duped Nuss with a series of “fabricated” crises: job problems on an oil rig, an arrest in Mexico, his mom’s stroke and even her funeral — all excuses to ask Nuss, 77, for money. When the scammers behind the profile tried to trick her into believing the man she was dating had died, she said, she realized it was all a scam.

“I have always been a very giving person my entire life, and I’ve always been a caregiver,” Nuss told NBC News last week. “And I fell prey. I was very vulnerable. I fell prey because of my personality and because I was lonely. And I was very ashamed of what happened.”
Days after what she thought was a budding online relationship fell apart, Nuss’ scammer showed back up on Tinder with the same profile, she said in an interview.

Soon, another group approached her claiming they could recover what she had lost. Then, through an elaborate cryptocurrency scheme, that group managed to scam even more money from Nuss. She believes both scammer groups were connected, the report stated. It added that, in total, she lost more than $700,000.

“I struggle. Some days are really bad days and some days are good days. I do get therapy. I’m starting a very special therapy next week called EMDR because it’s a trauma,” Nuss said. “I don’t trust my decisions now.”

Congress last month passed the Romance Scam Prevention Act, which would require online dating service providers to notify and warn any users who get messaged by potential scammers. The bill awaits President Donald Trump’s signature.

This summer, Hassan also introduced legislation with Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., to create a central reporting portal for victims of scams, an initiative that she said could give the federal government the tools to detect patterns in scams to shut them down more effectively.
Scammers stole more than $1 trillion globally in one year, according to a 2024 report from the Global Anti-Scam Alliance.

“Enterprises that run scams are now costing the global economy more than the illicit drug trade does,” Hassan said. “This is really important for individuals. It’s really important for our economy. And so, the more people speak up about the need to change the way the federal government handles scams, the faster it’s going to happen.”
For Subscribers

The Joint Economic Committee’s investigation sought to combat the prevalence of romance scams on platforms owned by Match Group, the biggest online dating company in the world, with a portfolio that includes Tinder, Hinge, Match and Plenty of Fish.

It found that during the third quarter of 2025, nearly 1.5 million scammers or other bad actors on Tinder and Hinge matched with someone. Nearly 500,000 of those accounts then exchanged contact information with other users.

Internal documents shared voluntarily with the committee noted that most of Tinder’s machine-learning detection scam models hadn’t been updated in years, and Match Group staff members found that scammers could quickly circumvent the company’s patchwork detection rules. Excessive false positives also overwhelmed the human moderators trying to detect dangerous accounts.
For Subscribers
The committee wrote that it welcomes the changes Match Group has made to address those concerns.

Match Group deployed new detection models throughout the latter half of 2025 and the first half of 2026 to better catch bad actors, according to the committee’s report. This year, it introduced 169 automated rules and “improved” 108 others aimed at targeting and removing inauthentic actors.

One of its key rollouts is a mandatory biometric face check for all new users on Tinder and Hinge, meant to prevent users from making multiple accounts and ensure banned users can’t make new accounts.

Yoel Roth, Match Group’s senior vice president of trust and safety, told NBC News the company is “grateful the Committee recognized our significant advancements to protect our users against romance scams.”

“That said, the report mischaracterizes both the historical scale of our investment and the work already completed.
